The set menus are changed up on a regular basis to showcase the ingredients of the season.

Name: Felicità Trattoria
Description: Opposite the village's small railway station, an elegant Bordeaux-stone building now houses a refined trattoria. Chef and owner Pierre Rigothier has waved goodbye to Lune and its bistronomy cooking to usher in the cuisine of Italy (a passion of his) in a cosy, retro-style setting – honey-coloured stone walls, a solid wood table d'hôte and cane seats with velvet upholstering. The apparent simplicity of the cuisine belies the rigorous and skilful cooking and seasoning that goes into it, whether vitello tonnato or the perfect risotto. Reflecting true know-how, the menu is quite varied and serves only food made in-house.

Name: Ma.Maison
Description: In this village so typical of Alsace set between Ribeauvillé and Illhaeusern, Manon Nasti and her partner, Italian chef Lucas Di Palma, have renovated this converted 18C hunting lodge in a simple and cosy contemporary style. The delicious Italian cuisine pays homage to the chef's grandfather. The set menus and à la carte options include classic dishes with a twist (risotto alla milanese, troccoli alla carbonara, lamb saltimbocca, "contemporary" tiramisu) and seasonal suggestions centred on top-notch ingredients (tagliatelle with truffle, scallops with carrots and guanciale emulsion). Modern and masterly!

Name: Brasserie Roseaux
Description: With this brasserie, Tabata and Ludovic Mey (whose other restaurant, Ombellule, is next door) prove that they have more than one string to their bow. Sit down to classic, bourgeois French cuisine: beef fillet with sauce périgourdine, chicken and veal sweetbread vol-au-vent, turbot with sauce bonne femme, savarin, millefeuille for two, cut and plated tableside… A tempting lunch set menu comes in at a lower price point to complement the high-calibre à la carte menu. The establishment serves the same wine list (around 600 wines) as the fine dining restaurant.

Name: Café César
Description: In a quiet little street, opposite a park, Café César is a modern bistro with a colourful, light-filled interior (red bricks, some painted white, blue zellige tiled counter, polished concrete flooring). From morning to night, people come and go, for coffee, lunch or dinner, the common thread being the precise and carefully prepared cuisine. The sauces and gravies, prepared to exacting standards, give layers of flavour to the dishes – crabmeat enhanced with curry, scallops served with a creamy fish roe sauce, or hot chocolate tartlet. Everything served here is house-made, the service is relaxed and, at lunchtime, the bill is more than reasonable. As Henry Miller would say, "Quiet Days in Clichy"!

Name: Elsass
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Counter dining,Interesting wine list,Wheelchair access
Description: Behind an anthracite-grey façade at the end of Avenue Parmentier, Elsass eschews the clichés and offers its own interpretation of Alsace. That means no checked tablecloths or rustic wood-panelled walls in this room with an open kitchen and a few seats at the counter; instead a clean-lined industrial loft-style space (it was previously a garage), softened by light hues of wood and flower arrangements. Everything here revolves around Alsace wines, the only ones on the list, and the modern cuisine that showcases them. The sauerkraut, a nod to the terroir, is served in unexpected ways: in crispy cromesquis or accompanying a house-made boudin blanc sausage and candied pork belly. At the helm, Guillaume Keusch, a food-loving lawyer-turned-restaurateur, has designed a place where tradition and creativity are perfectly allied.

Name: Le Plongeoir d'en Face
Description: An unusual setting for a restaurant: what was, in the 1970s, a municipal swimming pool, with raw concrete and colourful neon lights, has been converted into a bustling collaborative space. It is where Enzo Scaramuzzino, former right-hand man of Mathieu Pacaud, is swimming solo after clocking up experience in MICHELIN-starred kitchens. Every week, the short menu is written up on the blackboard – think cuttlefish fricassee, truffle risotto, farm-reared pork rack… Classics revisited without ostentation, impeccable jus and a fabulous béarnaise sauce on the rump steak, fresh and fruity desserts, such as pineapple carpaccio with an exotic condiment. Don't hesitate to dive straight in.

Name: MARMAR
Description: In a side street set back from the port, chef Claudio Marsico, who hails from southern Italy, and Jacopo Marini, a sommelier from Lombardy, have transformed a former burger joint into this charming, bright and welcoming Mediterranean restaurant. The fresh, spontaneous cuisine, with spicy notes and hits of citrus flavour, takes daily inspiration from the neighbouring Saleya Market: fried artichokes, lemon vinaigrette and carrot ketchup; duckling fillet, sweet potato, leeks sautéed in butter and white wine. A constantly evolving European wine list completes this pleasant culinary interlude.

Name: Le Mana
Description: At the entrance to the village, this restaurant is discreetly tucked away in a 19C red-brick building. Inside, light enters through the contemporary-style veranda, capturing the elegance of a decor dominated by black details and green velvet. In the kitchen, which opens onto the dining room, chefs Valentine and Maxime – also partners outside of the restaurant – can be seen intently focused on producing their tempting dishes with perfectly judged marriages of flavours. The fillet of pollock is topped with an anchovy viennoise and accompanied by a broccoli cream and almond milk and shellfish emulsion. For dessert, spiced clementine comes with date sorbet and an orange blossom zabaglione. Technical precision and generosity of spirit reveal a sincere desire to do things well, and naturally.

Name: Le Kermer
Description: This restaurant on the Rhuys Peninsula, the result of a fruitful collaboration between two seasoned chefs, is nestled in an authentic Breton building recognisable by its stone façade and blue door and window frames. The interior of this contemporary bistro blends traditional and modern elements, with exposed beams, a period fireplace and open kitchen. On the menu, hearty and perfectly executed recipes celebrate Brittany's terroir – the leek, andouille and mustard tart is the epitome of finesse and indulgence. In addition to an enticing lunch deal, the menu-carte is particularly appealing.

Name: Agave
Description: Located on a pedestrian street, with an open kitchen that is already visible from outside, Agave references the plant from which tequila and mezcal are made. Raphaël and Fernanda Pillon, a French-Mexican couple and trained pastry-makers, create a brilliant fusion cuisine of French ingredients and Mexican flavours. After a stint in Mexico, the pair returned to his roots in the Ain, where they create balanced dishes, discerningly complemented by a variety of sauces and condiments: scallops and macha salsa, pastrami-style roast beef given a boost by salsa verde, veal rump elevated by an intense mole sauce. Their expertise in patisserie brings the meal to a wonderfully indulgent close.

Name: La Chapelle de Guiraud
Description: The setting, located in a premier grand cru Sauternes wine estate and run by the Cercle Guiraud team, is certainly breathtaking: a spacious dining area beneath a lofty vaulted ceiling, an open kitchen and an inviting lounge with a fireplace… The menu rolls out flavoursome, mouthwatering dishes illustrated by poached egg and a sauternes sauce, pâté en croûte in a tribute to Mère Brazier, roast pork shoulder in smoked pepper or desserts like Belle Hélène pears. A well-crafted, patriotic Gallic lineup at sensible prices and a deliciously peaceful terrace.

Name: Tandem
Description: Behind a frontage with red window frames, this well-matched duo are forging their path and taking a simple approach. Trained in London, Lisa (front of house) and Tanguy (in the kitchen) have set up shop in this corner of the Lot. The bright, unfussy space has a pared-down aesthetic, with its white walls, exposed bricks and vintage objects lending it character. The food is in the same vein: clear, balanced and rooted in the ingredients. Enhanced by an orange vinaigrette and a scattering of almond splinters, the gravlax-style trout retains all its tenderness. The stuffed cabbage – a more rustic dish – gets a Middle Eastern makeover in the form of a lamb confit farce with dried apricots, accompanied by a subtly spiced sweet potato mash. The service is charming and the wine list is extensive enough that you can treat yourself to wallet-friendly labels.

Name: La Borie
Description: Chef turned farmer, Tanguy Hanoun has set himself the challenge of controlling his restaurant's entire food chain by sourcing (almost) everything direct from his farm in Haute-Loire (central southern France). Fruit, veg, aromatic herbs, eggs, poultry, lamb, honey, snails... even the butter is house made! Once a week, this ultra-fresh produce is delivered to La Borie's kitchen and into the capable hands of chef Raphaëlle Bathellier, who crafts surprise set menus that change in line with the seasons and the harvests. Dishes of disarming simplicity, enhanced by house-made vinegars, pickles and concoctions. (Very) short supply chains and a laser-like focus on produce are the DNA of La Borie.

Name: Il Ristorante Alain Ducasse Roma
Description: Housed in a 17C palazzo just a stone’s throw from the Piazza del Popolo, this restaurant run by Alain Ducasse, the chef with the most Michelin stars worldwide, is part of the Romeo hotel. The dining room, designed by architect Zaha Hadid, is panelled in ebony, while the open-view kitchen is in marble – luxury certainly takes centre stage here. The cuisine is on a par with the exquisite decor, featuring top-quality ingredients which young Jacopo Iualè transforms into dishes with a Mediterranean flavour.

Name: La Ripadoro
Description: Tucked away in the small medieval village of Rivalto, with stunning views of the surrounding Tuscan hills, the Ripadoro agriturismo is home to this rustic yet elegant farm-restaurant serving traditional Tuscan dishes made from produce grown on the property. There’s an authentic charcoal grill which is used to cook classic ribeye steak, as well as the superb “girarrosto” – boned pigeon and quail served with potato rosti, yellow carrots with ginger and Jerusalem artichokes in foil. Make sure you save space for one of the delicious desserts! In summer, it’s well worth booking one of the outdoor tables under the shade of large lime trees.

Name: Ego
Description: The experience begins at the moment of reservation, when guests choose the number of courses and prepare to place themselves entirely in the hands of the chef’s creativity. Ego is a reflection of the personality of Lorenzo De Lio, a young Roman talent with an international journey that emerges clearly in his dishes. His cuisine is a voyage without borders, where Mexican influences, Southeast Asian references, and unexpected inspirations coexist, constructed to stimulate the palate with spices, contrasts, and intensity. The dining room counts just five tables – to be reserved well in advance – entrusted to the gracious and knowledgeable care of Beatrice, who also curates wine pairings by the glass with great sensitivity.

Name: Vico Astemio
Description: Situated in the village centre surrounded by narrow alleyways, this attractive restaurant is housed in an old barrel warehouse. Here, self-taught chef Massimiliano Vasta serves colourful cuisine that is full of delicious flavours, showcased on two tasting menus and an impressive à la carte with an equal emphasis on meat and fish (despite the port being just a stone’s throw away). We focused on the main course and particularly enjoyed the Zuppa di Pietro, an updated version of the chef’s father’s favourite dish, as well as the tempting array of tasty welcome snacks. There’s an impressive wine list, while the family farm ensures that the extra-virgin olive oil is also of the highest quality.

Name: Ostaria
Address: Via Giovan Battista Perasso 10/12, Syracuse, 96100, Italy
Description: This restaurant in the centre of the modern city, yet just a stone’s throw from Ortigia, focuses exclusively on meat (local and from further afield, much of it aged on the premises), which is sourced from non-intensive farming and cooked using contemporary methods such as the Josper oven. The excellent wine list focuses mainly on Sicilian labels but also includes bottles from elsewhere in Italy, as well as from other important wine-producing countries. A typical Sicilian ambience, soft lighting in the evening and friendly yet professional service complete the picture.

Name: Essenza
FacilitiesAndServices: Car park,Garden or park,Great view,Terrace,Wheelchair access
Description: Essenza is housed within the Borghi dell'Eremo resort in a stunning setting surrounded by beautiful and tranquil natural landscapes. The spacious dining room, which is flooded with natural light thanks to the picture windows that look out at the Umbrian hills, provides the backdrop for a culinary experience that focuses on traditional cuisine. Our inspector particularly recommends the exquisite Borghi saffron tagliatelle served with a rabbit ragù (the rabbits are raised on the estate’s own farm).

Name: Locanda dell'Angelo
Description: This stylish, elegant restaurant occupying a historic 17C building in an attractive medieval village serves contemporary cuisine which is influenced by recipes and ingredients from Liguria and Piedmont alike. Dishes include Ligurian-style rabbit terrine with a pine nut and gravy sauce, and Piedmontese white suckling pig tomahawk on sauerkraut with a spicy, sour apple sauce.

Name: À Putia - Enoteca e Cucina
Address: via Umberto I° 456, Giardini Naxos, 98035, Italy
Description: This restaurant began life in 1946 as a grocery store (the name is the Sicilian word for shop) which, forty years later, was transformed into a very simple yet attractive trattoria-cum-wine bar (don’t be shocked by the paper tablecloths!). The cuisine focuses mainly on fish, seafood and fresh market produce, while the wines come from Sicily and further afield. Booking ahead is essential here, partly because there are only a few tables but also because the opening hours vary depending on the season. You may find it difficult to find somewhere to park between the main street and the seafront in the busy town centre, but it’s well worth the effort.

Name: Soluna
Description: At Soluna, which comes from the Spanish translation of the names of his children, chef Teppei Nii conjures up Japanese-inspired cuisine that strays a little from the norm as a result of its fusion with more Mediterranean-style cooking. At its elongated counter (with seating for six) and its functional tables, choose between menus (Soluna and Festival) that change approximately every two months. One particular dish everyone is talking about and you must try is the famous cod cheek “pizza" (okonomiyaki with cod cheeks pil-pil and tuna katsuobushi).

Name: Kaos
Address: Plaça de Sant Pere 14, Palamós, 17230, Spain
Description: Kaos is run by a couple, both trained in leading restaurants such as El Celler de Can Roca, Disfrutar, and Enigma. As you descend the stairs, you come to a pleasant bar crowned by an open-brick vaulted ceiling and, to one side, a modern dining room furnished in contemporary style. The à la carte takes its inspiration from what is available in the market, is reasonably varied and up-to-date in feel, and is always complemented by daily suggestions featuring local, seasonal ingredients (the famous Palamós red prawn, for example, is served as a carpaccio, cooked, or in croquettes). The rice dishes here are all prepared individually.

Name: Cal Viva
Address: Gutemberg 20, Morón de la Frontera, 41530, Spain
Description: This restaurant, surprising both for its pleasant decor and its location on an industrial estate, takes its name from the Spanish word for “quicklime”, highlighting the historical importance of this artisanal product on the local economy. Here, chef Leonardo Ramos conjures up an updated take on traditional cuisine, based around locally sourced seasonal ingredients and showcased on two tasting menus (Omakase Andaluz and Homenaje Omakase) that change daily and on which the chef chooses dishes for his guests. You’ll also find options that don’t feature on any of the menus, including soups, stews and rice dishes.

Name: KA-ORŪ SUSHIBAR & COCKTAIL
Description: A reinvented dining option that has taken on a new lease of life and name, the latter a combination of the Japanese words for family (kazoku) and olive tree (Orību). The cuisine here, which remains faithful to the traditions of Japanese cooking, is centred around two menus that need to be ordered in advance (Kazoku and Ka-Oru) and can either be enjoyed at the counter while watching the sushi chefs at work, or at one of the three tables. Options include top-notch nigiri, fresh wasabi, top-quality tuna etc. There’s also an interesting nod to local cuisine, such as the delicious Katsu Sando (a type of Japanese sandwich) filled with pork head.

Name: Ayantar
Address: Paseo de San Francisco de Sales 41, Madrid, 28003, Spain
Description: In the district of Vallehermoso, next to the sports and leisure centre known as the Parque del Tercer Depósito, you’ll find this restaurant in which the enticing and traditionally focused tasting menu has an unashamed focus on classic recipes, stews and slow-cooked dishes (veal tripe, cod with a pil-pil sauce, oxtail in red wine with a celeriac purée, truffled pigs’ trotters etc), a few grilled meat dishes, and excellent dishes of the day that don’t appear on the menu. Half-portion options are also available for the majority of the dishes here.

This simple, modern restaurant, which takes its unusual name by multiplying 12 dishes by a pairing of 12 signature cocktails, is one of the most bold dining options in the city, where a fun approach and global influences are very much at the forefront. On the menus (a ‘shorter’ option with 17 courses, and a longer one with 21), you’ll find constantly evolving fusion cooking, including enticing options such as their hamachi tartare with red curry tentsuyu and coconut ice cream or the prawn, peanut, vergamota and laksa soup. Here they say ‘every bite tells a story’!

Name: Delia
Address: 306 Santiphap Road, Pom Prap, Pom Prap Sattru Phai, Bangkok, 10100, Thailand
Description: Delia, a fresh addition to Bangkok's food scene, gives authentic Mexican flavours a contemporary twist. Greeted with a cheerful "Hola!", diners experience traditional techniques fused with quality Thai ingredients. Handmade tortillas, house‐fermented elements and bold, flame‐cooked dishes such as tostada with roasted cauliflower cream and taco de pastor – celebrate both heritage and innovation. Their unique spin on tamal de piña y umeshu rounds off the meal perfectly.

Name: K by Vicky Cheng
Address: 56F, The Empire, 1 South Sathon Road, Yan Nawa, Sathon, Bangkok, 10120, Thailand
Description: Chef Vicky Cheng's first restaurant outside Hong Kong promises an upscale dining experience that sees Chinese culinary traditions with a contemporary twist. His use of Cantonese and Teochew flavours with seasonal ingredients shines in the mud crab with olive leaf and garlic, inviting hands-on dining. In this stylish, refined and inviting setting, choose between private sofas or seating with splendid views of Bangkok's skyline.

Name: Carcasse
Description: An artisan butcher, Hendrik Dierendonck chose to open the first offshoot of his meat-lover’s establishment in Knokke’s Oosthoekplein. On entering, your eye is first drawn to the refrigerated counter and massive glazed aging cabinet, before it is distracted by the chefs in the open-plan kitchen as they craft outstanding produce that is Dierendonck’s signature. Delicacies such as Oedslach ribeye and tongue of Belgian red cattle are enhanced by subtle side dishes that add a wealth of nuances and refreshing notes. Grilled melt-in-the-mouth Menapii pork cutlet is coated in a creamy emulsion of tarragon and other fresh herbs and served on fregula seasoned with the same herbs and a mousse of thyme and coarsely ground hazelnuts. Diners are invited, even encouraged to share dishes, giving you more chance to taste the full scope of the appetising menu.

Name: De Lindehoeve
Description: Pallieter Vaes has breathed a new lease of life into this country hostelry, whose classical period details and fixtures have been retained, adding to the cachet and character of this airy establishment. The chef, who boasts an enviable CV, is manifestly a fan of top-notch produce. When he works with scallops, he may give them a crispy crust, which is then offset by side dishes like squash, ginger, a sea vegetable and a lovage-perfumed beurre blanc. You can expect a culinary lineup packed in gutsy flavours and delicacy. The à la carte is more traditional than the set menu, but both hit the spot every time. Even better, De Lindehoeve can stylishly put you up for the night in their lovely boutique hotel.

Name: Coprin
Description: This log cabin built entirely out of wood stands in quiet countryside amidst forest and woodland. The bucolic scene is set for Olivia, the exuberant lady of the house and chef Adrien to get to work and demonstrate how their shared love of nature has shaped their mindset. Genuine ambassadors of their local producers, they take real pleasure in showcasing outstanding produce. Chef Adrien may skin a perfectly ripe tomato, for example, before filling it with whipped cream jazzed up with horseradish, all of which to accompany velvety gazpacho and roast buckwheat. A fresh seasonal menu packed in rustic, wholesome flavours.

Name: Vintage
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Interesting wine list,Terrace,Wheelchair access
Description: Cyril Moulin crafts intelligent cuisine that is both bold and polished. Big-boned sauces and playful fresh nuances set the culinary scene. For example, he may pair textbook perfect cod with seaweed, pistachios and a zest of lemon, while velvety green asparagus, a light frothy espuma of seaweed and a pistachio crumble conclude the dish. The chef conjures up recipes in which outstanding ingredients are delicately and harmoniously assembled. Steven Wullaert suggests insightful food-wine pairings. The scene takes place in a tastefully revamped farmstead surrounded by meadows: huge windows, exposed beams and works of art. A gourmet getaway destination par excellence!

Name: L'Air de Rien
Address: Place du Vieux Tilleul 14, Esneux, 4130, Belgium
Description: A log-burning fire is the centrepiece of this stylishly converted 18C farmstead. In his splendid glass-fronted kitchen, chef Diffels can be seen barbecuing most of the main ingredients, which are largely locally sourced. These take centre stage in particularly creative dishes featuring rich sauces and complex flavours. Fermentation adds a vibrant twist. The chef has a gift for coaxing the best out of every ingredient. He celebrates the earthiness of celeriac, for instance, cooking it in a salt crust and combining it with Comté cheese and sherry. This chef has an artistic bent, and his dishes are truly original.

Name: Partage
Address: Rue des Fossés Fleuris 18, Namur, 5000, Belgium
Description: Charles Jeandrain of the starred establishment, Attablez-vous, has opened this buzzy eatery in Namur’s pedestrian centre. Diners can choose between a bargain-priced lunch menu, an enticing set menu and a few suggestions, all of which are in line with Jeandrain’s focus on authentic, unfussy flavours. Examples include a tartare of raw shrimp with finely diced celeriac and apple, a sweet curry emulsion and a crunchy salad, followed by a textbook perfect vol-au-vent. Just the ticket to share a meal with friends and family in Namur.

Name: L'Opéra
Description: Colourful artwork adds a vibrant note to the dark colour scheme. In fine weather, the front terrace is very popular. The extensive à la carte lineup, with an amusing set menu at lunchtime, showcases brasserie fare. Fish in batter with a tartare sauce, vol-au-vent of premium chicken or crispy sweetbread and crayfish, served with a fresh green salad and piping hot fries. L’Opéra, which tirelessly seeks to reinvent itself as it builds on its well-earned reputation, never fails to deliver the goods.

Name: Umā
Address: Rue de la Reinette 8, Brussels, 1000, Belgium
Description: Umā stands on a quiet side street near the bustling Porte de Namur. Its white-washed outer brick facade and modern artwork indoors are inviting and attractive. In an open kitchen, the chef skilfully blends frank Japanese cuisine with gutsy South-American accents in a suave bistronomic lineup. He adds his hallmark signature courtesy of subtle spicy notes. Examples include a sashimi of red tuna in a subtle stock perfumed with shiso oil and dashi or a medium rare fillet of duck with subtle sides of curry and vadouvan - intensity meets variety. Both the varied à la carte menu and the succulent set menu offer an opportunity to sample this establishment’s distinctive, drool-worthy fare.

Name: Wagyu
Address: Rue du Comte Théodule d'Ursel 1, Durbuy, 6940, Belgium
Description: Talented Wout Bru is at the helm of this chic BBQ restaurant in the heart of Durbuy. The stylish outer walls reveal a dark, inviting interior whose centrepieces are an imposing bar and a dry-ageing fridge. Unsurprisingly, prime beef, such as wagyu and other premium breeds, is the establishment’s raison d’être. Superlatively barbecued, the meat is served with knockout sauces and large portions of side dishes that each diner chooses themselves. There are a few fish courses on the menu, but this is really a place for meat eaters. First-class craftsmanship and lashings of respect for the produce.

Name: Compagnique
Description: Ideal for a romantic date night, this charming farmstead is the quintessence of poised and intimate and only offers tables for two (but there is a private room that caters to groups). Working hand in hand, Angélique manages the front-of-house while Tim runs the kitchen, in a bid to provide a personalised experience. Luxury ingredients enjoy the leading role on the menu and the chef might sign a high-flying combination of oysters and seaweed, caviar and a distinctive beurre blanc made out of curds. He has a soft spot for fresh, tangy notes, illustrated by the subtle sauce vierge that contrasts so wonderfully with the mild yet sweet flesh of turbot. A mouthwatering prospect…

Name: Auberge du Château de Leignon par Isabelle Arpin
Description: Today, the neo-Gothic Château de Leignon is home to a variety of businesses, including a brewery and, of course, this charming restaurant run by Isabelle Arpin, whose market-fresh cuisine showcases ingredients from local producers. Look forward to playful dishes that draw inspiration from all over the world – for example, she pairs brill with barley infused with coffee, artichoke, a creamy fish sauce and a sabayon with aged rum. Be sure to sample the creations of the local brewery, whose beers frequently find their way into the desserts.

Name: Lys d'Or
Description: Black marble, gilding and a grand piano set the scene in this swanky yet supremely tasteful Gent townhouse. The epitome of classy luxury, it provides the perfect foil to the high-flying, pedigree score signed by chef Wattenberge. Wagyu and North Sea crab, jazzed up with a tangy guacamole and radish cannelloni with furikake-laced sushi rice are emblematic of the talent and creativity of this virtuoso chef. Make sure you peruse the impressive wine list that stars a remarkable collection of Chateau Pétrus vintages (from 2000 on).

Name: ViEr
Description: Concrete, black and turquoise set the unusual scene in this imposing, yet nonetheless cosy venue. Fine produce such as cottage garden veggies and black chicken from Burgundy takes pride of place in the cooking of chef Bas. Natural, simple and seasonal sum up his ethos, all of which flanked by knockout sauces and at prices that make sense in the heart of Kortrijk!

Name: DOOR73
Description: The hip younger sibling of the starred OAK, DOOR73, has forged its own vibrant personality. A vintage tiled floor adds warmth to the modern interior while the open kitchen adds a buzzy vibe. The Josper oven rolls out skilfully crafted, international and unorthodox dishes to share. The chef embarks us on an intense journey with grilled hispi cabbage coated in a spicy sauce, toasted hazelnuts, chunks of grapefruit and a yoghurt dressing. The velvety pistachio-laced Basque cheesecake is to die for! You can expect a festival of flavours served in a refreshingly unstuffy ambience. Hits all the right buttons!

Name: Le Jardin de la Gaichel
Description: The cosy Jardin de la Gaichel is perfectly suited to its woodland surroundings and commands a splendid view of the huge garden. The chefs excel at crafting textbook perfect cuisine using traditional produce of outstanding quality, such as premium scallops. Examples include a generous slab of fish glazed in a subtle white wine sauce, while a heady mix of sweet and powerful flavours envelopes Challans duck, carved tableside (by reservation) or an amazing seafood platter (also by reservation)… This is unadulterated, uncensored generosity. We recommend staying overnight in one of the guestrooms to prolong the experience.

Name: L'O à la Bouche
Address: rue Armand de Wasseige 1, Wépion, 5100, Belgium
Description: The curtain rises to tightly packed tables, the characteristic hum of a busy brasserie and a warm, welcoming vibe, while the smiling faces of diners bear witness to the flair and talent of the chef. The latter has a knack for customising brasserie dishes: risotto is a staple of the menu, without forgetting fork-tender pork cheeks cooked in a velvety powerful sauce. Should there be pain perdu (French toast) on the menu (light, fluffy and served with vanilla ice cream and butterscotch sauce), don’t hesitate a minute – it is out of this world!

Name: De Koolputten
Description: These former coal shafts overlooking the Mirabrug bridge have been carefully restored and are now home to a comfortable B&B, an exhibition area, an events venue and this restaurant. A trendy, pleasant setting in which to sample contemporary fare with classical roots, with a very open feel. Up-to-date cuisine with gastronomic flair.

Name: Brimer
Description: Fancy a slap-up meal that won’t break the bank? The Brimers deliver just that – and with flair! Their magic formula: know-how, generosity and flavour. The chef works solely with premium produce, a passion he shares with his better half, who has a knack for foraging the tastiest mushrooms. Diners return again and again for familiar dishes like melt-in-the-mouth tenderloin served rare with a powerful pepper sauce, crunchy fries and subtle veggie sides. A feel-good, homely vibe reigns throughout this traditional hotel-restaurant.

Name: La Cuisine du Côté Vert
Description: The restaurant of Le Côté Vert Hotel unsurprisingly bears the hallmark of nature. Natural materials adorn the interior, whose floor to ceiling windows command a splendid view of the garden. Vegetables are the stars of the show in the chefs’ updated recipes, without forgetting meat and fish. The focus is on allowing each natural ingredient to shout its name.

Name: Le Val d'Amblève
Description: This handsome country house dating from 1934 is the quintessence of charming! The interior is modern from the guestrooms to the restaurant, whose floor-to-ceiling windows seem to invite the countryside indoors. The terrace and the garden are exquisite. The set and à la carte menus roll out a classical lineup, with the occasional feisty touch that makes the adventure exciting. The chef may pair rockfish with sweet-sour marinated white cabbage and a powerful shellfish sauce. You are in for a global dining experience at Le Val d’Amblève.

Name: La Cuisine d'un Gourmand
Description: Ambitious John Maes is a genuine good food lover. His mission in life is to source the best regional ingredients, to unfetter his creativity and to please or surprise his patrons with subtle fare. Outstanding quality at affordable prices. The tasteful, modern interior commands a fine view of the river Meuse.

Name: Au Petit Château
Description: Foodies are in seventh heaven in this elegant and endearing villa. The infectious friendly home-from-home vibe is the work of your cheerful hostess and her team. The traditional menu, which features the occasional modern tribute, reveals the hallmark of a seasoned chef, who is equally at ease when crafting fresh, acidic flavours as with a textbook tournedos Rossini or kidneys in a mustard sauce. The well-padded menu reads like an ode to soul-warming old-school cuisine in all its timeless, generous glory.

Name: Epices et Nous
Description: Chef Delvigne regularly calls upon oriental spices to add subtlety to his recipes. For example, a saffron sauce adds depth to a stew of megrim and lobster. Spices form the backbone of his cooking, oozing in generosity and free of fatuitous frills. Everything is crafted from scratch and the extensive menu further adds to the appeal. Finally, the casual serene vibe is delightfully contagious.

Name: La Régalade
Description: Peaceful, relaxed and friendly describe both the village of Toernich and the Régalade restaurant. The chef rustles up immaculately prepared contemporary fare whose value for money cannot be beaten.

Name: De Steenen Haene
Description: An irresistible friendly vibe echoes throughout this pretty modernised cottage, whose terrace-garden is set amidst fields and pastures. The family-run restaurant serves classical delicacies such as grilled lobster and the spring chicken and croquettes exhibit the chef’s talent. Flavour and generosity epitomise this establishment.

Name: Correspondance
Description: San Degeimbre’s vision of brasserie dining has become reality in the post-industrial mixed-use hub of Brussels’ former rail freight terminus. The contemporary establishment sports two rooms and our preference went to the mezzanine and its counter that hugs the open kitchen. The culinary score spans Belgium, Peru and Asia. For example, waterzooi with a kick of yuzu, or duck magret cooked in its skin and paired with an incredible orange sauce that features a jazzy blend of soy and a whiff of garlic. Correspondance unveils chef Degeimbre’s highly distinctive, no-holds barred, creative hallmark, which is embodied in signature dishes like his truly heroic masterpiece of sweetbread and langoustine.

Name: Charlu
Description: This imposing 1920’s villa in the heart of the Saint Job neighbourhood is home to a genuine temple of bistronomy. Wainscoting, mirrors and tightly packed tables set the scene. The working language is French in both the menu and the wine list, the owner’s passion about which he frequently waxes lyrical. Hearty wholesome recipes from southwest France are what you can expect, like textbook cassoulet made with proper duck confit, smoked ham and Toulouse sausage, unless you wouldn’t prefer fritters of pig’s trotters or crispy sweetbread. Traditional down to the core and crafted with love is the ethos of Charlu.

Name: Le bistrot du Kachatelier
Description: This sprawling bistro is housed in an amazing glass and wood arch-shaped structure fronted by a peaceful water feature. Harald and Maximilian Rüssel, first encountered at their Michelin-starred Rüssels Landhaus establishment in Germany, add their own inimitable touch to a regional culinary lineup courtesy of a concise menu packed in big-boned flavours. Examples include impeccably prepared cod à la meunière is garnished with a pumpkin-flavoured risotto, crunchy broccoli and a velvety beurre blanc to die for. Indulgent family favourites with a dash of stylish elegance.

Name: L'Orangerie de Moulbaix
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Garden or park,Great view,Terrace,Wheelchair access
Description: The bright and airy orangery at Moulbaix Castle presents itself as a tasteful blend of the old and the new. The terrace overlooking the vines, the castle and the windmill in the distance are simply idyllic! Maxence Bouralha and Charles-Maxime Legrand, the chef duo behind Quai no. 4, join forces with Philippe Lartigue to create meticulously prepared hearty French brasserie classics. Think sautéed mushrooms with finely chopped shallot topped with an indulgent potato emulsion, an œuf parfait (slow-cooked egg) that really lives up to its name, as well a touch of orange to provide a bright and zesty finish. Other tempting options are prawn croquettes, vol-au-vent or andouillette. The extensive menu is sure to please.

Name: OiO
Description: The pasta is prepared last minute, stuffed with a powerful ossobuco and then coated in a velvety parmesan and gremolata sauce. All the ingredients on the menu are as fresh as the homemade pasta. This fantastic Mediterranean osteria which boasts an exquisite riverside terrace on the banks of the Alzette, invites you to an Italian feast of great delicacy. Don’t miss the Negroni or the dessert trolley!

Name: Vonk
Description: Stijn and chef Bart are the fifth generation of the Hoonaert family, whose DNA is rooted in culinary excellence! The conservatory of the former café, planted with trees, is now a cosy gastrobar. A charcoal Mibrasa oven adds a distinctive flavour to market-fresh recipes, made with meticulously chosen ingredients (simple lunchtime menu, more varied in the evening).

Name: VAS
Description: Jolien and Robby have moved shop, but retained their win-win formula. Near the Gentseweg highway, VAS occupies an attractive street corner edifice whose interior sports a range of elegant materials and a tasteful colour scheme. The bubbly front-of-house team sets the scene as you peruse the interesting Franco-Belgian repertory dotted with trendy, spot-on twists. Fillet of duck cooked rare might be flanked by a champagne sauce and a creamy gravy jazzed up with hints of sea buckthorn for added vibrancy together with a velvety purée and a range of textured kohlrabi. VAS is the quintessence of warm and welcoming, enhanced by a festival of familiar family favourites underscored by feelgood flavours.

Name: Divino Gusto
Address: Square des Nations Unies 4A, Nivelles, 1400, Belgium
Description: Despite the Italian name of this elegant restaurant, Marc Grislain’s style is far from restricted to the bel paese. He may be a fan of Mediterranean panache, but that doesn’t prevent him showcasing his mastery of classical techniques together with Asian notes. For example, he might flank a rare rib of steak with veggies such as cream of squash and ginger and a gutsy cooking gravy flavoured with smoky black tea. The sommelier and owner, Gaëtan Poels, can be relied upon to ply you with insightful wine tips to create the perfect pairing. Hats off to this establishment that is enjoying a new lease of life!

Name: Klaver
Description: According to chef Korneel Verhulst, there is no reason you can’t start your meal with fries, even in a fine dining establishment. So should you wish to kick off with piping hot French fries and a caper mayonnaise, then go for it! Such is the down-to-earth outlook of this friendly, welcoming establishment. Before finishing your meal with a pancake and coffee, try out the chef’s main courses, some of which are enhanced with Japanese notes. Finely diced kohlrabi, seasoned with a sushi dressing garnish a tartare of Holstein beef, grated Belper Knolle cheese, caviar and curry. Klaver adds a brand-new youthful dimension to fine dining, embodied by Grace, your charming hostess.

Name: Bacon
Description: Your host, an enthusiastic champion of natural and organic wines, was a butcher in a former life. In the company of his partner, they have embarked on a new adventure in the shape of a cosy, trendy eatery. She woos diners with fresh cuisine, jazzed up with international seasonings and brimming with flavour in dishes – with or without meat! If you opt for the surprise menu, you will be delighted by her knack for playing with contrasts. An example: lamb cooked two ways – one spicy in pita bread, the other with lamb’s tongues cooked slowly in a tomato coulis and a madeira-laced gravy. Crisp, understated interior with a sober colour scheme and a fondness for plants.

Name: Origines
Address: Rue de la Coupe 25, Mons, 7000, Belgium
Description: A narrow lane near the main square of Mons leads to the endearing restaurant of Céline, the charming and ever cheerful lady of the house. The sunny rear patio features an olive tree in its centre. Chef Watteyne crafts a menu dictated by market availability, the seasons and his innovative ideas. Examples include his personal take on vitello tonnato or a fascinating tomato-strawberry-burrata dessert. Bold, distinctive cuisine crafted by a chef who takes pride in ensuring that each flavour is spot on and punchy.

Name: Le P'tit Gaby
Address: rue de la Croix Blanche 8a, Thisnes, 4280, Belgium
Description: The P’tit Gaby effortlessly combines elegance with a friendly vibe. You are greeted warmly and sincerely in this restaurant that is bathed in natural light and surrounded by the lovely Liège countryside. Chef Leruth rolls out a menu that allows his creative streak to run free. For example, he might pair turbot, crafted in several ways, with a range of side dishes such as samphire, razor clams and seaweed to enhance and exalt the main ingredient’s briny flavours. The cottage garden and exotic spices play a significant role in this chef’s culinary score.

Name: Quartz
Address: Rue de la Réforme 22, Ixelles, 1050, Belgium
Description: Local foodies still remember the street corner premises that housed La Canne en Ville for many years. Chef David-Alexandre Bruno has retained the soul of this former butcher’s shop with its wall tiles and floor mosaics. Bruno honed his skills and love of classical cuisine in upmarket establishments, as the personal spin he effortlessly adds to familiar recipes demonstrates. His take on Bellevue lobster is a splendid example: he pairs the tail with a skinned tomato stuffed with meat from the claws, samphire, a herby cream and vanilla-flavoured tomato stock. Sauces are one of the pieces de résistance of this chef, whose bold personality seeks to shine the spotlight on preferably local produce – simplicity and harmonious flavours are the goal.

Name: Primitif
Description: Augustin Massinon and Darius Van Hoef have returned to their roots as they roll out their nature-inspired gourmet concept. First of all, they tastefully refurbished this Ardennes edifice whilst maintaining its authentic character. We recommend booking a table downstairs to make the most of the view of the open kitchen. The chefs, who are committed to using locally sourced produce as much as possible, pool their creative talents to craft beautifully plated dishes. Impeccable handiwork underscored by local ingredients, exotic seasonings and fermented flavours, examples of which include a tartare of langoustine with fermented radish, green apples, poached and foamy oyster and a hint of blackcurrant. The menu, which changes every five weeks, both surprises and enchants.

Name: Château du Mylord
Description: Martin and Nuria Simonart have breathed a new lease of life into this English-looking manor house (1861), a landmark for foodies for many years. Rich in period charm, you can expect a log-burning fire to greet you in winter. The food is high-flying, with a quest for perfection that occasionally borders on daring. Cream of Jerusalem artichoke with coffee-flavoured mushrooms and scallops, all of which jazzed up by a tangy mandarin jelly. Delicacy is what best defines this establishment.

Name: LOF
Description: The Ghent Pillows Hotel sports a regal Louis XIV vibe, whose plush opulence also extends to the LOF restaurant, albeit in a less extravagant vein. A mouthwatering range of outstanding produce sets the sophisticated culinary scene with the odd Asian twist. The chef might cook monkfish on the bone to preserve the taste and juicy flesh, while a delicately sweet cream of carrots, a stock of lapsang souchong tea and a velvety emulsion of olives and carrot juice further underscore this subtle fish. Heaven for lovers of spot-on, up-to-the-minute French fare.

Name: Rock-Fort
Description: North Sea fish and natural wines are the bedrock of this bright, elegant bistro. Chef Laurent and Eline, in charge of the front of house, who first came to our notice at Amuzee in Zeebrugge, are going from strength to strength as they settle in here. The menu overflows in the generous produce of the North Sea with a distinctive subtle, sometimes spicy edge. The fascinating culinary score is depicted by almost translucent grilled langoustines, which are paired with a dashi umami edge or raw scallops served with green apples and jalapeno. Rock-Fort is alive and kicking – in every sense!

Name: Fleur de Sel
Description: You will instantly feel at home in this minimalist venture, two steps from the French border and founded by self-taught chefs, Slava and Antoine. The irresistible duo bowls us over - his passion and food-wine pairings and her delicate culinary flair and generous helpings. Slava’s meticulous attention to detail results in balanced dishes that combine fresh, acidic, spicy and many other subtle flavours. The ingredient takes pride of place in each carefully thought-out dish, whether it be asparagus that is enhanced in a ceviche, or lamb fillets underscored by an emulsion of beer and meat juices.

Name: Frenchette
Description: Frenchette may look like a warm traditional bistro, but it is also so much more! This becomes obvious as you peruse the set menus, to be shared or not, which showcase an authentic bistronomic slant that can only be described as exuberant. Wild mushrooms, snails and toasted bread are savvily combined, perhaps followed by a pot-au-feu of wild boar in Kriek beer… Forthright flavours and first-class produce paint the culinary portrait. After a day out in the easy-going town of Ostend, this is the perfect place to finish your trip on a festive note.

Name: Tablàvins
Description: This wine-decked, book-lined eatery sports a trendy colour scheme that reeks of the Flemish flair for interior decorating. The wine-food pairing suggestions are equally inspired. The food in the zeitgeist sports a subtle blend of tradition and exoticism: you may taste a generous saddle of rabbit or a sole sprinkled in Asian flavours. A deep-rooted respect for heritage paired with a streak of daring.

Name: Brasserie Rongese
Description: This characterful eatery is established in a former cafe in Runskt, a district that was once called Rongese. The owner, Peter Merken, is always on hand with excellent wine and beer tips to pair with the wonderful array of wholesome fare chalked up on the slate. Juicy rare entrecote steak with piping hot fries and al dente veggies followed by a Belle Hélène pear with vanilla ice cream and smothered in hot chocolate sauce: you can’t get more traditional than this brasserie score.

Name: Julienne
Description: This upmarket establishment dripping in marble, which is bright and airy by day and cosy by night, extends a warm welcome typical of the Kempen region, before presenting an enticing menu and list of daily specials. Seasoned chef, Tim Moeskops, knows his classics and skilfully turns out dishes ranging from crispy, generously filled shrimp fritters and fresh, juicy sole to flavoursome eel in sorrel or a Poire belle Hélène, straight from his own pear orchard. Julienne celebrates heroic classics and does so with flair and know-how.

Name: L'inizio
Description: Old family photos adorn the walls of Fabian Dichiara's sleek establishment, near the centre of Herve. The open kitchen is the focal point in the cosy dining space. The chef here combines familiar Italian flavours in his own special way, ensuring you leave satisfied. Whether you opt for the al dente calamarata pasta with wild mushrooms and bacon, or the stuffed tomato with its juicy meat and bold tomato sauce, this cuisine is sure to warm the cockles of your heart. Only a set menu is served at lunchtime; in the evening you can order à la carte.

Name: Cuichine
Description: House-made Peking duck with crispy skin, fresh veggies and pancakes ready to be stuffed, all of which flanked by a gutsy sweet and sour hoisin sauce. This signature dish embodies the philosophy of Cuichine: a modern version of old-school Chinese nosh, starring all our favourite Cantonese recipes. The interior of this eye-catching establishment is ideally suited to the trendy vibe and the restaurant also boasts a pleasant terrace.

Name: Delys
Description: Delys is a haven of design depicted by a chic black colour scheme. Intimacy and mystery set the stage, while floor-to-ceiling windows seem to invite the countryside indoors. Be it for a quick lunch or a more leisurely dinner, chef Doucet’s modern approach always hits the spot. He avows a weakness for crisp, legible, contrasting flavours. For example, he may add an exuberant edge to lightly poached Atlantic cod courtesy of lemon zest and a subtly smoky mushroom stock. Doucet leaves his heroic, distinctive stamp on each dish thanks to sensitive nuances.

Name: Caillou
Description: Caillou is a hip, modern restaurant, strewn with passing nods to ‘pebbles’ (its namesake). The kitchen team prepares the food on a central table that sets the scene for their culinary show. The performance continues in the plate, with an appetising blend of flavours and textures and enticing veggie dishes. The chef doesn’t hesitate to spice up traditional recipes, flanking lobster and turbot, for example, with deftly crafted side dishes such as asparagus flan, a gutsy lobster béarnaise and a poivrade of fried artichokes. The sommelier may suggest an elegant mineral wine, echoing the establishment’s name, to pair with your food.

Name: Antoine
Description: Lisa’s old family home has lost none of its welcoming allure. Today it is a magnificent restaurant, where Lisa has curated an excellent, mainly German, wine list. Chef Mirko concocts elegant dishes whose distinctive flavours are revved up with a bold individual touch, all of which founded on modern techniques. Examples include a subtly sweet carpaccio of strawberries paired with a bergamot granita and a yoghurt ice cream. The menu keeps pace with the seasons with a view to using the best of the moment, but you can always be certain to taste a festival of flavour.

Name: L'Atelier Windsor
Description: Escoffier, Bocuse: the pedigree sources of inspiration immediately set the tone in this restaurant that champions classical cuisine. The chef wows our senses with excellent produce, spot-on preparations and savvy sides. This culinary know-how extends to the dining room courtesy of tableside service, like a juicy pepper steak flambeed in cognac and then paired with a creamy sauce to die for! Carefully crafted, heroically wondrous food. At lunchtime, this trendy bistro (picture windows, vintage tiles and stylish furnishings) is a hit with a business clientele.

Name: Le Bouton d'Or
Description: Roch and Florence’s friendly restaurant bears witness to the couple’s love of nature. The veggies come from a neighbouring farmer and the chef hunts the game himself. Generous, unfussy cooking at its best. You can expect dishes such as succulent sole meunière or rare tenderloin steak underscored by a punchy pepper sauce. The set menu with choices is always a safe bet. Florence seamlessly supervises the front-of-house and can be trusted to suggest insightful wine-food pairings.

Name: Le Plëss
Description: The opulent Le Plëss brasserie is just as elegant as the swish Place d’Armes Hotel in which it is housed. A quick glance at the menu will reveal that rotisserie and carvery dishes feature prominently in the classic lineup. The veal cutlet is grilled to perfection and flanked by a punchy gravy. You have the choice of side dishes, from Robuchon mashed potato to seasonal veggies, while other delicacies include foie gras in red wine and balsamic vinegar. The meat is carved at the table in traditional brasserie style. A mouth-watering "plëss-ure"!

Name: Domaine la Forêt
Description: This elegant, classical restaurant commands a stunning view over the Luxemburg Moselle valley. Chef, Claude Wallerich, concocts tasty dishes of traditional inspiration that will introduce you to delicious regional produce. The well - stocked wine cellar is an added bonus!

Name: La Rameaudière
Address: 10 rue de la Gare, Ellange, 5690, Luxembourg
Description: Daniel Rameau is a connoisseur of luxury produce, among which foie gras, lobster and pigeon, which he prepares refreshingly simply in dishes that blend generosity and tradition. The equally enticing wine list features a savvy selection of Luxemburg vintages. This former village train station and its flower-decked terrace are steeped in vintage charm.

Name: Bosque FeVi
Description: If your tastebuds start to tingle at the idea of biting into a “croquetas de jamón” and a “crema catalana” with a hint of citrus fruit, then book a table straight away in this exquisite restaurant, depicted by a striking “undulating” wooden wall-cum-artwork. Fernando Andreu conjures up a Mediterranean score with a dash of modernity by delving into his Spanish roots and the odd international influence like kimchi or tikka masala. If you’re in the mood for tapas, make a beeline for FeVi Gaudium, under the same roof of the Seven Hotel.

Name: Bleuet
Description: Time seems to have stopped still at Bleuet, which is confirmed by the view over the rolling hillsides of the Flemish Ardennes from the exquisite terrace and the cosy interior of this cosy cottage. Pieter-Jan is in the kitchen, while Yoran makes sure the dining room never gets too crowded to ensure optimum quality. Yoran can be relied upon to open a bottle of wine for you to taste, which is something of a rarity these days. The chef plays with familiar flavours and international accents, as his seabass fillets in a miso and champagne sauce with a risotto of wheat and crunchy veg demonstrates. Food that throbs with flavour and a felicitous feast of unexpected associations.

Name: Max & Moi
Address: Grand Place Baudouin Premier 4, Braine-l'Alleud, 1420, Belgium
Description: Max & Pina have set up shop on Place Baudouin 1er in a tastefully refurbished town house dripping in understated glamour and sporting a suitably tasteful colour scheme. The couple works with a talented youthful chef, Julien Hauspie, who prefers to work with local produce while rolling out his experience gleaned in worldclass establishments at home and abroad. The chef’s know-how can be tasted in the beurre blanc that flanks seabass or in his way with carrots, which he might pair with a béarnaise sauce and tarragon and lemon oil, also demonstrating his creative side and fun-loving personality. Vibrant, exciting cuisine that comes in a four- or five-course menu.

Name: le Petit bon bon
Description: Christophe Hardiquest has opted to uphold his idea of a luxury brasserie in the Corinthia Grand Hotel Astoria. In this plush, stylish setting, the open kitchen has been cast in the star role. The brasserie lineup is as purebred as the traditional tableware in which it is served, but Hardiquest has assembled a team, who adds a distinctive signature and spin. The intense filling of the shrimp fritters, the bordelaise sauce enriched with a perfectly runny egg yolk and the elaborate vol-au-vent stuffed with a creamy concoction of sweetbread illustrate how difficult it will be to make up your mind when you peruse the enticing brasserie menu.

Name: De la terre à l'assiette
Address: Rue de la Poste 13, Arlon, 6700, Belgium
Description: Magali and Guillaume Lempens’ colourful venue is the quintessence of comfortable and steeped in feelgood vibes, a large proportion of which are courtesy of their bistronomic cuisine. The latter includes fried cod flanked by a subtle bouillabaisse, white asparagus, homemade gnocchi and a knockout aioli mayonnaise. Big-boned, punchy sauces and impeccable technique bear witness to the experience of seasoned chef Guillaume. Rather than fussy frills, you can expect wholehearted authenticity and no-nonsense rustic fare.

Name: Table Rase
Description: At Table Rase, chef Ludovic focuses on allowing the ingredient to shout its name, simply and emphatically! His flavoursome set menu with options keeps pace with the seasons as it highlights regional produce. Examples: tartare of langoustine with asparagus and a kombu-laced sabayon or fork-tender ribeye steak with morels and a knockout jus. The décor is cosy and colourful and the vibe is casual and cheerful. Bargain prices further add to the establishment’s appeal. Don’t miss the house signature – tiramichoux (tiramisu cream puffs).

Name: Colonel Fort Jaco
Description: An offshoot of Colonel, a temple of red meat, this stylish brasserie sports a tasteful colour scheme that is the epitome of suave urbanity. Diners are invited to choose one of the juicy cuts of meat from the butcher’s counter near the open-plan kitchen. The knife-edge precision offered by the Josper charcoal oven, the exquisite flavour of the cured meats, the made-to-order sauces and the crispy fries are indeed admirable, but that is not all. Side by side this traditional Belgian lineup, you will also find dishes like carpaccio or filet américain, and more nostalgic dishes like their excellent vol-au-vent. We recommend a seat at the counter to make the most of the show in the kitchen.

Name: Les Potes au Feu
Address: avenue de la Plante 4, Namur, 5000, Belgium
Description: A couple of pals, Damien Gorjanec and François Schepens, have added a new spin to the bistronomic concept with creativity as their baseline, depicted by locally grown veggies, unorthodox combinations and throbbing sauces. For example, they might mix black and Morello cherries with a cocoa crumble and vanilla ice cream made with unpasteurised milk. A casual, fun vibe bordering on rock ‘n roll with masses of taste in the plate.

Name: ATELIER D THE BISTRO
Description: Diego De Baets is clearly at home in this sophisticated bistro, in which art and authenticity go hand in hand with a truly romantic vibe. The chef loves popping into the dining room to add a finishing touch to his dishes. You can expect a Franco-Belgian lineup starring outstanding ingredients, truly memorable sauces and big-boned flavours. Examples include crispy sweetbread coated in a flavoursome gravy further enhanced by sakura vinegar, or a match made in heaven of finely sliced wagyu and scallops paired with a knockout consommé made with the cooking gravy. The à la carte menu, which will have fine food connoisseurs slavering in anticipation, is a treasure trove of Belgian and French staples with a twist. Sheer bliss from start to finish.

Name: Restaurant Cloche
Description: The bright, elegant venue of Tobias Clocheret and Wim De Mulder stands in the shadow of the belltower of Hofstade church and the front terrace is heavenly in summertime. Top-drawer produce like langoustines and sweetbread is pampered and delicately crafted into succulent recipes. The chef slices scallops into wafer thin carpaccio, adding a beurre blanc enhanced by fermented asparagus peelings, lovage oil and cauliflower textures. A felicitous feast designed to appeal to today’s tastebuds courtesy of a range of enticing textures.

Name: Nonam
Description: Nestled in the heart of Ghent's Patershol neighbourhood, Nonam has an authentic and cosy ambience with a touch of vintage charm. After stretching out in one of the luxurious guestrooms, pop into the the restaurant, where the set menu presents a playful take on fusion cuisine. The chef transforms his grandmother's rice pudding recipe, for instance, with exciting textures of apricot and a koji-based ice cream. Or he boldly combines beetroot, blue cheese and umeboshi. The selection of fine wines, by the bottle and by the glass, has plenty of gems in store.

Name: Palais Royal by David Martin
Description: As soon as the doorman ushers you into the luxurious Corinthia Grand Hotel, you will be entranced by its period charm. The restored stained-glass dome of the Palm Court is truly magnificent, while the dining room immerses you in a romantic Belle époque ambience. A marble fireplace, lovingly restored details and fresh flowers set the scene in the spacious, characterful restaurant, which also offers privacy and intimacy. David Martin has assembled a team that invites you to sample subtle creations enhanced by familiar Japanese flavours in a vibe that is both classy and casual. An example: juicy fillet of red mullet lacquered in a sweet-sour chorizo sauce and flanked by a rich chorizo oil, subtle vegetable sides and chunks of merguez… You can expect a culinary banquet that intelligently combines a few carefully chosen ingredients to create a genuine explosion of flavour. A banquet of royal proportions indeed!

Name: Artis
Description: Hao Guo entirely redesigned the interior of Artis with a brand-new colour scheme of soft shades and a cornucopia of contemporary comforts. The food is emblematic of the veteran chef’s experiences in top establishments in Belgium and abroad. While the backbone of his cuisine may be Gallic, he doesn’t hesitate to add international influences. For example, his bouillabaisse reveals the full depth of the salty seafood and is underscored with a rich, yet subtle stock. Chef Guo has an undeniable knack for sauces and his culinary technique is second to none. The extensive menu impresses, as does the spot-on selection of French and Luxembourg wines.

Name: Tabernakel
Description: Brothers Steven and Bart refuse to be hampered by a single style. As a result, you may sample an appetiser of fresh, mildly spicy baba ghanoush or a playful new twist on the traditional tomato-mozzarella bruschetta, followed by a rack of lamb in a rosemary jus. Versatile and talented, they create appetising set menus and a splendid à la carte lineup. Kim enthusiastically supervises the front-of-house, bending over backwards to ensure that you savour every morsel of your meal to the full. An elegant, neoteric industrial vibe with just the right dose of authenticity.

Name: Cella
Description: One half of the restaurant commands a view of the kitchen team crafting all sorts delicacies, while the other overlooks the Antwerp docks and skyline. There is never a dull moment at Cella, starting with the industrial cachet of this stylishly repurposed warehouse by the team that used to run Het Pomphuis. The menu features a tempting lineup of pedigree Belgian fare with matured meat grilled over charcoal embers, fresh fries and a last-minute sauce, together with a smattering of ubiquitous international dishes of the likes of ceviche and sushi. Flawless technique and aromatic sauces are the hallmark of the gifted chef.

Name: Nage
Description: (Temporarily closed) The character of this medieval mansion has been intelligently enhanced by the cosy, trendy revamp. Niki shares his know-how in terms of choice of excellent natural wines to pair with the modern French recipes crafted by Koen. The chef sprinkles his cooking with the occasional unexpected note in a bid to further highlight the ingredients’ authentic flavours. Examples include saddle of lamb cooked in butter with suave, flavoursome side dishes based on wild garlic. A word of warning: à la carte only at lunchtime and set menu only in the evening.

Name: La table du Royal Snail
Address: avenue de la Plante 23, Namur, 5000, Belgium
Description: This laid-back restaurant is appointed in the same trendy, glamorous vein as the Royal Snail Hotel in which it is housed. The welcoming, casual vibe provides the perfect foil to sample Carl Gillain’s bistronomic vision. The slate menu features a pageant of unconventional bistro dishes and sensibly priced wines. He might add depth to ravioli of turnip with a stock of roast onion and veal, imparting subtle umami, but then again, he may simply pair a juicy entrecote with a fresh, wonderfully light, silky bearnaise sauce. Most of the dishes are designed to be shared, although you may not always wish to do so…

Name: Le Flore
Description: A restored farm-castle near Bergenvaart, whose rustic characterful charm sets the scene of the stylish interior, without forgetting the idyllic terrace overlooking sheep grazing in the meadow. Sheer bliss! Chef Verlande rustles up an enticing lunchtime lineup that changes daily and a varied à la carte offering. You will immediately be struck by his passion for premium produce, such as lobster, turbot and hare, to which he adds his inimitable hallmark. Take his scallops gratineed with cheese and paired with wild garlic, a velvety poultry cream and creamy unctuous asparagus. Le Flore allows the ingredients to shout their name.

Name: Huize Alberic
Description: From the ironwork and the restored fireplace to the wooden floors, the former home (1920s) of Alberic Plettinck, ironworker and artist, has been tastefully and respectfully refurbished in a stylish vein. After being welcomed by your gracious hostess, you will sample an updated version of classical recipes in which chef Bram demonstrates his flair for plating. His consummate craftsmanship shines through in the intense creamy gravy that flanks pheasant or in his modern spin on eels in sorrel.

Name: Hors-Champs
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Garden or park,Interesting wine list,Terrace
Description: Stefan Jacobs has metamorphosed the Ernage farmstead. This gifted chef has opened a B&B, a bakery and a tasteful restaurant that sports a rough, brutalist look. His sustainable ethos can be tasted in subtle dishes, rife in unorthodox and playful combinations. His devotion to the produce of his own cottage garden and that of local market gardeners is unwavering. He may use cucumbers in a myriad of ways, such as in a concoction of mussels, briny seaweed and fresh veggies. Or would you prefer a veggie burger stuffed with different textures of courgettes, radish and turnip and served with a veggie gravy that is reminiscent of a big-boned BBQ sauce? This light-hearted culinary ethos is paired with an unconventional wine list that has been savvily curated to enhance the food’s numerous nuances. A generous ode to the region!

Name: LESS Eatery
Description: Love Eat Share Smile is the baseline of this hip urban eatery, which is equally suited to a hunger-obliterating snack at the bar as to a full-course feast with all the trimmings with all the family. You can expect an international culinary repertory with a definite Asian slant. From steak tartare with a Korean kick and ceviche scattered with distinctive fresh, spicy, tangy Peruvian notes to Hong-Kong-style young turbot, the extensive menu is a treasure trove of premium produce and creativity. A trendy, suitably casual vibe depicts one of Bruges’ most popular foodie hotspots!

Name: Cosma
Description: The bright, hip, relaxed vibe of this restaurant immediately sets everyone at ease. This enthusiasm is further enhanced when you take a glance at the menu which sports a wide range of dishes to be shared, countless vegetarian suggestions and excellent side dishes – bravo! An unusual formula and heart-warming international influences.

Name: Nyde
Description: The decision to call their restaurant Nyde, which means “to enjoy” in Danish, was far from ingenuous. Chef Céline, flanked by Martijn, your host, bend over backwards to make sure their guests enjoy their meal. The restaurant, whose vibe is serene and boasts a gorgeous patio to the rear, offers a set menu and a selection of cocktails and mocktails and insightful food-wine pairings. Céline underscores each ingredient’s purity as she seeks to sensitively enhance their flavours. She may garnish a lemon-flavoured mackerel tartare with a delicate concoction of diced cucumber and briny oysters, all of which is further offset by a lemon and cucumber dressing. Feelgood food that is guaranteed to lift your spirits.

Name: Brasserie Daefnis
Description: It isn’t easy to nab a table in this luxury brasserie, which is always a sign of top-notch quality. Daefnis specialises in first-rate produce: North Sea sole, lamb shoulder and Hereford côte à l'os are just a few of the delicacies that are showcased on the up-to-date brasserie menu. Familiar flavours are nonetheless respected, albeit with judicious nuances.

Name: Tafeltje Rond
Description: Tafeltje Rond enjoys something of a reputation as a romantic venue. Parisian chic defines this brasserie which sports parquet floors, elegantly laid tables, a black and white colour scheme and tableware that is as classy as the wine list and chef Slangen’s polished Gallic score. Old school classics like seabass in a salt crust, tournedos Rossini and hop shoots in a divine hollandaise sauce are rich in the distinctive flavours of yesteryear and the ethereal profiteroles filled with rich vanilla ice cream and smothered in intense dark chocolate are to die for! Don’t hesitate to give the chef your feedback directly as he loves popping out of the kitchen to add a final touch to dishes and say hi to his guests. Set menu at lunchtime only; à la carte in the evening.

Name: Ristorante Roma
Description: Opened in 1950, Roma was the first Italian restaurant of Luxembourg, and it remains true to its founding authentic values. Seventy years on, little has changed and the venue, adorned with Venetian chandeliers, is still as vibrant and colourful as the food is wholesome. The pasta is homemade and oozes with crisp Mediterranean accents. Examples include pasta stuffed with seafood and a velvety vongole-type sauce or why not order a melt-in-the-mouth medallion of lamb, flanked by a gutsy gravy, mashed potatoes and scamorza? Themed festivals and a varied menu with something for everyone transform each meal into a feast.

Name: Le Bouchon et l'Assiette
Description: From the outside it is a small brick farmstead nestling in the green countryside, inside, however, diners are greeted by a surprisingly airy and contemporary décor. A family - run establishment that specialises in generous dishes with a dash of originality prepared on the spot. Fantastic wine list.

Name: Jacob's
Description: Juicy red meat straight out of the wood-burning Josper oven is the signature of this hip joint done up in dark colours. The staff is both jovial and professional and it is a pleasure to watch the chefs in their open kitchen deploying their talent to craft spot-on food packed in flavour. Whether it is impeccably cooked hanger steak garnished with a bearnaise sauce and fresh fries or their take on French toast (to die for!), generosity defines the ethos of this establishment. It is of course heaven for meat lovers, but the menu also offers fish and lobster.

Name: Manoir de Lébioles
Description: The chef working at this manor house creates his own personal style of up - to - the - minute cuisine using the highest quality ingredients. Chic, modern decor and lovely panoramic terrace.

Name: La Cour de la Reine
Description: The ‘Queen’s Courtyard’ aims to serve creative bistronomic dishes with strong classical overtones. The chef, a seasoned stalwart, has no qualms about letting creativity guide his inspiration and you will taste the chef’s personal version of a Belgian classic, shrimp fritters, together with a cutlet of venison with a heroically wondrous pepper sauce. A distinctive metal structure forms the centrepiece of the elegant establishment, which also offers swish guestrooms.

Name: Les Plats Canailles de la Bleue Maison
Address: rue du Pont d'Oye 7, Habay-la-Neuve, 6720, Belgium
Description: The picture postcard scene features a blue-shuttered gingerbread house poised between two rivers. The exquisite neo-rustic interior exudes a romantic vibe. Brice and Martin Thiry have added gusto and verve to this family business. They favour local produce and juggle with modern flavours such as acidity whilst respecting the ethos of traditional recipes. So, fancy sharing a rib of beef, carved in front of you, washed down with a glass of full-bodied wine? Good food and good vibes are the backbone of this endearing eatery.

Name: L'Amandier
Description: L'Amandier is a family business that is going from strength to strength. Martin Volkaerts took over the establishment a few years ago, before moving it to this characterful edifice, which sports a modern interior. It even boasts two guestrooms for overnight stays. Creativity dictates Volkaerts’ culinary skill, which is depicted by made to order cooking and exquisite sauces. His interest in exotic flavours adds depth and intensity to his score and he enjoys letting the produce from his cottage garden inspire his recipes as he creates a fine balance between spicy and acidic notes. Stéphanie and the team are responsible for the warm cheerful vibe, further confirming that hospitality is truly part of the Volkaerts’ family DNA.

Name: Atelier de Bossimé
Description: Ludovic Vanackere’s converted this old farm in line with his sustainable vision. If the produce doesn’t come from his own impressive kitchen garden, which can be admired from the floor-to-ceiling windows, it is sourced locally. The surprise menu showcases the best of Namur and the region. Veggies take the limelight, prompting extra creativity in the winter season, illustrated by the chef’s work with different cabbage textures enhanced by a sauce packed in fermented veg, peanuts and sate-flavoured spices. Regional cooking founded on throbbing recipes and powerful sauces.

Name: Mout
Description: Walk past the Damse Brouwers microbrewery to the cosy dining space and treat yourself to a brew straight from the tank. What a lovely prelude to a fine meal in a convivial setting! Chef Monteyne's passion shines through in the restaurant's exciting, modern dishes. In the afternoon, you can tuck into light snacks and lunch options; the evening menu offers a wider selection. He has a penchant for bold accoutrements, such as salt-crusted celeriac and the tangy beurre blanc emulsion that he uses to elevate plaice.

Name: Les Tilleuls
Description: The former village hall of Céroux-Mousty has been converted into a welcoming bistro. Marc Volkaerts throws all his enthusiasm into crafting his own version of classical cuisine, such as shrimp fritters, sole fish fingers or duck shepherd’s pie. He adds a personal and distinctive spin, courtesy of his extensive experience, creating dishes that stand out with crispy crunchy details or delicately, tangy touches. The market fresh menu changes daily and is chalked up on a slate.

Name: Commotie
Description: Commotie radiates a sense of zen-like tranquillity. The verdant surroundings and minimalist Japanese decor create a harmonious whole and the terrace is an oasis of alfresco calm, until the arrival of the food interrupts your quiet contemplation. Chef Thomas expresses his originality through fermentation, vegetables, tart flavours, barbecue notes and intense sauces... His inventiveness is captivating, and his nose-to-tail vision is an inspiration. An example of his fascinating approach is monkfish in seaweed, lacquered in butter before being seared over an open flame. He further underscores the delicacy of this exquisite fish with a vin jaune and razor clam bearnaise sauce, crafted like a beurre blanc. Each dish tells a story, complemented by the insightful choices of sommelier Lara, who avows a penchant for natural wines.

Name: Casello
Description: This former toll station on the Turnhout-Antwerp road has morphed into a sophisticated restaurant. The sleek annexe drips with designer luxury and gilt details, and the open kitchen is sure to draw the eye as soon as you arrive. The chef works with top-notch ingredients, elevating them regularly with subtle Asian touches and the bold flavours of Italy. Whether in the form of langoustine with wawasai and enoki, or tagliatelle with truffle and horn of plenty, this modern approach to the principle of "less is more" is captivating.

Name: Alexandre
Description: This 18C doctor’s home, set in the picturesque village of Herzele and a well-kept secret among discerning foodies, is depicted by a snug interior, a superb terrace and Tamara’s attentive service. Tim Ritserveldt deploys his virtuoso culinary skills, rustling up a set menu overflowing in creativity. Hearty, gutsy flavours are his hallmark, such as feta, watermelon sorbet and guacamole cream which enhance the character and depth of thinly sliced Duroc ham. Full-bodied, spot-on food that enjoys straying from conventional culinary paths.

Name: Atelier Noun
Description: Bert and Sandra’s workshop sports a cosy, lounge vibe, underscored by Scandinavian accents and a splendid leafy al fresco area. The couple’s passion can be felt throughout the restaurant and Bert adores rustling up fascinating modern recipes, scattered with Asian nuances and incisive, acidic notes. Paradise for foodies!

Name: Schéiss
Description: Schéiss sports a classy contemporary brasserie slant paired with classical culinary know-how in a match made in heaven. The seasoned front-of-house team ensures that you lack for nothing as they seamlessly provide tableside service with flair and talent. The score shines the spotlight on a cast of patriotic classics like shrimp fritters and Liège-style meatballs, all of which with a weakness for powerful sauces and delicate new spins on traditional recipes. The fillet of seabass, impeccably cooked on the skin, is paired with a frothy girolle-flavoured cream, mashed potatoes and steamed spinach. Rather than surprises, you can expect a serious lineup of family favourites that never fails to deliver.

Name: Les Jardins d'Anaïs
FacilitiesAndServices: Car park,Garden or park,Interesting wine list,Terrace,Valet parking
Description: These gardens are the epitome of posh elegance from the conservatory overlooking the lush greenery to the guestrooms, without forgetting the champagne trolley. All of which doesn’t prevent the chef from occasionally erring from the path of classicism and giving a free rein to his creative streak. Fillet of smoked sturgeon is paired with a striking gin and caviar sorbet and subtly offset by asparagus, foie gras and grapefruit. Bold, daring, spot-on cuisine!

Name: Bistronome
Description: In this chic bistro, chef Hospital imparts a daily lesson in bistronomy, giving popular dishes and flavours a gourmet spin. The food is as exquisite to behold as it is to taste. Throw in the occasional creative twist and a liberal sprinkling of generosity and the scene is set. In addition to dishes that have been revamped with seasonings from around the globe, the menu also features classics such as meatballs in tomato sauce or rib steak with a silky bearnaise sauce and hand-cut fresh fries. Making your choice from the set and à la carte lineups is always a challenge!

Name: La Paulée Marie-Pierre
Description: This friendly establishment is named after an ancient Burgundy wine festival, which is far from a coincidence. It is even possible to buy a bottle to take home from the sensibly priced wine bin. The culinary score errs towards the traditional, albeit with a more contemporary lineup of suggestions. Examples include tender juicy veal garnished with a poultry sauce enriched in Comté cheese and a gratin of sliced potatoes and onions. The lunchtime menu embodies the big-hearted mindset of this culinary landmark of Tournai.
