The concept is a success, with its remarkable choice of 110 wines by the glass, and nicely done traditional food (pâté en croûte, bavette steak with a peppercorn sauce etc). Elegant and inviting decor.

Name: Les Roseaux Pensants
Description: This quaint historic village is the lair of a self-taught couple, who sources their organic ingredients entirely locally thus enabling them to develop close ties with producers. The gutsy result demonstrates a weakness for veggies and fermentation illustrated by vegetarian black pudding paired with apple and black garlic pickles, although the menu also features a sprinkling of meat and fish dishes. A delightful patio shaded by linden trees in fine weather and swish, slick service complete the portrait.

Name: ASPIC
Description: After ditching the world of finance to enrol in the Ferrandi Culinary School, the chef went on to hone his skills in a variety of establishments (including the French Ministry of Foreign Affairs and L'Épi Dupin). He then went it alone and opened this restaurant. With its vintage vibe and open kitchen, the chef devises a surprise set menu that is unabashedly creative and showcases carefully selected ingredients: free-range meat and poultry, line-caught fish from small boat fishing, citrus fruits, herbs and spices, all sourced as locally as possible.

Name: À l'Échevin
Description: In the heart of Colmar's Little Venice, this half-timbered building houses the Le Maréchal hotel as well as its restaurant, which is done out in a very classical style. Try to reserve a table in the blue room with exposed timberwork and a view of the River Lauch. Expect modern cuisine that revisits the classics of the local terroir and gastronomy.

Name: Kazumi
Description: Japanese-born Kazumi Hatakenaka originally came to France to work in a traditional inn in the Beaujolais region. Behind his counter, he now crafts a tasting menu devoted entirely to pedigree Japanese cuisine that is the epitome of delicate and fresh. Drool-worthy dishes and flawless cooking and seasonings. Expect to spend three hours to do full justice to this culinary experience.

Name: Zen
Description: This succulent restaurant combines a pleasantly traditional interior with authentic Japanese fare. The extensive menu stars a lineup of staples: sushi, grilled dishes and tempura, together with the house signatures of gyoza and chirashi - even the mochi are made in house. A word of warning: no bookings possible at lunchtime (more concise menu) and it fills up quickly – so come early!

Name: La Cage aux Fleurs
Description: Flowers and colours abound in this spruce-looking bistro, both in the decor (floral wallpaper, varnished porcelain knick-knacks) and on the plate: tuna tartare, pumpkin seeds, grilled butternut condiment, anchovies with green pepper; roast fillet of sea bass, panisse (chickpea fries), saffron, fennel. This cuisine in tune with the zeitgeist is delivered by a professional couple – themselves the offspring of restaurant owners – who work in tandem. French classics that are the winegrowers' favourites and cuts of meat to share are also present and correct.

Name: Sagan
Description: A stone’s throw from the iconic Odéon Theatre, this dinky restaurant, depicted by bare stone walls and a counter with seating, serves inventive, razor-sharp Japanese fare: sashimi of semi-cooked salmon and caviar, miso soup with clams marinated in sake. The wine list is a treasure trove of Bordeaux and Burgundy tipples.

Name: Boutary
Description: The ideal place to discover or brush up on your caviar know-how (osetra, sterlet and baeri), as the owners have been raising sturgeon in southern Bulgaria for several generations. The plush smart interior and the chef’s “carte blanche” menus, with a traditional tasting session served on the back of the hand, are very popular.

Name: Tavline
Description: Between Saint-Paul and Hôtel de Ville, a slice of Tel Aviv, a taste of Morocco, a hint of Lebanon – such is the formula of Tavline. Spices supplied by Shuk Ha'Carmel, the largest market in Tel Aviv, adorn the fine cuisine served here, including ksitsot daguim – grilled fish balls with herbs and spices on a bed of lentils with yoghurt and candied lemon, or the memorable memoulam (onions stuffed with lamb), a recipe passed down to the chef from his mother.

Name: Allard
Description: In the heart of bustling Saint Germain des Près, this authentic Parisian bistro, dripping in charm and now part of the Ducasse empire, has changed very little since it opened in 1932. The culinary score wavers between bistro fare and heroic brasserie staples. Attractive lunchtime menu.

Name: Dersou
Description: In a pleasant side street near Bastille, Dersou proposes the original experience of pairing food and cocktails in a trendy atmosphere complete with music. A dish of leeks with a coarse grain mustard cream and sorrel vinaigrette is accompanied by a dill, yuzu, gin and Granny Smith apple cocktail; guinea fowl with tangy beetroot puree is paired with a whisky, port and orange cocktail judiciously. The ingredients are top quality and the mixology does not disappoint.

Name: Le Bon Saint-Pourçain
Description: Tucked away behind St Sulpice Church in the heart of arty St Germain des Prés, this former 'bougnat' eatery pulls out all the stops against a backdrop of tiled floors, fake leather banquettes and the cheerful chatter of regular patrons. Start with a house-made peppery black pudding terrine, followed by tender, crispy-skinned free-range chicken, melt-in-the-mouth potatoes, chard, mushrooms and a gutsy pepper sauce, to finish with a glorious vanilla millefeuille. The epitome of a Parisian bistro. Booking advisable!

Name: Le Christine
Description: This restaurant has been in this quiet little street for over 20 years; the abbey next door has been converted into a delightful boutique hotel. A talented young chef, who has worked in some top kitchens, is making his mark here with his cosmopolitan cuisine, which is influenced by fermentation, smoky flavours and his childhood memories: onion soup pimped up with foie gras and Appenzeller cheese; charcoal-grilled red mullet with a full-bodied bouillabaisse and a dash of chicken liver cream; île flottante, rice pudding, crème anglaise with grilled koji and shio koji caramel. Vegetarian options are also available.

Name: Toyo
Description: In a former life, Toyomitsu Nakayama was the private chef of fashion designer Kenzo. Nowadays, he excels in the art of fusing flavours and textures. Breaded monkfish, Buddha's hand, seaweed and Mimolette; beef, myoga ginger and red shiso sauce… This is fresh, fragrant cuisine, perfectly washed down with a glass of Burgundy and served up by an attentive but unobtrusive team. Terrific.

Name: Baffo
Description: Originally from southern Tuscany, cooking enthusiast Fabien Zannier pays tribute to the flavours of his childhood in this small, colourful Italian restaurant that packs a tasty punch. Fresh organic ingredients, often sourced directly from the producer (arborio rice, Colonnata bacon, artisanal pasta from Pitigliano). Unusual antipasti, set menus for sharing (on seafood or truffle themes) and a cellar stocked in great Italian wines – just the place for a "pranzo con i baffi" – a meal so good, you’ll want to lick your whiskers!

Name: L'Apibo
Description: In his small bistro in the Montorgueil neighbourhood (hushed atmosphere, oak floorboards, exposed stone), Antony Boucher, a chef with a strong track record, creates beautifully original and delicate cuisine that fêtes ingredients. He is renowned for his two classics: filet of sea bass, black rice and paprika sauce and the eight-hour confit pork with sweet potato mousseline. The laid-back (and very professional) service evokes the rough and ready spirit that used to characterise Les Halles.

Name: L'Ardoise
Description: This restaurant, whose walls are covered in slate, wears its name well! It pays a pleasing tribute to bistro heritage by means of its style and also its food – chicken pâté en croûte, foie gras and ceps; fillet of beef with black pepper and pommes Anna; lemon meringue tartlet; crème brûlée – a feast of generous, fresh and tasty dishes!

Name: Nacl
Description: Nestled within the medieval ramparts of Vence, this small restaurant, whose name refers to salt (cast your mind back to chemistry lessons: NaCl is the chemical formula for sodium chloride), serves authentic seasonal cuisine that takes a no-nonsense approach. The menu changes depending on the food markets, and the lunch set menu is a great deal. Friendly service.

Name: 19.20 by Norbert Tarayre
Address: Prince de Galles, 33 avenue George-V, Paris, 75008, France
Description: Built in 1928, the Prince de Galles is a legendary jewel of the Parisian Art Deco movement. It has chosen to democratise luxury hotel cuisine by entrusting its kitchens to Norbert Tarayre, the firebrand chef discovered on French TV show Top Chef in 2012. In a cosy setting that pays tribute to artistic life in Paris, the chef serves up traditional cuisine that channels the tasty regional cooking of yesteryear: grated carrot salad, leeks in vinaigrette, celeriac in remoulade dressing, pork shoulder and pommes Anna, salmon tournedos – not to mention the dessert trolley. It's all lovingly prepared and delivered. Incredibly reasonable price of the menu.

Name: Yen
Description: The stripped-back decor of this eatery will appeal to fans of minimalism. You will taste a festival of Japanese delicacies: sushi, tempura, black cod marinated in miso and grilled, sakura mochi… The house signature is soba (buckwheat noodles) served hot or cold. Authentic fare and slick, seamless service.

Name: Restaurant de l'Écluse 16
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Garden or park,Wheelchair access
Description: This restaurant standing beside the Canal de la Sarre towpath was once a coaching inn, along which horses used to tow coal from the mines. The chef, from Morbihan in Brittany, cooks up delicious and meticulous cuisine, such as saffron risotto with chorizo served alongside premium quality poultry with wild prawns, or his truly unforgettable take on tarte Tatin. He occasionally uses ingredients from the local terroir, enhanced with condiments or home-made aromatic oils.

Name: Racine
Description: Just a stone's throw from Place Stanislas, youthful chef Martin Debuiche orchestrates a market-fresh score inspired by regional produce. Carefully sourced ingredients and deftly crafted cooking: good food in a buzzy, friendly vibe.

Name: Ô Gayot
Address: 2 avenue de la Ferté-Macé, Bagnoles-de-l'Orne, 61140, France
Description: This chic bistro in a pretty stone house certainly has its finger on the pulse. On the menu find good bistro recipes that change on a weekly basis. These include, soft - boiled egg with cream of mushroom soup and Calvados baba. A taste sensation!

Name: Odette
Description: Two steps from Les Halles, in the luxurious Albar Hotel, the Rostang family demonstrates that they haven’t lost their touch in this urban inn. Odette regales us with succulent dishes to be shared: seabass in a pastry crust, one of the house signatures, veal cutlets, roast guinea fowl. Her score is spot on and dotted with fanciful notes, like veal belly paired with Gala apples or lightly seared scallops with parsnip and cashew nuts. The addictive desserts are to die for, illustrated by a hazelnut and pistachio millefeuille sprinkled with confit of orange zest.

Name: Black Bass
Address: Black Bass Hotel, 921 route d'Albertville, à Sevrier, Annecy, 74000, France
FacilitiesAndServices: Car park,Garden or park,Great view,Terrace,Wheelchair access
Description: A smart trendy vibe, a hip interior design and a sweeping view of the lake set the scene for bistronomic dining. Fish from local farms play the lead role in a concise culinary score strewn with creative flair.

Name: Sandikala
Address: 9 rue de la Barsogue, Galan, 65330, France
FacilitiesAndServices: Car park,Garden or park,Interesting wine list,Terrace,Wheelchair access
Description: Australian-born chef Luke MacLeod welcomes guests to this old farmstead, which has been done up in a tasteful country chic vein. He concocts generous seasonal cuisine that allies local produce with Asian ingredients, in a nod to his travels: pan-fried foie gras and kimchi; spaghetti squash tempura and fresh wasabi. The ingredients are firmly rooted in the terroir, and the seasonings are a blend of tangy, sweet and spicy flavours.

Name: La Corniche - Sainte-Barbe
Description: Sainte Barbe Hotel offers a choice of Instagrammable views looking out to sea or of the harbour. La Corniche sports and elegant contemporary vibe. Finely crafted cuisine, recipes of bistronomic inspiration with a distinct preference for local fish and seafood. The rooftop bar is heaven for a drink before or after dinner.

Name: La Table des Climats
Description: Within the Cité Internationale de la Gastronomie et du Vin, this restaurant is just a few metres from the Chapelle des Climats et des Terroirs. The contemporary furnishings highlight the building's historical features like the exposed stonework and a coffered ceiling. This splendid setting provides the perfect foil for cuisine that fetes produce from the region: pôchouse (sort of hotpot) of freshwater fish, aïoli, ham and Chablis; Dombes duck with apricots, aubergine and hyssop and a dessert of Burgundy blackcurrant, water mint, crème anglaise and blackcurrant pepper. Food and wine pairings are taken very seriously here.

Name: es/pacìo
Address: 201 nouveau port des Lecques, Saint-Cyr-sur-Mer, 83270, France
Description: Local seasonal veg and fruit, freshly caught wild fish, an on-the-ball team (including the former sous-chef from La Chassagnette), a concise, savvily curated list of local natural wines: the scene is set for lip-smacking, heroic fare in which everything tastes of something. Examples: red tuna, raspberry and coriander harissa; line-fished dentex, borlotti beans, tomatoes, pilpil and combava; duckling, caillette, broccoli rabe and blackberry juice. The picture windows of this seafront bistro, appointed in a lowkey vein, overlook a terrace and the marina.

Name: Auberge aux 4 Saisons
Description: Venture over the threshold of this large regional-style 1920s building with oriel and stained-glass windows into a handsome, inviting dining room. Poultry pâté en croûte and confit lemon; honey-lacquered loin of pork, cream of sweetcorn and sautéed seasonal mushrooms; chocolate soufflée tart: the young chef delights diners from start to finish. A concise wine list with a focus on organic and biodynamic wines; possibility of gin and tonic pairings (with local gins of course!).

Name: Le Terroir des Vignobles
Address: CC Le Valaisan 2, Montvalezan, La Rosière, 73700, France
Description: Terroir and vineyard: the name says it all, summing up this young couple's passion for good food, good ingredients (local, but not exclusively – you'll see tuna and sea bream on the menu) and fine wines; the wine list features an organic selection from Savoie and elsewhere. Whether after or before skiing, mountain biking or hiking, the chef's recipes will whet your appetite: saddle of rabbit, red cabbage compote; cod loin, parsnip purée and mixed vegetables; vanilla sablé, blueberry cream and sorbet, pistachio cream. This pleasant rustic-style mountain bistro is perched on the top floor of a building in the resort.

Name: Le 21
Address: 21 rue de la Plage-de-la-Birochère, Pornic, 44210, France
Description: Although a little out of the way, this restaurant enjoys an enviable location overlooking Plage de la Birochère, whose sandy cove surrounded by rocks is visible from the restaurant. Chef Sylvain Belouin and oenologist and sommelier Valérie Belouin are the brilliant couple behind this Pornic institution. The experienced chef (for a decade, Sylvain headed up the kitchens at Le Pigeon Blanc in Vern-d'Anjou, where his efforts were crowned with a Bib Gourmand) certainly knows his stuff. His simple way of treating guests to dishes centred on local ingredients, meat (pigeon, pig) and fish, eg his beautifully crispy sole meunière, is testament to this. The wine list features 500 wines (mainly biodynamic). Laid-back and friendly service.

Name: Bonnotte
Description: A 10min walk from the Albert Kahn Museum, Manon Negretti-Guichard and Antoine Guichard's restaurant has a simple, warm aesthetic. The pair of chefs have a solid track record to their names and pay homage to the Île de Noirmoutier and its famous bonnotte potato, a painting of which hangs on the wall. Manon runs the kitchen; Antoine also takes care of diners during service. The bistronomy cuisine gives pride of place to fresh produce and vegetable flavours: grilled courgette with feta and black olives; roast chicken leg (poulet jaune des Landes) with potato purée and a fragrant jus; apple crumble.

Name: Bassas
Description: The Bassas couple, whom we first encountered at Deymier (also in Pamiers), has renovated this old town centre building from top to toe. The striking result is both understated and smart and provides the perfect foil to the food which shines the spotlight on local producers. Inspired selection of local wines.

Name: Le Saint Jean
Description: By a winding road through the Bauges mountains, this establishment is the epitome of a country village inn whose recently refurbished wood-rich chic interior pays tribute to the surrounding countryside. Romain Bonnier works with local produce and a veggie-centric ethos, without forgetting meat and fish from the lake. His delicate mousse of catfish with spinach and his fragrant tartlet of crunchy white asparagus are packed with flavour, while his Chartreuse lamb cooked several ways is in a class of its own. Sweeping views over the Chambéry valley and surprise menus that invite the diner to “let go”…

Name: La Table - Sébastien Gravé
Cuisine: Farm to table, Cuisine from South West France
Description: After the success of Pottoka in Paris, the chef, a key figure on the Bayonne bistronomy scene, is back on his home turf. All smiles behind the stove, he prepares dishes inspired by the best produce South-West France has to offer, including natural hake from Saint-Jean-de-Luz, marinated and charred mackerel and Ibaïma pork shoulder. You can eat at the zinc-topped counter, at the large table d'hôtes with friends or in the kitchen (there is a table for two, for a more immersive experience). An inviting restaurant with a convivial atmosphere!

Name: Nolinski Le Restaurant
Description: On Avenue de l'Opéra, near the Comédie Française, a chic brasserie whose vintage interior mixes Art Deco and the 1970s, with mirrors, gilding, yellow marble and corduroy upholstering. The culinary is big-boned and Gallic down to its core (pot au feu, poultry and sweetbread vol au vent, veal cutlet with morels).

Name: POPS
Description: Pops is the nest of two fledglings who have flown the snug Mare aux Oiseaux, a recognised talent hatcher helmed by Éric Guérin. In their eatery just off the seafront, Corentin Leverger and Océane Maisonneuve bend over backwards to regale diners with fresh premium, often organic produce such as girolles mushrooms or red mullet. Their creative bistronomic score rolls out a festival of textures and forthright flavours illustrated by a scrumptious tartlet of mushrooms, prepared in several ways (raw, cooked, in jelly, creamed and pickled).

Name: Ombelle
Address: 7 boulevard du Président Wilson, Dinard, 35800, France
Description: After stints in a number of top establishments, chef Alexandre Frin and his partner Ludivine La Rosa, who manages the restaurant floor, have set up shop in this attractive early-20C red-brick house with picture windows with small panes and white frames. The chef composes a modern, open-minded and 100% seasonal menu that keeps things simple: just good ingredients (preferably with short supply chains) and herbs and aromatic flowers from their grandfather's vegetable garden. Pearlescent scallops; the subtle scent of cinnamon blossom in an ice cream paired with sweet potato and clementine: a delicious culinary journey.

Name: a.lea
Description: a.lea is the quintessence of appetising bistronomic cuisine: creamy soft-boiled egg, cream of green peas, apricots, feta and verbena; duckling breast, sweet potatoes, blood orange, mild curry seasoning and gravy… Chef Léa’s spot-on recipes demonstrate a market-fresh slant with a bargain-priced lunchtime (including Saturdays) menu. More elaborate and polished in the evenings. The front-of-house experience is in the capable hands of William Atlan, also a chef.

Name: Les Jardins du Léman
Description: In the heart of the pedestrianised medieval city, this appealing restaurant is laid out over several levels and furnished in a contemporary style. It proposes modern, impeccably crafted and generous dishes, all washed down with the best Savoie wines. Attentive welcome and service. Be sure to book if you wish to enjoy the splendid panoramic terrace overlooking the château and Lake Geneva.

Name: Ilô
Description: This tastefully decorated bolthole, which is hidden behind a noren (a vertical fabric divider hung across the doorways of shops in Japan), provides the backdrop to a well-designed omakase menu. High-flying food-wine/saké pairings.

Name: L'Alentour
Description: This quintessentially cosmopolitan, downtown eatery of Beaune is the joint brainchild of Tatenda Mhende, in charge of the dining room, who hails from Zimbabwe, chef Natasha Watson, who is from Calgary (Canada) and Marc Marchetti, also a chef, who is a Beaujolais lad. This alchemy of buddies has sparked a particularly appetising culinary offering that is depicted by a concise menu of hearty dishes packed with punchy flavours, to be shared (or not!): barbecued oxheart tomatoes, smoked tomato water and mozzarella; crunchy fritters of mushrooms with marrow, chardonnay-flavoured vinegar gel; pork belly, patty pan squash and courgettes.

Name: Auberge de Monceaux
Description: This inviting country restaurant strikes a tasteful balance between authentic rural charm (terracotta tiles and beams) and pared-back modern comforts. Two sisters oversee the front-of-house operations, while their partners pour their culinary enthusiasm into this cheerful family venture. Crispy tomato, smoked trout, harissa mayonnaise and gelée; matured beef cooked two ways, dauphine potatoes and caponata of Swiss chard; sorrel, poached fruit, jam and meringues: polished, colourful dishes, in which freedom and tradition go hand in hand. The menu changes regularly.

Name: Bulle
Description: Chef Guy Lassausaie masterminded the stylish top to toe refurbishment of this restaurant in a former Jesuit seminary (1853). You enter through a bar which boasts a jaw-dropping panoramic terrace, before heading downstairs into the restaurant, passing by the building’s Gallo-Roman foundations on the way! A swish, historic interior (crystal lighting, parquet floors and a view of the kitchen) sets the scene for colourful seasonal food, such as brook trout, fennel and seasonal mushrooms…

Name: Brut maison de cuisine
Description: This tasty bistro with a contemporary feel has an open kitchen, shelves filled with jars of fermented vegetables and books… and just a handful of tables, so it's best to book. The chef, who has a solid track record, devises a short menu that changes regularly. The three pillars of his cooking are seasonality, local ingredients (such as Racan poultry) and modern, often bold cuisine, for example his dessert that combines a naturally sweet Jerusalem artichoke cream and a coffee ice cream with a pronounced flavour. Short list of natural and organic wines.

Name: Le Quincy
Description: A cosy ambience prevails in this utterly timeless establishment, which was dominated by its larger-than-life boss, “Bobosse”, for so many years. Even though he doesn’t pop in quite so often anymore, his personality continues to underscore the DNA of this haunt of foodies. For fifty odd years, fine food lovers have been digging into wholehearted, rustic dishes from Berry or Ardèche. The chef scrimps neither on quality nor quantity when it comes to the house terrine of cabbage and garlic, poultry in cream or the rum-flavoured ice cream! An establishment whose existence is almost anachronistic in today’s restaurant universe.

Name: Passerini
Description: In his convivial restaurant, Giovanni Passerini treats us to tasty, carefully prepared Italian dishes, such as his trippa alla romana, which could hardly be bettered. Here, it's all about the produce and authenticity: sharing plates are a house speciality, as is Black-Headed Manech suckling lamb or whole pigeon in two courses. This place is very popular, so be sure to book!

Name: Le Cornichon
Description: Armed with an iron-clad CV (Atelier Guy Martin, Lucas Carton, Grand Véfour), Sébastien Dagoneau has been weaving his magic since he took over Le Cornichon in January 2020. Born in the Perche, the chef works directly with producers and suppliers from his homeland, in particular pork and poultry breeders. Examples include guineafowl cooked in morel mushrooms or melt-in-the-mouth pork and potato gnocchi, followed by a crunchy yet fluffy chou filled with Bourbon vanilla cream. Fine selection of organic and natural wines.

Name: Le 703
Description: Navigating between France and Japan, chef Naomi Ogaki trained in Alsace and Provence, under the tutelage of Antoine Westermann and Christian Étienne respectively. In his lovely bistro complete with a long counter, he serves high-quality traditional French cuisine that draws on influences of Alsace in autumn and winter, and of the South of France in spring and summer. House classics include pâté en croûte, game, spaetzle, home-made boudin, fish aioli – not to mention some first-rate classic desserts.

Name: Le Noyo
Description: A few minutes’ walk from the covered market, this dinky eatery, refurbished in a tasteful modern vibe, is the brainchild of François Liebaert, a well-known local chef. His enticing seasonal menu is occasionally jazzed up with creative notes, such as line-caught hake served with a gutsy Spanish sauce, flanked by spot-on balanced seasonings and artistic plating. Estelle efficiently and cheerfully manages the front of house.

Name: Auberge d’Aillon et d’Ailleurs
Address: 795 route de la Correrie, Aillon-le-Jeune, 73340, France
Description: In the Bauges Mountains, an unspoilt natural haven, this contemporary hotel has a lovely restaurant run by a young chef who has both technique and ideas. He throws himself into his work to get the best out of the Val d'Aillon terroir: vegetable garden, cooperative cheese, farm lamb, wild herbs... The menu changes regularly.

Name: Miro
Address: Rue de la Nachtweid, Ostwald, 67540, France
Description: This restaurant stands in bucolic grounds on the banks of the River Ill. Familiar with South American, Japanese and French gastronomy, the chef regales diners with tasty and uninhibited cuisine inspired by his many travels, for example Thai-style sea bass ceviche and his superb Argentinian beef entrecote finished over burning embers. The lunch set menu is a steal.

Name: 52 Faubourg St-Denis
Description: Fans of neo-bistro aesthetics will love this place done out in bare concrete and exposed stone, where diners tuck into cuisine infused with Asian flavours, as well as time-honoured bistro classics such as pâté de campagne (rustic-style pâté) or leeks in vinaigrette. The food is nicely washed down with fine wines or craft beer, and you can round off your meal with coffee selected and roasted by the owner. Please note: no reservations.

Name: La Condesa
Description: Designed by Camille Flammarion, this pint-sized, sleek restaurant stands on a street corner in the 9th district of Paris. On entering, you will admire the kitchen where the chef, who learned the ropes in nine countries, enjoys explaining his philosophy. He rolls out a 3-, 5- or 7-course surprise menu – the latter of which provides the best insight into a globetrotting tasting journey that spans numerous world cuisines. The delightful on-the-ball staff is always close at hand and there is a half glass food-wine pairing option.

Name: Les Résistants
Description: These résistants believe that taste and traceability should be the backbone of all food. Indeed, the credo of owner, Florent Piard, is none other than "good food that respects natural cycles! " and he amply proves his case in this cheerful establishment. The concise menu changes daily in keeping with market availability and the prices are never outlandish. Natural wines bien sûr!

Name: La Régalade Saint-Honoré
Description: Bruno Doucet regales foodies in the Halles neighbourhood with dishes that sing an ode to fresh market and country produce. After titillating your tastebuds with the chef's delicious terrine, dig into pan-fried snails, mushrooms and chorizo, followed by braised chuck steak with a bourguignon garnish or the “famous” rice pudding with a dairy caramel. Fine wine list.

Name: Bistrot Augustin
Description: Taken over by Guy Martin in 2020, this bistro still lives by the same values: a cosy setting, a small terrace on rue Daguerre, and lovely market-fresh cooking that is all about the ingredients. Rabbit terrine and red onion compote; sautéed farm-reared quasi of veal, seasonal vegetables with country bacon. Table d'hôte to the rear and an appetising menu-carte.

Name: Regain
Description: In the trendy Le Camas neighbourhood, this friendly bistro is in the competent hands of experienced chef Sarah Chougnet-Strudel and sommelier Lucien Salomon, who deploys his flair and talent front of house. Whether seated at the traditional chestnut wood and zinc counter or in the leafy courtyard, which is open in fine weather, you'll love the flavoursome market-fresh cuisine, which highlights local produce, particularly vegetables and artisanal fish. Think rack of pork with kale, sorrel cream, lentils and limequat, or a delicious tartlet with maple syrup, coffee mousse and candied celery. To accompany your food, pick a bottle from the enticing selection of around 200 "living" wines. An energising harvest of flavours!

Name: Le Duc
Description: Despite being in the heart of the Left Bank, you would be forgiven for thinking you were in the cabin of a yacht packed with seafaring acolytes… The chef works with first-rate fish and seafood and is a consummate craftsman: tartare of langoustine with black lemon, sole meunière, lobster sautéed with orange, grilled John Dory… All aboard!

Name: L’Oyat
Description: Even in Paris, near the Place de la République, a Ch'ti chef from Dunkirk like Jérémy Sergeant continues to hark back to the beaches of his native region. There, marram grass – oyat – is a small plant capable of holding in place the sand of the dunes. He uses good market produce in his modern, light cooking, which smacks of sincerity. Excellent value for money at lunchtime; in the evening, the menu is subtly embellished with premium ingredients. Cosy, contemporary atmosphere.

Name: Kigawa
Description: Kigawa is named after Michihiro Kigawa, the chef at this refreshingly simple restaurant. Buoyed by his experience in a French restaurant in Osaka, he now finds himself in Paris, delighting guests with classic French dishes such as pâté en croûte and roast pigeon.

Name: Ciasa Mia
Description: In a side street near the Pantheon, this charming little restaurant with exposed stone walls and wooden furnishings has a rustic feel that calls to mind a chalet. At the helm is an Italian couple in their forties: he is in charge in the kitchen, she takes care of proceedings front of house, dressed in the traditional attire of the Dolomites. The food is presented in surprise set menus, in which an inventive spin is put on local ingredients and bitter flavours are subtly explored – a hallmark of refined Italian cuisine. A good selection of wines completes the experience.

Name: Neva Cuisine
Description: The Neva is not only a river in Russia, but also the name of this restaurant, headed by Mexican chef Beatriz González, after completing stints in top establishments including Lucas Carton and La Grande Cascade. In a friendly, modern Parisian bistro setting, she conjures up modern, multi-facetted cuisine, illustrated by blow torch-seared foie gras, smoked eel and dashi stock, or skate meunière with spring vegetables and a gutsy aïoli. Everything tastes of something here.

Name: La Grande Ourse
Description: This bistro named after the Ursa Major constellation has a down-to-earth decor done out in a palette of grey, plum and orange. The mouth-watering menu, concocted by a professional and focused chef, gives pride of place to fish, but doesn't exclude other fare; the cooking is technically sound, the flavours distinct, and the ingredients of high quality.

Name: Les Délices d'Aphrodite
Description: In this charming tavern-style restaurant, you could be forgiven for thinking you are in Greece! Freshly made, sun-drenched dishes such as marinated peppers, spit-roasted leg of lamb on a skewer, etc., all prepared with top-notch ingredients.

Name: Le Tertre
Description: In a small cobbled street in the village, this restaurant has been given a new lease of life by an accomplished professional couple, who took over in 2020. Building on classical foundations, the creative dishes are inspired and harmonious. They showcase produce from the region: Landes duck, Basque country trout, fish from the ports of Aquitaine. In an extension to the dining room, the wine cellar hewn out of the monolithic stone has a table for four that is in great demand in the evening.

Name: Terrae
Address: 7 avenue de la Mairie, Cambo-les-Bains, 64250, France
Description: A former fishmongers has been savvily repurposed into a charming pocket handkerchief restaurant. Lucile Voisin and Grégory Ménard (Choko-Ona and Grand Hôtel de Saint-Jean-de Luz) have left nothing to chance from the terracotta walls, linen-coloured banquettes and pale wooden tables to the exquisite tableware: silverware, hand-crafted Basque ceramics and cutlery. The menu is inspired by the availability of fresh local produce and the chef’s boundless creativity. Barbecued venison steak, shoulder as fritters and variations on the butternut; citrus fruits in a meringue nest with a yuzu-laced house-made lemonade: hard work, impeccable taste, colour and creativity.

Name: Drouant
Description: This iconic, yet resolutely sprightly restaurant provides the smart, elegant stage where the Goncourt and Renaudot Book Prizes have been awarded respectively since 1914 and 1926! After learning the ropes with legends such as Cyril Lignac and Yannick Alléno, gifted chef Romain Van Thienen rolls out a pedigree lineup of French classics, from vol-au-vent and sole meunière to last-minute steak tartare and the famous "madeleine de Proust". As you take a seat in the plush interior you can expect to taste beautifully crafted, flavoursome dishes whose ingredients are nothing if not fresh, served by a front-of-house team that is both on the ball and cheerful. The wine cellar boasts nearly 2000 references and a very respectable range of wines by the glass.

Name: Aux Lyonnais
Description: This bistro established in 1890 has a delightfully retro decor and serves delicious cuisine that explores Lyon's gastronomy in all its riches. The terrines, pike-perch quenelles with crayfish, and the chicken liver terrine vie with the specials chalked up on the slate, and the desserts are enough to awaken anyone's sweet tooth.

Name: Clover Grill
Description: Mouthwatering dry - aged meats – Baltic black beef, Bavarian beef, Blonde d'Aquitaine, Black Angus – take pride of place in the window, drawing in diners keen to try them for themselves. From the starters to the desserts, everything is cooked over coals or roasted on a spit, giving the dining experience its own particular flavour. A great success.

Name: Charbon Kunitoraya
Description: Outside, the attractive timber façade has a Japanese feel. Inside, you'll find an old zinc counter, Paris Métro-style tiling, mirrors, wood panelling, mouldings and two long solid wood tables. In this chic setting with a vintage feel, chef Nomoto – a pioneer of udon restaurants in France – serves up mainly multi-course tasting menus composed of traditional dishes, including poulet de Bresse yakitori, one of his specialities. Be sure to try one of the wagashi – traditional Japanese pastries that change with the seasons.

Name: Loulou
Description: The Arts Décoratifs Museum promises an enchanted interlude opposite the Louvre gardens. In the kitchen, Benoît Dargère reinvents Mediterranean classics by means of meticulously selected produce. On the terrace or in the elegant dining room, the service is as exquisite as the food (risotto of the day; piccata of milk-fed veal al limone and sage; grilled octopus and aioli). Cosy, refined and delicious.

Name: Thaï Spices
Description: Between Quai des Célestins and the village of Saint-Paul, this restaurant is run by Willy Lieu, who was once Jacques Chirac's personal chef! Now his own boss, he serves up a short menu of authentic Thai cuisine, including generous and flavoursome classics such as pad thai and tom yam. Prices remain reasonable; good service. It is a popular haunt for local residents on account of its friendly, unpretentious atmosphere.

Name: L'Atelier de Joël Robuchon - St-Germain
Description: Bathed in a studied semi-darkness, two bars face each other around a central kitchen where the dishes are prepared under the gaze of the guests, seated on high stools at the counter. This "chic canteen" is a Western version of Japanese teppanyaki and sushi bars, with a menu that can be “tailored” into small portions and plates that boast superlative ingredients. Caviar on a soft-boiled hen’s egg and smoked salmon in puff pastry and the house staples, king crab ravioli, suckling lamb chops, Joël Robuchon's famous mashed potatoes...

Name: La Roche Le Roy
Description: This pretty little manor house on the outskirts of town has recently been refurbished and modernised, all the way from the decoration to the kitchens, the domain of chef Maximilien Bridier. Taking an enthusiastic approach to high-quality ingredients, he presents elegant, precise dishes with no frills. Without fail, the menu features a vegetarian option. There is a fine selection of wines by the glass, and the service is attentive. Sit out on the terrace on warm days.

Name: Le Pavillon Bleu
Address: 315 rue de la Reine-Blanche, Olivet, 45160, France
Description: A "guinguette" atmosphere pervades this 1903 building on the bank of the Loiret, where you can sit on the terrace in the shade of old plane trees, right by the water's edge. Fun fact: the dining area is actually an old boathouse. A few comfortable guestrooms available for overnight stays.

Name: L'Auberge d'Allex
Description: Between Valence and Montélimar, this erstwhile village inn is continuing its vocation as an eatery thanks to a young couple who have turned it into a cosy and inviting bistro-style restaurant with a smattering of contemporary decorative touches. The food, too, is in a bistro vein – think simple, contemporary cuisine designed for the modern palate. The fillet of hake with citrus sauce, red cabbage and butternut takes no prisoners.

Name: Soces
Address: 32 rue de la Villette, Paris, 75019, France
Description: A gem of a Parisian brasserie, where Marius de Ponfilly, formerly chef at Clamato, has teamed up with Kevin Deulio. Previously at Bar Vendôme in The Ritz, the latter has taken to the restaurant floor like a duck to water. The pair have found a formula that is as irreverent as it is on point: choice cuts of meat and plates to be shared between friends (aka soces in Parisian slang), not forgetting their trademark fish and seafood… We recommend the Pyrenean trout and its indulgent basil sauce, or the delicious wedge clams from Le Guilvinec in a spicy parsley sauce.

Name: Marius et Janette
Description: This elegant yacht-style décor, replete with fishing rods, nets and copper portholes, caters to discerning food lovers. The chef highlights fish and seafood, with a menu that is renewed daily, according to the catch. Carpaccio of salmon and basil, grilled seabass to share or linguine with lobster (a house speciality): a festival of flavours!

Name: Auberge de Port Vallières
Description: This slate-roofed country inn built of white stone stands on the banks of the Loire. The restaurant serves traditional family-style cuisine made from premium ingredients: prawns, creamed sweet potato with rosemary; braised calf sweetbreads, full-bodied Banyuls jus, mushroom fricassee; apple tarte fine with a snow shower of vanilla ice cream. Small terrace to the rear.

Name: Le Bénétin
Address: 4 chemin des Rochers Sculptés, Saint-Malo, 35400, France
Description: For starters, a tender, flavoursome carpaccio of sea bream, invigorated by a citrus fruit sauce; then, precisely cooked pollack with a spicy curry sauce; and, finally, to round off your meal, pear and apple tart with crispy pastry and house-made vanilla ice cream. All aboard for a culinary cruise in the comfort of this delightful, bright and airy space that is reminiscent of a boathouse and commands a bird's-eye view of the steep coastline and its rocky reliefs.

Name: Bistro Gaby
Description: The restaurant’s name and wholesome French country cooking are a tribute to Gaby, who was the chef’s grandmother. Market- and garden-fresh ingredients take pride of place in this attractive homely interior, adorned in soft provençal colours.

Name: Café Brunet
Address: 18 place Gabriel-Fauré - à Annecy-le-Vieux, Annecy, 74940, France
Description: This café dating back to 1875 is a real haven. It has managed to keep intact its soul of an authentic and convivial bistro (terrace, boules). As time meanders by, enjoy a good hearty meal or tasty little dishes.

Name: La Cheneaudière - Le Chêne
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Garden or park,Great view,Interesting wine list,Wheelchair access
Description: After a visit to the hotel spa, why not treat yourself to a meal in the chic natural setting of Le Chêne? The refined menu features a concise range of tempting proposals: seasonal vegetable gazpacho with preserved vegetables on crispy bread and black garlic vinaigrette; prawns with fresh thyme, a vibrant bisque, house-made tagliatelle with Taggiasca olives; cheesecake with Alsace cream and fruit compote.

Name: Le Petit Lucas
Address: 9 place de la Madeleine, Paris, 75008, France
Description: The bistro counterpart of Lucas Carton is accommodated on the first floor of the fine dining restaurant, in a space with a more low-key vibe (but with a view of the Église de la Madeleine). Chef Hugo Bourny's cuisine follows in the footsteps of fine French tradition (sole meunière, pâté en croute, chocolate mousse etc), thanks in particular to the quality of the ingredients used. The business menu, albeit without options, is a notable bargain in this upscale neighbourhood.

Name: L'Unisens
Description: This modern building just outside the village of Vagnas harks back to traditional Provençal architecture. In its spacious interior, which is done out in a contemporary style and has an open kitchen, sample the cuisine of Tarik Mezri-Charmasson, who ticks all the boxes, remaining true to the seasons and letting the ingredients speak for themselves.

Name: Le Quai
Description: On the banks of the Saône, this quayside brasserie boasts a very pleasant terrace right beside the river. In charge of proceedings is chef Valéry Meulien. His dishes focus on the region's classics, including pâté croûte, ham terrine with parsley, calf's head, and sweetbreads with morel cream. The flavoursome red wine sauce sprinkled with chopped parsley that accompanies the œufs en meurette is proof that the chef has by no means lost his touch. Booking is highly recommended.

Name: L'Arborescence
Description: Between Annecy and Geneva, a chef, who trained with the greats (Lionel Giraud, Christian Constant, Laurent Petit), crafts a range of surprise menus using fresh and often local ingredients. Charming service courtesy of the chef’s spouse.

Name: Leptine
Description: The sound system is an integral part of this place with its long corridor bathed in red light, its open kitchen behind a counter and its tables lining the wall. The name ("leptin" in English) refers to the hormone that signals to your brain when you are satiated – no question of leaving here on an empty stomach! The chef deftly draws on the culinary traditions of France, Asia and beyond, treating diners to siu mai, an array of fermented foods and Japanese seasonings. It's brilliantly done, and the seasoned team is more than happy to tell you how. Two to three savoury dishes plus one sweet should do the trick. Natural wine list, an interesting selection of wines by the glass and savvy recommendations.

Name: Restaurant Côté Marais
Description: A starter of ceviche of white mullet (a fish rarely found on restaurant menus) with rhubarb for a hint of tartness, followed by a savoury/sweet main course of pollack fished by small boats, French peas al dente and a smattering of sweet cherry condiment. The young chef applies his own personal culinary style to local ingredients, while his partner works the restaurant floor in this outlying establishment surrounded by marshland (and with a lovely terrace).

Name: L'Œuf de Coq
Description: A fine arts student in a former life, chef Mathieu Lacaze takes great care over the presentation of his dishes. His artistic sensibility shines through in his resolutely modern market-fresh cuisine. In keeping with the seasons, his dishes are prepared using quality local ingredients selected from organic market gardeners and small-scale livestock farmers. The space is contemporary, with exposed tiles and stone walls; in fine weather, make a beeline for the small patio terrace. A surprise set menu is served in the evening, along with a fine selection of independent wines, mainly organic and natural.

Name: À la Maison
Description: This house rustles up wholesome bistro fare that shines the limelight on regional produce. The chef particularly likes devising dishes around a single ingredient, such as pork or lamb. House specialties include black pudding, a 64° egg and Guéméné andouille. Well worth discovering.

Name: Colibri
Address: 14 rue de la Mittrie, Dinan, 22100, France
Description: In the heart of medieval Dinan, this modern bistro sports wood furnishings, oak parquet flooring, a fireplace and a view of the kitchen from the dinky dining room. Vibrant, often surf ‘n turf recipes set the culinary scene: lobster, green peas and strawberries, mullet, black pudding and figs; raspberries, red pepper sorbet and chiffon cake…

Name: Auberge de la Haute-Joux
Description: A former philosopher (and the epitome of courtesy and discernment when it comes to her wine recommendations) plus a globetrotting chef who grew up eating at Michelin-starred restaurants have taken over this family-run inn: just the ticket in the middle of this rural village. This pair promises diners a delightful dining experience that combines rustic surroundings and cuisine that nonchalantly switches between regional and more contemporary dishes, and is littered with nods to the chef's many travels: here you see vin jaune and saffron from Franche-Comté, peanut vinaigrette, seaweed emulsion alongside Thai-style mussels from Bouchot.

Name: Les Mérovingiens
Description: On the ground floor of a residential building in the centre of Noisy-le-Grand, this brasserie pays homage to the history of the town, which was built on a Merovingian and Carolingian necropolis. The culinary focus is on intelligently revamped classics, served in an attractive trendy interior.

Name: L'Atelier
Description: Originally from Vendée, chef Stéphane Chenneveau must have been a little crazy – or "fada" in the Nice dialect, to dare to revisit the city’s ubiquitous socca, flatbread made with chickpea flour... And yet it remains a firm fixture of the menu. The chef has never ceased to evolve, crafting flavoursome regional recipes, together with a more ambitious carte blanche menu which is seasonal and reflects his mood of the moment. Splendid biodynamic wine list.

Name: Daniel et Denise Créqui
Description: Joseph Viola, Best Craftsman of France, reigns over this dyed-in-the-wool, patina-aged bolthole, oozing in authenticity. Patriotic line-up of Gallic recipes, high-flying technique (calf’s head, quenelle of pike) founded on superlative ingredients with an eye on the seasons. His signature dish is a “porkpie” of sweetbread and foie gras – to die for!

Name: Cinq Mains
Description: This warm, modish bistro, which occupies two floors, rolls out seasonal, spot-on cuisine, savvily tweaked with seasonings like fermented pickle sauce or blackcurrant pickled gel that add a kick to calf’s sweetbread fried in breadcrumbs. The knowledgeable staff can be relied on for insightful tips regarding the wine list that unveils a soft spot for natural wines.

Name: VIVE, Maison Mer
Description: Alsace-born restaurateur Adrien Rech opened this institution dedicated to seafood in 1925. After Ducasse, it is now the turn of David and Stéphanie Le Quellec, whose Breton name alone smacks of the ocean, to celebrate fish and shellfish cuisine. The decor is sumptuous, with its huge bar, dining area on the first floor and long banquette seating. David Le Quellec serves food that is good for sharing and made with excellent, ultra-fresh ingredients from fish markets spanning France, from the Atlantic to the Mediterranean. The ceviche of sea bream with coconut milk, lime and coriander is already a house classic – not to mention the dishes prepared from fish matured on site in the maturing cellar.

Name: Le Restaurant
Address: 9 bis avenue de la Gare, Saint-Priest, 69800, France
Description: Le Restaurant is 10 minutes from Lyon Saint-Priest Parc Technologique. Sit at your table surrounded by artwork by young artists and enjoy well-crafted traditional cuisine, with a few exotic twists. The menu is rooted in the terroir: lentils and runny poached egg flavoured with bacon, or artisan-made hot sausage poached in wine and cut into good generous slices!

Name: Le Sully
Description: A small bistro, opened by Julien Gautier (owner of neighbouring M Restaurant) in a modernised bouchon vein, tantalises diners with dishes such as chicken liver gâteau, veal liver en persillade (with parsley and garlic) and calf's head with sauce ravigote. It is tasty, well made and you will be going back for more!

Name: Oiseau - Oiseau
Description: Sven Chartier and his wife Marianne have built their new nest in this tiny Perche village, opposite a church several centuries old. Far from the madding crowd, the chef is flourishing in this country chic setting, pampering diners with wholesome fare that respects tradition: scallops, almond milk, cauliflower and citron; crispy chuck steak. Culinary precision meets comfort food…

Name: A Nepita
Description: English born chef Simon Andrews, a former Michelin star holder, fell head over heels with Corsica. He goes to the market every day to painstakingly select local ingredients, which he then meticulously crafts: red tuna, denti, seabass, brocciu, veal, etc. Some of his signature dishes are always on the menu, such as grilled squid or his medley of local fish, to the delight of regulars and tourists alike. The chef also enjoys scattering his dishes with wild marjoram (“nepita”, after which the restaurant is named). The cheerful front-of-house service is managed by Simon’s wife, Corsican born Roberta.

Name: Le Grenier à Sel
Address: 26 place de l'Éperon, Le Mans, 72000, France
Description: At the entrance to medieval Le Mans, the team of this former salt loft has one goal in life: to please themselves and their customers! A contemporary vibe and top-quality ingredients (lobster, turbot, foie gras) with bold, authentic flavours, all of which washed down with a fine selection of Rhône, Loire and Bordeaux tipples.

Name: Le Bistrot des Voraces
Description: Do you just have a healthy appetite or are you downright starving? Either way, this bistro in the Croix-Rousse district will sate you. Youthful Cédric Blin honed his skills in top establishments like Les Crayères (Reims), before going solo here. Genuinely eater-friendly, almost bargain prices – not to be missed!

Name: Le Canut et les Gones
Description: This authentic neighbourhood institution, decked in an understated façade, has been going strong for over 30 years in a relatively little-known part of Croix Rousse. A warm vibe with a retro feel sets the scene courtesy of a Formica bar, vintage wallpaper and a quirky collection of old clocks and other paraphernalia. Chef Junzo Matsuno deftly crafts polished traditional Gallic fare, to which he may add the odd low-key Japanese twist, together with a strong focus on veggies (which he grows himself). The lunch menu is a steal.

Name: Le Voilier
Description: Drop anchor in the marina and climb on board this elegant yacht to sample fresh Mediterranean cuisine (fish soup and carpaccio, ceviche, courgette blossoms) in which the local catch (whole or in portions) takes pride of place. Meat lovers are, however, not forgotten and the menu also offers dishes such as a thick juicy veal cutlet or stuffed saddle of lamb.

Name: Au Jardin d'Eden
Description: On the way into town, this eatery ticks all the boxes: an owner-chef with a fine CV – including 15 years at Le Grand Véfour, who has returned to his roots in Évian and generous, traditional cooking that keeps pace with the seasons. Fricassée of sweetbread and green peas; free-range chicken, lemon confit and roquette; tartare of Charolais beef; fillets of fresh perch…

Name: Le Comptoir de la Mère Germaine
Description: Wood dominates the contemporary interior, alongside an imposing counter-cum-kitchen and a gleaming spit-roast oven. The bistronomic lineup is strewn with South American accents. Pleasant shaded terrace

Name: La Flèche d'Argent
Address: Hôtel Princesse Flore, 5 place Allard, Royat, 63130, France
Description: La Flèche d'Argent – the name is a nod to the incredible "Silver Arrows" Mercedes-Benz Formula 1 cars of the 1930s – references the nearby Circuit de Charade racetrack. In a plush decor, chef Clément Lorente serves up his contemporary cuisine in a multi-course set menu format. His dishes display excellent technique and incorporate creative touches. The ingredients are of the highest quality: foie gras from the Plaine de Limagne, artichokes from Roussillon, saffron from Mazayes, bluefin tuna from the Mediterranean. For dessert, a tribute to the chef's grandmother's Agen prune flan is a real hit, flambéed tableside. Market-based set menu at lunchtime; brunch on Sundays.

Name: La Table du Marché
Description: Owner-chef Stéphane Cuzin has been at the helm of this street corner bistro with a distinctive red façade and a snazzy, modish interior for many years now. It faces Bergerac’s covered market, where Stéphane sources the majority of his ingredients. Creative recipes and unusual seasonings set the tone: tonka, nutmeg, cumin and coffee may underscore veal, spinach or asparagus.

Name: Auberge de Cassagne & Spa
Address: 450 allée de Cassagne, Le Pontet, 84130, France
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Garden or park,Interesting wine list,Terrace,Wheelchair access
Description: This old Provençal bastide on the outskirts of Avignon upholds the traditions of Gallic bourgeois establishments devoted to good food. Noble produce and classical recipes are the name of the game, albeit with the occasional more modern creation, such as tataki of house smoked salmon on a pannacotta of green vegetables. Southern Côte du Rhône wines take pride of place in the cellar. Lovely terrace in fine weather and polished service.

Name: Le Collet
Address: 9937 route de Colmar, Col de la Schlucht, 88400, France
Description: “Instinctive, last-minute” regional dishes, rustled up by a seasoned veteran who has trained many a local chef. In a picture postcard swish Alpine chalet décor, each dish celebrates and pays tribute to authentic regional produce.

Name: L'Atelier des Saveurs by Stéphane Garcia
Description: Fruit and veg from local producers, fish from local fishermen, meat from southwest France and a knockout lineup of Basque cheeses: the “flavour workshop” more than lives up to its name! Examples include fillet of Galician beef with a gravy laced in Espelette pepper and mashed seasonal veg… A 100% Basque menu is available to order, in tribute to the chef’s roots.

Name: Le 5ème Péché
Address: 16 rue de la Fraternité, Collioure, 66190, France
Description: This small restaurant in Collioure's old town is run by a chef from Tokyo, who is passionate about French food and wine. Here, Japan meets Catalonia in fusion cuisine that stars ultra-fresh fish. A prime example is the rockfish soup with coconut milk, braised ox cheek with banyuls and prawns. Remember to book well in advance.

Name: L'Écureuil
Description: This modern bistro with its chic country decor serves appetising market-fresh cuisine: duck breast with black olives, pork cheeks braised in red wine, French toast made with brioche... The short menu is chalked up on the blackboard, and a simpler lunch deal is available at a snip.

Name: Le San Felice
Address: 3001 route des Hauts-du-Camp, au Circuit Paul Ricard, Le Castellet, 83330, France
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Garden or park,Great view,Terrace,Valet parking,Wheelchair access
Description: San Felice is not only a Dumas novel: at the Hôtel du Castellet, it is also a swish, imaginative bistro! The menu is deliberately concise, with a seasonal line-up and a mouth-watering focus on matured meats and fish flame-cooked over hot coals. The terrace by the swimming pool commands a knockout view of the golf course and greenery. Treat yourself to the lunchtime "Menu Gourmand" set menu (daily). And on Sundays, it's all about the barbecue!

Name: La Table by La Villa
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Great view,Interesting wine list,Terrace,Wheelchair access
Description: La Table is part of La Villa, whose luxurious decor fades in front of the jaw-dropping view of the bay, citadel and mountains. The focus is on premium regional produce which is married with Italian-inspired recipes: Milanese veal cutlet, carpaccio of marinated Corsican veal “al Limone”, a new take on parmigiana, etc. Everything is served alfresco on the incredible panoramic terrace. Simpler (but equally delicious) lunch menu.

Name: Le Lancelot
Description: In the centre of the village, this welcoming flower-decked place with a garden and terrace is a real oasis of calm. Cosy setting and cuisine that navigates between tradition and modernity (notably the melt-in-the-mouth pithivier pie, rum crème brûlée, pistachio ice cream), not forgetting Sologne game in season.

Name: Le Florida
Description: While regional delicacies remain firm fixtures on the menu of this welcoming traditional establishment (in business since the 1930s), a few discreet nods to the Mexican roots of the new owner have found their way into the culinary score. Examples include crispy crackling chicharron appetisers or a smoked, spicy tomato sauce that adds a kick to a starter of thinly sliced carpaccio of stuffed duck neck, apples and mayonnaise made from Gascony mustard. Healthful, fresh, throbbing with flavour and top-drawer quality. On sunny days, the shaded alfresco patio is blissful.

Name: Kitchen Ter(re)
Description: In his third establishment devoted to pasta, William Ledeuil crafts a kaleidoscope of pared-back tastes and flavours, starring high-flying creations from spelt, durum wheat, einkorn or tender Roussillon wheat by artisan Roland Feuillas. Chef Julien Jéquier (with stints at Le V and L’Écrin) orchestrates a balanced score in which Asian notes and fresh herbs play major supporting roles. From the exquisitely laid tables to the plating, balance is the key word, as is illustrated by his dish of coquillettes (small pasta shells) made out of fresh milled khorasan wheat flour with chicken wings, Taggiasche olives, spinach and Thai broth! Vibrant, lively and the epitome of charming!

Name: Villa Morelia
Description: Villa Morelia exudes a certain discreet charm. The setting offsets the refined, tasty and inventive market - based cuisine. You can really taste the freshness and savour the flavours.

Name: La Deuvalière
Address: 18 rue de la Monnaie, Tours, 37000, France
Description: Julien and Alexandra have poured every ounce of their enthusiasm into successfully wooing local and visiting gourmets. Their seasonal cuisine is a treasure trove of culinary gems. The charm of their old country house, appointed with bare beams, terracotta tiled floors and a fireplace, together with the odd contemporary detail, further adds to the experience!

Name: L'Hostellerie d'Acquigny
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Interesting wine list,Terrace,Wheelchair access
Description: This small village inn with a buzzy modern streak has been run by the same couple for over 25 years. As enthusiastic as ever, chef Éric Georget rustles up generous, modern cuisine that makes the mouth water, presented in a set and à la carte menus. Painstakingly selected produce goes into dishes that are packed with flavour: gravlax of Scottish salmon and medley of beetroot; Black Angus flank steak and a voatsiperifery pepper sauce. Pleasant terrace and guestrooms for overnight stays.

Name: Le Clos du Château
Description: Adjacent to the Château de Proméry, this imposing contemporary building has been run for 17 years by Pascal Avertis, who hails from the village. The chef is equally at ease with traditional recipes (braised chuck with an excellent Mondeuse sauce, potato croquettes to dip in a delicious home-made ketchup) as he is with more modern and creative creations, such as leek and nori maki with Thai vinaigrette and smoked caviar – absolutely delicious! To be savoured on the pleasant terrace, in the shade of the plane trees.

Name: Elmer
Description: Close to République, this terribly chic bistro is officiated by a chef with an impressive career (including L'Oustau de Baumanière, Pierre Gagnaire, travels in Asia and Latin America). He composes a flavoursome menu that packs a punch, with fine meats cooked on embers or on the rotisserie.

Name: Les Années 30
Description: This restaurant may be named after the 1930s but that's where the connection to that period ends. The decor is chic and trendy, with walls in hues of terracotta and verdigris and retro dining chairs. Diners will love the appetising cuisine based on fresh ingredients. Tables on the terrace in fine weather.

Name: Le Stofflet - Château Colbert
Description: This magnificent 17C tuffeau and granite château is already worth a visit for its rich chequered history and its 800m² cottage garden, voted the most beautiful cottage garden of France in 2016 and 2021. Guests are welcomed beneath a 13m-high dome, before progressing into one of two dining rooms, both of which sport high ceilings and crystal chandeliers. This glamorous interior is fully equal to the fine dining experience of contemporary cuisine: wafer-thin tartlet of aubergine caviar, prawns and radishes; guinea fowl, herb butter, mashed potato and autumn veggies; roast figs in port wine, almond cake, honey and vanilla ice cream.

Name: Le Senso
Description: On the market square, this spruce, well-kept restaurant provides the perfect foil for simple, unfussy cuisine in which local, seasonal produce takes pride of place in chef Allan Castellote’s artistic plating. His brother Tristan supervises the wine cellar, wine bar and next-door wine shop. The house speciality, kouign amann, is to die for!

Name: La Bastide
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Garden or park,Terrace,Wheelchair access
Description: In the small spa village of Cazaubon, this swanky 5-star Relais & Chateaux hotel, owned by the Guérard family, has been refurbished in a tasteful chic country house vein. The chef crafts a score founded on the classical, dietary recipes invented by the late Michel Guérard: the food is light, healthy, modern and overwhelmingly mouthwatering and each dish is generously laden in first-class, locally sourced seasonal produce, all of which is consummately crafted. Spot-on service and a swish, tasteful setting.

Name: Fouquet's
Address: Le Royal La Baule, 6 avenue Pierre-Loti, La Baule, 44500, France
Description: A restaurant in the Royal Hotel, typical of the large seaside hotels of the early 20C. The cosy wood panelling and the photos of actors by Studio Harcourt recall the atmosphere of the Parisian Fouquet's. The menu is inspired by brasserie fare (seafood, sole meunière, fillet of beef with Béarnaise sauce, andouillette, profiteroles), but there are also light dishes – as you would expect at a seawater therapy resort.

Name: La Superb
Description: Located in the heart of the old town, this contemporary "dining bar" serves market-fresh dishes that are in tune with the seasons. Take a seat at the counter for views of the chef cooking fine mature meats or his tuna Rossini a la plancha, or alternatively in the small dining room with stone walls and glassed-in wine cellar, and prepare to enjoy tasty, no-frills cuisine. Bargain-price set menu at lunchtime!

Name: Marnage - Hôtel La Marine
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Credit cards not accepted,Great view,Wheelchair access
Description: With its panoramic view of the sea and the port, this local institution on the Cotentin peninsula faces the Channel Islands of Jersey and Guernsey. In a pleasant contemporary interior, you will sample modern, elegant cuisine that shines the limelight on Normandy produce, with a weakness for local seafood, illustrated by pollock, fennel (confit and roasted) and a lemon-flavoured butter emulsion.

Name: Thiou
Address: Hôtel Norman, 9 rue Balzac, Paris, 75008, France
Description: Chef Apiradee Thirakomen, who goes by "Thiou", has set up shop on the Right Bank, in a small hotel just off the Champs Élysées. In a chic, intimate atmosphere, you can sample the Thai specialities that have made her reputation. Some have a French twist: prawn ravioli with coconut cream flavoured with lemongrass, pad thai, "Crying Tiger".

Name: Les Petits Parisiens
Description: A buzzy, friendly vibe and bistro fare in the zeitgeist at prices that won’t break the bank. This eatery specialises in adding a virtuoso new spin to timeless family favourites of the likes of veal blanquette or stuffed cabbage, to name but a few. Those with a sweet tooth will adore the vanilla-laced rice pudding and the dark chocolate tart. A happy marriage of delicate craftsmanship and finger-licking flavour.

Name: Relais de l'Abbaye
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Garden or park,Terrace,Wheelchair access
Description: This modern Relais, looking out onto the surrounding meadows, is anchored in local culinary traditions. The chef is passionate about fine ingredients and showcases regional producers (Charlieu andouille, Charolais meat, cheese etc) in contemporary, hearty dishes. Pleasant guestrooms for an overnight stay.

Name: Bistrot du Bac
Address: 19 rue du Bac, à Sainte-Marine, Combrit, 29120, France
Description: This quaint Breton eatery, located on the quayside of Sainte-Marine's little port opposite Bénodet Island, celebrates the sea. The terrace affords picturesque views over the River Odet, the dining area is painted blue and white, as are the guestrooms, and the maritime theme is pursued in the no-frills seafood score.

Name: Claire et Hugo
Address: 77 avenue du Général-Galliéni, à Sainte-Savine, Troyes, 10300, France
Description: An enthusiastic self-taught young couple runs this restaurant with a subdued decor composed of raw materials. The premises also house a bakery and delicatessen leading onto a lovely terrace and indoor garden (including a citrus tree greenhouse). The ingredients, which are 95% organic, make for healthy, tasty and balanced dishes.

Name: La Vieille Fontaine
Address: Hôtel d'Europe, 12 place Crillon, Avignon, 84000, France
Description: Wood panelling, mouldings and a fireplace set the elegant Provençal scene of this venerable establishment. Pascal Auger is in his element, crafting Mediterranean fare steeped in the aromas and flavours of the south. On sunny days (you’re in Avignon!) you can enjoy these delicacies beneath the ancient plane tree on the terrace facing a fountain.

Name: Ermitage de Corton
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Garden or park,Interesting wine list,Terrace
Description: In this house set in vineyards opposite Corton “mountain”, the chef aims to shine the spotlight on local producers. His modern meticulous cuisine draws upon his classical training and features a traditional Gallic line-up, including snails and œufs en meurette (poached eggs in red wine) crafted with text-book precision. Stylish interior, inviting patio and spacious guestrooms to prolong your stay.

Name: Ko-sometsuke 2K
Address: 156 boulevard de la Plage, Arcachon, 33120, France
Description: Originally from Cambodia, the Khong family settled in Arcachon, and now they are the ones inviting diners on a journey: from China and Japan to Southeast Asia, using regional ingredients. Don't miss the dim sum, the real stars of the show, wrapped in a remarkably fine dough.

Name: Le Bouillon
Address: 9 rue de la Gare, Annecy, 74000, France
Description: In addition to meaning stock, a bouillon also refers to the first restaurants opened in Paris in the 18C. In a recently refurbished modern interior, the chef crafts tasty market-fresh recipes, with the odd Asian twist, such as a splendid loin of croaker in a chorizo crust underscored by a red curry and curcuma stock.

Name: La Bourse et la Vie
Description: This bistro owned by an American chef is a big hit. So what is the secret of his success? Distinctly French dishes, slightly tweaked, quality ingredients and flavours that are on point. Leeks with vinaigrette; onglet de bœuf (a skirt steak) with peppercorn sauce; chocolate mousse: all manner of bistro classics that you'll be delighted to come across (again).

Name: Semilla
Description: In a street teeming with restaurants and art galleries, Semilla ("seed" in Spanish) is a bistro with an exceptionally friendly atmosphere and trendy, industrial-style decor. In the kitchen, which opens directly onto the restaurant floor, a young and enthusiastic team work exclusively with fresh, selected produce: sea bream ceviche, leche de tigre, quince confit with hibiscus and kohlrabi; roasted cod, Granville cockles, Roscoff onion, Poiré sauce. Delicious and brilliantly done!

Name: Kodawari Ramen - Yokochō
Description: In a decor dripping in nods to urban Tokyo (lanterns, fake street fronts and a soundtrack of street noises), the visitor is transported to Japan. Liquid (shio) or thick (shoyu) broths, made from free-range poultry and artisanal Shibanuma soy sauce, simmer on the stove. The ramen, made with wheat that is grown and ground on site, unveils incredible depth of texture and taste. The house speciality is kurugoma ramen made with black sesame seed and pata negra pork. Bright, bubbly and bustling, this venue is steeped in an authentic Japanese ramen-ya vibe. Avoid peak times, when it can be packed to the seams.

Name: Huître Brûlée
Description: Don’t worry, the oysters aren’t burnt - despite the name! Updated recipes, quality ingredients, locally sourced whenever possible (organic veg, fish from small boats) and a concise, seasonal menu. This friendly bolthole is run by an enthusiastic couple: local lad Paul Lacheray, in the kitchen, and his partner, Chloé Woestelandt, who runs the dining room.

Name: La Table d'Edgar
Description: Chef Sébastien David signs an enticing score using top-notch, mainly local Brittany ingredients. Expertly balanced flavours, consummate cooking and a sprinkling of bold combinations define the score: pollock paired with papaya-samphire-marjoram seasoning or a fennel-themed dessert flanked by a white chocolate ganache and bergamot seasoning. This painstaking attention to detail is also mirrored in the bright, relaxed interior whose pleasant lounge-dining area is set in a conservatory, adding both warmth and light to this town centre establishment.

Name: Tandem Saveurs Nomades
Description: The title says it all – a duo of chefs who trained under Thierry Marx and innovative fusion cuisine in which South American and Asian influences rub shoulders with pedigree French ingredients. The aubergines are underscored by miso sauce; pollock is flanked by creamy green peas, risotto of quinoa and Thai herbs sprinkled with grilled buckwheat for a roasted flavour; beef dumpling and a teriyaki sauce: everything is intelligently and patiently combined and assembled by our gourmet duo. This warm, colourful bistro, fully in tune with its era, is good news for the town centre of Saint-Maurice!

Name: Rhapsody
Description: This spruce eatery in the Parisian suburbs works with first-class produce to rustle up appetising, well-curated bistronomic recipes. Examples include puréed chicory in flaky pastry and seasoned with cancoillotte (sort of cream cheese) and pomegranate; fillet of hake with squash spaghetti, seawater and bergamot stock and for dessert, a wickedly decadent creamy chestnut and Corsican clementine delight. Ask for a table on the lovely rear patio with a view of the kitchen.

Name: Tabi - Ippei Uemura
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Counter dining,Notable sake list,Wheelchair access
Description: Tabi, which means journey in Japanese, says it all! Born in Kyoto, the chef has adopted the city of Marseilles as his own. He incorporates locally caught fish into traditional Japanese recipes, prepared in front of customers. Food-saké pairings for aficionados. One of a kind!

Name: Parapluie
Description: This lilliputian restaurant serves globetrotting food in the zeitgeist, with a sprinkling of spices and based on seasonal, mostly local, ingredients. The culinary offer is rolled out in a single set "mystery" menu comprised of several courses at dinner, and a reasonably priced lunchtime menu with options. Fine selection of wine, beer and spirits (whiskies, eaux de vie etc).

Name: PY Restaurant
Description: In this dinky brasserie in a smart neighbourhood, Pierre (in the kitchen) and Yuko (front of house) make the magic happen. In this contemporary decor, diners sample generous, well-crafted dishes. The à la carte menu in the evening is enriched with premium dishes such as hare pâté en croûte.

Name: La Mangeoire
Address: 2 rue du Castrum (Le Bourg), Floirac, 46600, France
Description: In this picturesque Lot village, the traveller cannot fail but notice the handsome limestone edifice with a slate roof, flanked by a terrace and Belle Époque conservatory. The globe-trotting chef demonstrates a weakness for exotic combinations: velvety, humus-like aubergines, burnt rye bread, fried Camus artichoke and pork fillet dried in the hearthplace; lightly seared secreto pata negro pork with peanuts and ginger, roast fennel and whole wheat noodles. Bistronomic in style, internationally sourced and strewn with tributes to Asia and North African spices.

Name: Penati al Baretto
Address: 94 boulevard de la Tour-Maubourg, Paris, 75007, France
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Interesting wine list,Valet parking,Wheelchair access
Description: It is no secret that Italians have great taste. Milanese chef Alberico Penati has set up shop in this chic bistro with honey-coloured wood panelling, and bay windows overlooking the garden of the Invalides – a highly prized location indeed! Tradition is the chef's passion. With no concessions to passing fashions, his menu features a selection of Italian classics made out of carefully selected ingredients. Home-made pasta remains the forte of this place, eg ravioli del plin piemontesi with a very good roast beef jus. The 100% Italian wine list highlights Piedmontese wines, particularly Barolo and Barbaresco.

Name: L'Attanum
Address: 64 place de la Nation, Saint-Yrieix-la-Perche, 87500, France
Description: The ground floor of this 19C sous-préfecture is now home to a fashionably appointed restaurant that welcomes with a cheerful vibe. At the helm, Ludwik Crosnier, with stints in some prestigious establishments under his belt, signs a seasonal score depicted by local ingredients, stellar technique and delicately balanced flavours. Claire cheerfully and attentively supervises the front-of-house, adding a gracious flourish to this fine dining experience.

Name: L'Inattendu
Address: 18 avenue de la Plage, Saint-Gilles-Croix-de-Vie, 85800, France
Description: Tucked away amidst villas and holiday homes, L'Inattendu is as unexpected as its name suggests. One pleasant surprise follows the next from the appetisers to the dessert, as diners sample deftly crafted, creative cuisine. Chef Paul Bonneau has a knack for enhancing locally sourced ingredients: veg from market gardeners, hibiscus, saffron and lemon jellies, ice creams and mousses. Dishes you may taste range from sardines, blueberries and potatoes; pearlescent cod, cucumber and sunflower; squab breast, tomato and strawberries. You can bank on a warm welcome and wholehearted enthusiasm from the front-of-house team. A culinary hotspot that is a hit with locals and tourists alike.

Name: Le Lien
Description: The bond here (‘lien’ in French) is that which ties this young couple (he’s in the kitchen, she in the front of house) to the winegrowers and producers whose work is showcased in the plates and glasses of this friendly bistro. Modern food with a creative twist founded on first-class seasonal ingredients that are allowed to shout their name. Two lunchtime menus and a more elaborate offering in the evening. Highly recommended.

Name: Sao
Description: On the quayside of the River Odet in Quimper city centre, Sao is the brainchild of talented young chef Kevin Gourret, formerly of the restaurant Le Goyen in Audierne. In an inviting contemporary setting, he serves up his original recipes inspired by regional ingredients (langoustine, local fish, seaweed, buckwheat, buttermilk) and Asian influences (such as ponzu, gomasio, sesame and ginger). The more ambitious evening menu reveals the full extent of his technical prowess, particularly his robust sauces and jus. The desserts are on a par – for example, a creation bringing together vanilla, chestnut and yuzu.

Name: Âma Terra
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Garden or park,Terrace,Valet parking,Wheelchair access
Description: Diners are faced with a dilemma in the restaurant of this magnificent hotel. You can opt to dine in the inside space, with its Second Empire glass roof, crystal chandeliers and imposing china cabinet, or on the gorgeous terrace, with the gentle sound of water tinkling in the pools and fountains and the scent of typical Mediterranean fragrances hanging in the air. The Chef cooks up gourmet cuisine with Provençal overtones and a backdrop of original and striking associations.

Name: La Table de l'Europe
Description: Opposite the country town’s listed covered market, this tastefully appointed guesthouse and restaurant with a terrace to the rear invite you to sit down, relax and take your time.
