Description: The clean-lined interior was created by a tea-house craftsman. The ground floor has private rooms in a modern Japanese style; the upper floor features counter seating with the chef holding court. Tempura is fried in cottonseed oil for a light texture. The prix fixe menu alternates between seafood and vegetables, ensuring constant variation. In a creative touch, tilefish is wrapped in perilla leaf. The restaurant is managed by a ryokan; in hope that guests will return to dine here even after their stay is over, tendon is offered at lunchtime.

Name: Kurubushi
Description: The chef of an izakaya opened this kappo as a sister establishment. He favours items with a salty taste, the better to keep the sake flowing. Vintage Japanese serving vessels and antique Western glasses delight the eye. The meal wraps up with seasonal takikomi-gohan or curry rice—with free refills, a welcome bonus. Omakase cooking bursting with creativity—enjoy it to your heart’s content.

Name: Kamado
Description: A wood fire blazes in a kamado, or traditional wood-fired stove. Echoing the shop’s name, the meal begins with a bowl of freshly cooked rice straight from the kamado. The style is fusion of Italian and Japanese cuisine, with wood-fired cooking the unifying concept. The hearth is a primaeval scene of meat roasting over glowing embers, yet the flavours are distinctly contemporary. A dish of pasta wraps up the evening. Continuing the theme, the pottery on which the fare is displayed was also fired in a wood-fuelled kiln.

Name: ku:de kiyo
Description: ‘Kuude’ is ‘let’s eat’ in Osaka dialect, the chef’s nickname is Kiyo, and the whole name has a French sound to it. A colour scheme of bright blue and green declares the shop’s freedom from convention. The theme is ‘unforgettable cuisine’: each dish features no more than three items, arrangements are minimal, and portions are generous. At lunchtime, set meals of Western items paired with rice and miso soup make ku:de kiyo a local favourite.

Name: Shunzen Kiraku
Description: This Japanese restaurant is in the style of a Naniwa (Osaka) kappo. The procession starts with a combination platter of seafood, vegetables and sushi. The menu ranges from grilled and simmered items that hew close to the basics to offerings with a creative spin such as bisques and frites. The chef’s greatest joy is concocting dishes that connect on an emotional level: indicate a preference and he is happy to prepare your dish the way you like it. He keeps in his heart the teaching of his mentor: the true measure of a chef is the ability to tailor each dish to the taste of the diner.

Name: genso
Description: The venue, a remodelled ironworks, exudes an industrial vibe. Guests are greeted with cuisine styled on the concept of the four elements of fire, earth, wind and water, represented on the menu by elemental symbols of ancient Greece. A platter of vegetables, each grilled with a variety of techniques, represents cuisine of the earth; soup redolent with herbs and other ingredients expresses water; and so on, with each item conceptually linked to a classical element.

Name: Masaki
Description: The chef learned at a ryotei how to produce rich flavours by combining ingredients. Having been responsible for the simmered dishes and soups there, he pours his strength into wanmono. His search for ever greater depth of flavour led him to combine first-draught dashi with fish bone broth. The chef’s pride and joy is surinagashi, with a distinct sense of season. The power of dashi makes ingredients all the more impressive. As a counterpoint to the varied tone of the menu, the meal ends simply, with white rice and clear soup.

Name: WASHOKU TOKU
Description: À la carte is the focus, so guests can freely sample the cuisine of the season. The menu ranges widely, beguiling diners with items from appetisers to more creative offerings. The sashimi plate is garnished with green peppercorns. Refreshing flavours draw out the sweetness of seafood. ‘Kamo Wasa’, quick-boiled duck tenderloin, draws inspiration from the yakitori technique. The wide range of items includes rice dishes, donburi, rice soup and fried rice. The flexibility to make portions larger or smaller is much appreciated.

Name: Le Nez
Description: Not surprisingly for a restaurant whose name means ‘the nose’, aroma is the unifying theme here. The house is redolent of ingredients in season and the fragrances of fresh cooking. An amuse-gueule named ‘Hakoniwa’ is, as the name suggests, like a miniature seasonal garden in a little box. Scattering the blessings of Wakayama, Le Nez carries the hometown breezes of that prefecture. Nanko plums, for example, are a speciality of the chef’s birthplace of Minabe. The aroma of meat, adroitly grilled over Kishu-binchotan, wafts on the air and beguiles the nose.

Name: Higashiyama Tsukasa
Description: The menu is always original, thanks to the insatiable curiosity of the chef. Declining to be bound by Japanese cuisine, he makes pleasing diners his top priority instead. Rice paper rolls, an idea from Vietnam, are made with Japanese ingredients that change with the season. Meals conclude with dishes such as spicy curry rice or rice topped with raw egg and XO sauce. A freewheeling imagination entices with familiar ingredients such as dashi and miso used in unpredictable ways.

Name: middle
Description: The Kamo River provides a serene backdrop to this house near Kitaoji Bridge. Inspired to become a chef in Paris, the chef studied French cooking in Osaka and Japanese cuisine in Kyoto. This life story is evident in his prix fixe menus, which blur the boundaries between Western and Japanese gastronomy. Sauces are lovingly prepared, fish and meat grilled over charcoal flame. The style is freely expressive, with hints of Middle Eastern and South American influences scattered here and there.

Name: Doshincho Washoku Zui
Description: ‘Zui’ means ‘fresh and lively’, which applies equally well to both fare and chef. His cheerful personality and energetic expression reflect his passion for cuisine and service. As a restaurateur who studied in Kyoto, the chef makes Rishiri kombu and light-coloured dried bonito flakes the foundation on which he works. Each dish is restricted to just two ingredients, so each component leaves a strong impression. He is especially adept at pairing ingredients with their own dashi, as seen in the sea bream sashimi accompanied by a jellied broth of sea bream dashi.

Name: Kappo Shinatomi
Description: Keen to earn the affection of locals, the chef named his restaurant after the ancient word for this part of Kyoto. Offerings are determined by customers’ à la carte preferences, the chef’s omakase menus, and how he feels that day. The quality of the seafood Kappo Shinatomi sources is top-notch, so we recommend the sashimi assortment. Boiled greens redolent with bonito stock and stewed dishes warm the soul. The meal ends with sweets prepared by the lady of the house. The couple’s personality is stamped on the ambience of this kappo restaurant.

Name: Mescita Pane e Vino
Description: ‘Mescita’ is an old Tuscan word for a bar or tavern. Come here to try the steak of aged beef and organic wine. The chef sources rump, aitchbone and rib roast, which he chargrills in the Florentine style. Seasoning is restricted to salt and pepper and portions start at 200g. Order appetisers to tide you over while the beef is grilled slowly. If you still have room, the pastas are recommended.

Name: Washoku Iikura
Description: More than an izakaya but not quite a kappo. The addition of ‘Washoku’ to the name promises enjoyment of Japanese cuisine in a relaxed setting. Commitment to guest satisfaction shines in the extensive menu. The chef excels at grilling, simmering or deep-frying items from the extensive fish list simply, yet with ingenious touches of his own. Individual portions are modest to encourage diners to sample widely. Rice dishes, cooked in clay pots, are similarly varied.

Name: L'angolo
Description: The husband studied cooking in Nice, the wife in Tuscany. Today the two of them express simple, honest home cooking and regional dishes using Japanese ingredients. Pairings courses combine food with organic wines favoured by the couple. Working in shifts, the wife serves Italian cuisine at lunchtime, while the husband provides cuisine based on French cooking for dinner, each making the most of their area of expertise.

Name: tamanegi
Description: Onion-shaped lamps hang from the ceiling. In this couple-run restaurant, the wife has studied Italian cuisine and the husband was a sommelier at a French restaurant. They chose the name (‘tamanegi’ is Japanese for ‘onion’) because of the bulb’s familiarity in both Italian and French cooking. Taking her culinary cues from her experience in Italy’s Piemonte region, the dishes are bold yet delicate in flavour. Pasta is made by hand the way she learnt in Piemonte; completely free-range beef is paired with organic wines.

Name: Temmabashi Fujikawa
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Counter dining,Shoes must be removed
Description: The uniquely elegant counter of Yoshino cedar reflects the taste of the chef. Kaiseki meals showcase the chef’s original vision. In the middle stage of his prix fixe menu, the chef offers tempura, with each piece individually deep-fried. At lunchtime, appetisers delight the eye as well as the palate; in the evening, offerings increase in number, with sharpened focus on the ingredients. As the tempo of the menu gradually rises, the diversity of skills on display in the open kitchen piques interest.

Name: TEMPURA HANAGATAMI
Address: 5F, The Ritz-Carlton, Osaka, 2-5-25 Umeda, Kita-ku, Osaka, 530-0001, Japan
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Counter dining,Interesting wine list,Wheelchair access
Description: Boxed sea urchins, foods from both land and sea, and tempura to start. The tempura, fried in blended oil, is light and airy. The secret is in the batter: to reduce gluten, wheat flour is chilled to below freezing before frying. One inventive dish is tempura of sea urchin and nori seaweed. Combinations are delightful, including eel grilled without seasoning then brushed with wasabi, and Orient clams dressed with pepper flowers.

Name: DuKKAh
Description: The restaurant is temporarily closed. It's planned to reopen in April. A counter restaurant serving the cuisine of northern Spain. After spending considerable time in Galicia and the Basque Country, the chef drew inspiration from the guardians of those regions’ culture and food. Both regions face the Bay of Biscay, so their cuisines, blessed with bounties of sea and land, are delightfully varied. Overlaying these traditions with Japanese foods such as kudzu, soba and green pepper flower creates expressions of unique character. A marriage of Spanish local cuisine with Japanese ingredients.

Name: Sushidokoro Hirokawa
Description: When you order sake, the chef presents a box of paulownia wood containing Satsuma and Tenma kiriko cut-glass drinking cups. These craft traditions of Kagoshima and Osaka tell of where the chef was born, and where he apprenticed. Fish is selected at Tsuruhashi Market. The meal starts with snacks before proceeding to more creative preparations, attesting to his experience. Nigiri are formed small, in the hope you will sample as many different items as possible. The chef’s ready smile is another factor that keeps diners coming back.

Name: La Lucciola
Description: A small light shines from a back alley. The restaurant’s name means ‘firefly’, and the chef’s sunny smile lights up the spirits of his guests. The fare is Italian, yet Japanese sensibility lives within it. Counter seating is kappo-influenced, while the charcoal grill reflects use of longstanding Japanese methods. Japanese and Western serving-ware are used to suit each dish; the chef personally repairing pottery with kintsugi gold and lacquer comes from the Japanese spirit. Many customers frequent La Lucciola to enjoy the presence of the good-humoured chef.

Name: Kawahara
Description: The interior of the restaurant, an old family home, exudes warmth. The affable owner-chef, Koji Kawahara, is creative too, as his menu abounds with ingenuity. Rishiri kombu kelp is used only for soup dishes, ensuring an elegantly flavoursome broth. In cooked items, however, ma-kombu is favoured, to bring out flavour. In an innovative touch, fish is marinated in miso before frying. An assortment of items come together in a single dish, creating a unique expression that adds variety to the meal.

Name: Sushi Marumine
Description: The husband-and-wife team have previously managed a fishmonger and a caterer. As a discerning connoisseur, the chef’s ability to source great ingredients is impressive. The menu, written in a beautifully flowing hand, is crammed with a rich miscellany of fish. Many of the patrons are regulars, freely ordering snacks and nigiri with cups of sake; they drop in for friendly conversation amid their daily lives in this intimate restaurant with its congenial atmosphere, a radio playing in the background.

Name: Sushi Yuden
Description: This is how we remember it: the chef at work behind the old-time sushi counter, in the customer’s line of sight. ‘Sushi is a traditional cuisine of Japan’, says Yuya Nishimura. True to the food culture of Osaka, which prizes freshness above all, Nishimura seeks out the finest of the catch at Kuromon Market with the eyes of a seasoned connoisseur. The ‘Yu’ in ‘Yuden’ is a Chinese character meaning ‘calm’ or ‘everlasting’. Nishimura carries on the traditions, techniques and spirit of sushi with a style indelibly his own.

Name: MOTOÏ
Description: Housed in a remodeled Taisho-era residence, with a dining room looking out on a courtyard, MOTOÏ is suffused with the atmosphere of Old Japan. Kyoto native Motoi Maeda boasts careers in both Chinese and French cuisine, so he assembles prix fixe menus applying Kyoto customs to Chinese and French techniques. Sichuan-style tofu mousse is a chilled hors d’oeuvre. During seasonal festivals, Motoi cheerfully mixes elements of traditional events into his dishes.

Name: Unkaku
Description: ‘Unkaku’ is a traditional pattern depicting cranes dancing in the clouds. Masaharu Shimamura sees himself as a crane; the image expresses his wish to fly high in the culinary world. In the thrifty spirit of Osaka cooking, he uses every part of his ingredients. His signature dish, ‘Nozaki-style grilled small sea bream’, is testament to that conviction. Recalling that the area around Nozaki Kannon Temple (Jigen-ji) was once famed for its canola, Shimamura simmers the fish in rapeseed oil so that even the bones of this fish served whole can be eaten.

Name: Yuyu
Description: The shop’s name recalls the phrase ‘yuyu-jiteki’, ‘a life of leisure, free of worldly cares’. True to this proposition, Yuyu offers dining à la carte in the evening, so guests can relax and dine at their own pace. Sashimi plates are accompanied not with soy sauce but with Daitokuji natto. Beef tongue is dressed with white miso, resembling a stew. Yuyu respects the boundaries of Japanese cuisine while mixing in creativity for a distinctive spin. For the final item, flexibility is the order of the day, as guests can choose from rice with toppings, noodles, curry or a wide range of other options.

Name: Gion Kajisho
Description: Making Kyoto cuisine accessible to all is the goal of this chef and proprietress. ‘Kajisho’ combines the husband’s surname with his wife’s maiden name, signifying their bond of matrimony. Rolled omelette preserves the legacy of popular delivery items and box lunches from the chef’s apprentice days while recreating the air of a kappo. Seafood sourced from Nagasaki and Goto-udon noodles convey the flavours of the couple’s hometown. À la carte items such as braised pork and chawanmushi are offered in the evening.

Name: Sushi Hayashi
Description: The rice is seasoned with rice vinegar and salt; the chef doesn’t use sugar, preferring to draw out sweetness from the fish instead. To ensure compatibility with the sushi rice, he pays attention to the temperature of the toppings. Though it depends on the preparation, he likes to start the hand-formed sushi with light-flavoured squid, so you can taste the sushi rice. Blueback fish are seasoned with buds of the pepper tree, white-fleshed fish with a paste of chilli peppers and yuzu zest. Mackerel sushi and steamed sushi are served from autumn to winter, in true Kyoto style.

Name: Gion Nishimura
Description: The aim of this chef is to serve cuisine that is simple in appearance but makes a lasting impression. He places great store by elements the customer never sees, such as dashi combinations and knife techniques. In the eel and rolled omelette dressed in starchy sauce, for example, he creates synergistic effects by varying the dashi used for the omelette and the sauce. For the assortment of simmered vegetables, each vegetable is cut in a unique way, adding up to a harmonious whole. Customer demand has made the unforgettable sesame tofu and mackerel sushi standard dishes.

Name: ortensia
Description: The chef has gained experience in many parts of Italy, but Sicily remains closest to his heart. Pasta made with dried tuna roe, and ‘matalotta’, a stew of whitefish and vegetables, are traditional flavours. To grow a clientele that drops in casually, ortensia is decorated in a burnt-orange tone, recalling the blood oranges of the Mezzogiorno. Familiar items such as clam sauce pasta and spaghetti peperoncino grace the menu as well.

Name: Varier
Address: 2F, Nakanoshima Daibiru, 3-3-23 Nakanoshima, Kita-ku, Osaka, 530-6102, Japan
Description: Tables sparkling in the light of opulent chandeliers. Taking ‘classic modern’ as his theme, the chef jealously guards traditional techniques while incorporating Japanese ingredients: French cuisine, but à la japonaise. Thus, he also uses a Japanese-style dashi made from kombu and katsuo. ‘Varier’ is French for ‘to change’, expressing how ingredients shift with the seasons, and the changes to the aroma and flavour of each dish. Crockery, much of which is Mino ware, is richly varied.

Name: Yoshitaka
Description: Oden fashioned in the manner of a simmered dish in kaiseki fare. Toppings such as dried kombu shavings for tofu and ground sesame for soft-boiled eggs are served one piece at a time to offer a twist on familiar flavours. Each serving-dish is different, an influence from the chef’s experience in other cuisines. The meal ends with ramen flavoured with dashi or, taking a page from Edo cooking, peppered rice. Osaka has been a port of call for kombu merchants since the Edo period, and this is a place to savour stewed items from that rich dashi culture.

Name: LACERBA
Address: 2F, Shin Daibiru, 1-2-1 Dojimahama, Kita-ku, Osaka, 530-0004, Japan
Description: Masaaki Fujita reaches deep into the character and history of Japan and Italy to conjure his cuisine. Eel, Chinese yam and red rice on a single plate fuse the gustatory senses of the two countries, both rooted deeply in cultures of river fish and rice. Zest of Japanese pepper married with the bittersweet of red wine sauce is somehow nostalgic. Fujita’s motto is ‘to be master of one is to be master of all’. His long study of hometown cooking followed by his own innovations proves the point.

Name: xiang hua
Description: True to its name, which means ‘serving the cuisine of every region of China’, the menu features a rich variety of regional dishes. The background to the recipes is a tale worth telling. As the chef used to teach at a cooking school, he is well-versed in his craft. He follows Confucius’s teaching of ‘Bù shí bù shí’, that people should eat foods in season. Tour the regional cuisines of China and taste its many fascinating flavours.

Name: Sui Okazaki
Description: Intent on breathing novelty into Japanese cuisine, the chef does not shrink from making changes. He pulls out all the stops in both creativity and skill, with innovations such as sashimi marinated in soy sauce or wrapped in nori. Dashi is drawn in an enamelled pot, on the theory that this elicits its pure umami. ‘Sui’ is a tribute to the restaurant where the chef apprenticed, whose lessons he applies in his own cuisine. Giving thanks for techniques learned while moving ever forwards defines this chef’s mission.

Name: Gion Rohan
Description: Gion Rohan runs the gamut from seasonal favourites to creative Japanese cuisine. Potato salad is paired with fermented crucian carp sushi as a drinking snack. Sandwiches of mackerel pickled in vinegar pique the interest. Fish of the day is served salt-grilled or stewed. A good choice is to choose one of the rice dishes in clay pots and supplement it with ginger-fried pork or sukiyaki. Quantities can be adjusted according to taste, so you’ll want to try a range of offerings.

Name: PONTE VECCHIO
Description: Daisuke Yamane’s culinary goal is ‘optimal cuisine’. Cooking and composition are kept to a minimum, so that beauty flows from function. Each ingredient serves a purpose. The chef rejects needless decoration, knowing too much can be as bad as too little. Disparate elements judiciously balanced create harmony—for example, the luxury of caviar meeting the familiarity of potato.

Name: Oryori Matsumura
Description: Tomonori Matsumura built the foundations of his career at a ryotei before travelling to France to add Western techniques to his toolkit. His creed is ‘Make ingredients taste even more like themselves’. For example, shrimp dishes use reduced shrimp stock to enhance the star ingredient. Butter, garlic and fresh cream are sometimes used to lend subtle notes to his seasonings. Matsumura’s aim is to create recipes that will resonate a century from now; Japanese cuisine that will be talked about for generations.

Name: Le Logis h
Description: The chef’s attention focuses on spices, herbs and fruit. These are used freely in everything from appetisers to dessert. Foie gras offerings drive home the concept with creative use of fruits and spices. Millefeuille and tarte Tatin are prepared with a playful spirit. Only a chef who apprenticed in Périgord, famous for its foie gras, could imagine dishes that are this much fun.

Name: Tokumaru
Description: À la carte fare is the star here, to ensure that diners can taste whatever takes their fancy. To convey the passing of the seasons through food, the chef updates the menu every day. A full range of wanmono spoils diners for choice. Potato salad swaps ham for beef; isobe-age is topped with aosa nori, a laver seaweed, to bring out the scent of the sea. Nonchalant twists such as these form lasting impressions.

Name: Washun Taiki
Description: The name ‘Washun’ means ‘complementing the seasons’. The purport here is to bring together ingredients that draw out each other’s goodness, using proper techniques but with splashes of creativity. Noting bread’s affinity with fats and oils, Washun Taiki created baguette sandwiches, breaking new ground with fillings such as grilled seafood and deep-fried items. With orthodox techniques as the baseline and smiling guests as the goal, Washun Taiki is not afraid to break a few rules.

Name: TOKI
Address: 1F, Hotel The Mitsui Kyoto, 284 Nijo Aburanokojicho, Nakagyo-ku, Kyoto, 604-0051, Japan
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Counter dining,Interesting wine list,Wheelchair access
Description: Water from Kyoto’s Fushimi district supports TOKI’s contemporary cuisine. In accordance with its concept, that ‘fond’ equals ‘dashi’, the restaurant harmonises elements from France and Japan. A wide range of dashi are used: vegetable, fish, meat. The chef brings out the flavour of each ingredient, such as pairing duck meat with duck dashi. Western and Japanese ingredients are combined into new harmonies, including salmon with sweet, white Kyoto-style Saikyo miso and foie gras with sake lees.

Name: Aoikonshin Yamada
Description: The owner-chef makes the extra effort to offer gorgeous presentations of elaborately prepared cuisine. The menu, which begins with a hassun appetiser, conveys a joyous love for the seasons. In sweetfish season, come for the rock garden platter. A clear stream and waterfall are drawn in salt on a black lacquer panel. The sweetfish on the platter is posed as if swimming upstream as mist rises from the spray of the waterfall, recalling the natural beauty of the valleys surrounding Kyoto. The scene imparts cooling thoughts as you dine.

Name: Miyagawacho Hotta
Description: The cobblestone street where the Kaburenjo Theatre of traditional dance is located is lined with teahouses and geisha houses, lending the quarter a distinctive air of elegance. Here in the crossroads of performing art and that is Miyagawacho, the restaurant seems at first glance to break the mould. Yet the inclusion of familiar beef cutlet in the procession of less conventional fare feels somehow nostalgic. Cuisine unbound by convention and the handiwork of the reliable chef delight the spirit.

Name: Tempura Urakami
Description: In his tempura creations, Dai Urakami prizes lightness above all. Frying in light safflower oil brings the flavour of each piece to the fore. The meal begins with two tiger prawns. To ensure that the sweetness of the flesh makes an impression, fragrant prawn legs are served afterward. Tempura items such as abalone and milt are imaginatively paired with vinegared rice stuffed with sea urchin. The painting of Mount Fuji on the wall reminds Urakami always to seek greater heights.

Name: anu
Description: Adding fun to good taste makes the experience of cooking all the more fulfilling. For example, a chef who explains his cuisine with humour brings smiles to diners’ faces. The name, French for ‘as it is’, reflects the restaurant’s philosophy. There are no fences or borders between cuisines here. Ingredients are expressed as they are, service flows with a calm, natural grace. Let go of preconceptions and enjoy everything as it is.

Name: Luca
Description: The restaurant name comes from Lucas, ‘bringer of light’ in Latin, out of the chef’s desire to make it a place of bright smiles. He delights in creating beautiful arrangements where every plate is a medley of elements. Aromas, textures, tastes modulate gracefully as the meal progresses. Amuse-bouche arranged like the sun seem to give physical form to light, presenting a rich variety of expressions.

Name: Yakitori Kyoto Tachibana
Description: Tomonori Sakata turned his attention from Japanese cuisine to yakitori when he fell in love with Kyotamba chicken. Many dishes are served wrapped in skin, because of its tenderness and to bring out the flavour of the fat. Unique inspirations from Japanese cuisine include chicken meat marinated in kombu broth and chicken meatballs mixed with takikomi-gohan. In a clever twist, yakitori is served atop vegetables, which absorb flavour from the many types of skewer placed on top of them, then are grilled last.

Name: OIMATSU Tempura Suzuki
Description: The tempura here shows an awareness of the start and end of each ingredient’s season, reflecting the chef’s experience in Japanese cuisine. Thinly battered items are lightly fried in safflower oil to convey their flavour plainly and honestly. Tiger prawn and cod milt are wrapped in perilla leaves for added fragrance. Wagyu fillet is grilled to a rosy pink with consummate skill. Red pickled ginger added to kakiage (all-in-one seafood and vegetable tempura blend) is a unique touch that is pure Osaka.

Name: Shokudo Tanoshi
Address: 2F, Shin Daibiru, 1-2-1 Dojimahama, Kita-ku, Osaka, 530-0004, Japan
Description: The down-to-earth name, ‘Shokudo’ or ‘cafeteria’, was chosen because the restaurant aims to be one where people can drop in casually, while ‘Tanoshi’ (from tanoshii, ‘fun’) reflects the fun atmosphere created by Hirata, who handles service, and the chef. Indeed, it’s fun just to peruse the extensive menu. The inventive items, which weave together Japanese, Western and Chinese influences, offer no end of variety. Abalone-like shrimp croquettes and Chinese-style fried chicken-wing tips amply exemplify the spirit of Shokudo Tanoshi.

Name: L'aparté
Description: An intimate French atelier where refinement and warmth come together. At the helm are a French chef who honed his skills under Alain Ducasse and a proprietress who is a graphic designer. Tailoring its cuisine to the season, the restaurant showcases Japanese ingredients. Menus and wine lists feature maps of France and Japan, while napkins are embroidered with the restaurant’s logo. Everything is made lovingly by hand, weaving the threads of husband and wife together like warp and woof.

Name: Kassen Iritani
Description: Genki Iritani apprenticed at a number of kappo in Osaka. He flexes the skills and ingenuity he developed there, responding nimbly to customers’ preferences. He focuses on live seafood dishes, as the restaurant name ‘Kassen’ (‘sliced fresh’) suggests. Being able to select drinking snacks such as squid cut into thin strips like noodles with caviar or oysters simmered with pepper is fun. Crumbed beef fillet and beef tongue simmered to tender perfection are flavours neither Western nor Japanese, yet quintessentially Osaka.

Name: Koryu Keishin
Description: ‘Naniwa’ is an old name for Osaka; ‘kappo’ derives from the words meaning to chop and cook ingredients. And to convey the character of Osaka people and the foods they love, the ‘Naniwa kappo’ was born. That spirit living on through the extensive menu reflects Osaka’s culinary ethos of preserving the native flavours of ingredients while pursuing the preferences of guests. Being spoilt for choice, unable to decide which of many tempting choices to order, is all part of the fun.

Name: COPPIE
Description: The aproned staff greet arriving guests as if welcoming friends into their home. The nostalgic interior of this old Japanese-style house oozes serenity. The concept is fare that complements sake and wine. The chef, not binding himself to any genre, serves up an imaginative medley of Japanese, Chinese, Western and ethnic influences. Using fermentation to impart flavour and tartness is the chef’s forte. Enjoy pairing innovative cuisine with compatible sakes.

Name: Kitashinchi Yumiba Shinnosuke
Description: The owner-chef prizes nothing more than the temperature and aroma of his cooking. All dishes are prepared and served fresh, so counter seating is arranged around the preparation surface. In a twist, the sashimi is served with unconventional dressings such as nori seaweed soy sauce and monkfish liver with ponzu. Char-grilled beef and, in winter, shabu-shabu of bear and boar are prepared in front of customers. To finish, a selection of takikomi-gohan, rice seasoned with various ingredients, allows diners to enjoy comparing flavours.

Name: LOUISE
Description: The Cameroon-born chef co-stars with the hospitable sommelier. What prompted a chef who pursued gastronomy in Paris to set up shop in Osaka. Simply put, a fascination with the foodstuffs of Japan. Layered ingredients, effectively seasoned with herbs and spices, bring out a distinctive character. The counter, where you can chat with staff and enjoy the delicious aromas wafting from the kitchen, offers the best seats in the house.

Name: Pontocho Masuda
Description: The mood is the Showa era, when Pontocho was a much sleepier place. Two generations, father and son, man the kitchen, displaying their talents in ryotei cooking. ‘Obanzai’, a style of cooking beloved by Kyoto families, exudes the warmth and familiarity of the good old days. Side dishes are simply simmered and unadorned: okara (soy pulp), hijiki (black seaweed), nishin-nasu (Pacific herring with eggplant). Grilled seafood and seasonal stews are popular. ‘Daimyotaki’, dried daikon pickled and simmered in dashi, was born of the wisdom of previous generations.

Name: Funaokayama Shimizu
Description: You’ll find this Japanese restaurant in a residential area close to Funaokayama Park. The chef draws his water from Daitokuji Temple, gets his vegetables from farmers in Takagamine, and buys ingredients from various regions at the Central Market. He chose this location so he could focus fully on his craft. To honestly convey the flavours of his painstakingly selected ingredients, the chef avoids reliance on garnishes. Stripped to the bare essentials, his fare speaks with its own clear voice.

Name: Mokubei
Description: Mokubei serves Kyoto cuisine in Hanamikoji Street. The fourth-generation chef weaves the customs of Kyoto into his menu, along with the inquisitive spirit he learned as an apprentice. To pass on the legacy of the ancient capital, dishes are accompanied by waka poetry and Buddhist blessings written in the chef’s own hand. Eel cuisine, the signature fare, is patiently deboned to draw out the fish’s distinctive texture. Painstaking handiwork and graceful service embody the teachings of the chef’s mentor.

Name: Shimogamo Saryo
Description: Shimogamo Saryo began as a water-wheel teahouse on the approach to Shimogamo Shrine in the late 19th century; hence the name, which means ‘Shimogamo tearoom’. Traditionally crafted accoutrements and the garden are beautiful, and the dining hall and private rooms on the upper floor afford views over the Takano River and the Hiei Range beyond. The chef advocates the principle of ‘dosan-doho’: local ingredients prepared the local way. Pamper your tastebuds with traditional Kyoto cooking.

Name: Hachiraku
Description: ‘Urban Chinese’ that uses no garlic or lard. The starting point for Hachiraku is the spirit of graceful service as only the ancient capital can offer, so these ingredients are banned to prevent odours from transferring to the kimono of gentlemen, geishas and maikos. The chef applies the richness of top-grade soup stock to his cuisine to good effect. Stir-fries are paired with wasabi, fried rice with Kyoto pickled vegetables. Spice use is restrained, as befits the urbane refinement of Kyoto.

Name: Tempura Mizuki
Address: B1F, The Ritz-Carlton, Kyoto, 543 Hokodencho, Nakagyo-ku, Kyoto, 604-0902, Japan
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Counter dining,Interesting wine list,Notable sake list,Wheelchair access
Description: Ingredients are presented before frying begins: vegetables from Takagamine and Shūgakuin, seafood from Awaji and Shizuoka. Safflower oil is used to achieve a light tempura coating. While some items, such as shrimp and conger eel, are fried on their own, other items are ingeniously paired, such as sesame tofu with sea urchin, wagyu with perilla leaf, and egg yolk with caviar. Gracious hospitality accompanies.

Name: en
Description: His father was an artist specialising in maki-e, gold and silver decorations on lacquer; his mother the latest in a long line of tea-ceremony instructors. Overseas, he spread the word about the virtues of shojin-ryori. ‘En’ means ‘swallow’; the chef named his restaurant for this migratory bird in reference to himself, a man who had lived away from Japan but had come home to Kyoto. The menu is broad in scope and includes some dishes incorporating Western elements. The swallow is said to bring good fortune, and the chef’s personality and the reputation of his cooking bring customers flocking to him.

Name: Hirosawa
Description: The restaurant is a forum for his self-expression, so the chef named it after himself. Its modern Chinese fare incorporates elements of Japanese dishes and French techniques. Garlic is toned down to allow the aromas of ingredients to speak for themselves. Roasted pork fillet is cooked twice, sparing neither effort nor time. Hot pots, which layer the flavours of Chinese shinesāhi soup stock with seafood dashi, show imaginative flair. Plating Chinese food on Japanese vessels is a distinctive touch.

Name: Takocho
Description: The rich aroma of dashi broth fills an interior that recalls the warmth of the old days. The restaurant name in kanji is framed on the wall; copper saucepans are polished till gleaming. Preserving tradition at this restaurant, which has been in business since the late 19th century, are the fourth-generation owner-chef, resplendent in bow tie, and the proprietress, dressed in a traditional smock-style apron. The name ‘Takocho’—with ‘tako’ meaning ‘octopus’ —was adopted in the mid-20th century as a nod to the shop’s popular octopus dish. In addition to the menu inscribed on wooden tags, off-menu items are intriguing as well. Light-flavoured broth and Kujo spring onion are quintessentially Kyoto.

Name: Jikiba Ono
Description: ‘Jikiba’ is the name of the region in Amakusa, Kumamoto, where the chef was born. Attesting to the richness of the seas of Kyūshū, seafood is sourced from local waters and from the Bungo Channel. To bring out the goodness, seasoning is minimal. Appetisers, decoratively arranged sashimi and soup dishes are all decided by the chef, out of a determination to impart the flavours of the season. After these, grilled and stewed items can be selected from the menu.

Name: Être à l'aise
Description: The intimate dining space wraps you in the warmth exuded by the couple at its heart. The chef’s cuisine and the wine pairings of his sommelier wife are a perfect match. French duck and lamb are dressed in rich sauces, their flavours supported by patiently prepared consommé and soup stock. The couple work in tandem like a well-oiled machine to put their guests at ease.

Name: Raiz
Description: The chef collaborates closely with producers who have deeply impressed him. From those encounters spring recipes from vegetables grown by farmers in Nara and Kyoto. Vegetables match the fragrance of the good earth with seafood and meat, combined through Spanish techniques into simple, modern arrangements. As the name ‘Raiz’, Spanish for ‘roots’, suggests, the restaurant expresses its unique character through the deep connections it maintains with food producers.

Name: LES SOUVENIRS
Description: The chef layers Japanese elements over French cuisine. Insisting on only the finest Japan-grown ingredients in season, he uses kombu dashi and soy sauce as subtle accents of flavour. The chef values knowing the people behind his produce, and deepens his ties with them, while crockery and cutlery are specially commissioned from artisans. The restaurant name is French for ‘memories’, reflecting the chef’s desire to make it a place that recalls the happiness of chatting contently around a dining table.

Name: Michino Le Tourbillon
Description: Tadashi Michino has been a driving force in Kansai’s French-restaurant community, powered by his avant-garde spirit. Michino ran a restaurant focused on vegetables before his current project, in which he partners with a biologist to explore the future of food. ‘Tourbillon’ means ‘whirlwind’. Being a chef is life itself, he says, and he is determined to always be a fresh wind that stirs up change and moves people’s souls.

Name: Niomon MUI
Description: A counter kappo that is ready to serve whatever takes your fancy. The menu is crammed with the names of dishes and ingredients, and the chefs will adapt each dish to guests’ preferences. To begin, guests enjoy an assortment of appetisers as they select their meals. Ingredients change daily and are prepared simply, whether grilled, simmered or deep-fried. The meal wraps up with a variety of possibilities, including donburi, chazuke and somen noodles in soy-sauce broth. The flexibility of the chefs, who will even make you sushi if you want, is much appreciated.

Name: Tosara
Description: The book ‘Tosara no Ryori’ (‘Ten-Plate Cuisine’) became the guiding light of the chef’s life. One line in the book defines ‘cuisine’ as ‘a word that conveys boundless gratitude to the greatness of Nature for the vast bounty the Earth provides’. Deeply moved by the author’s values and perspective on life, the chef expresses the fascination of the natural world and food producers through a prix fixe menu of ten courses. Cuisine formed from his bonds with others is the tale of the chef’s journey.

Name: Asador ROCA
Description: A pairing prix fixe menu plumbs the appeal of Spanish cuisine coupled with wine. The house brings together seasonal ingredients of Japan with Spain’s local cuisines and wines, shaped by that country’s diverse climates. Examples include seafood paella and asado of chub mackerel with mushrooms, or of shrimp with shiitake. The bounty of mountain and ocean gathered on one plate delivers flavours that are simple yet striking. Discover a cuisine born of nature, the land and the people.

Name: Benoit
Address: The Hotel Seiryu Kyoto Kiyomizu, 2-204-2 Kiyomizu, Higashiyama-ku, Kyoto, 605-0862, Japan
Description: Curated by Alain Ducasse, the Benoit chain spreads the bistro charm beloved of Parisians to locations that span the globe, anchored by its flagship in Paris. A soaring glass wall commands views of Yasaka Pagoda. The modern interior, appointed with antique silverware and furniture, is a harmonious fusion of old and new. Prix fixe is the rule here; classic French cuisine prepared with a modern sensibility from appetiser to dessert.

Name: Yassan
Description: Yassan is a meat kappo of long renown. The shop is busy night after night, filling up as soon as the shop curtain is posted outside. Staff use German as a sort of code, calling tongue ‘Zunge’, heart ‘Herz’, stomach ‘Magen’ and so on. The practice began at a time when many of its regulars were German physicians. ‘Yassan’ is an affectionate contraction of the restaurant’s original owner-chef’s name, ‘Yasuo-san’. Calabashes hang from the rafters around the counter, recalling that Yasuo-san liked sake in these gourds.

Name: Artisan
Description: The meaning behind the name ‘Artisan’ is twofold. Firstly, it reflects the career of the chef, who left carpentry to take up cooking. Secondly, it denotes respect for farmers, fishermen and potters. A devoted fan of a popular Japanese manga, the chef wears its protagonist’s trademark straw hat on his back, as he sees himself in that character. Duck in pie crust, dubbed ‘Shinjidai’ (‘New Age’), resembles the prow of a pirate ship, showcasing his artistry. Humorous sensibility and skills polished in Paris shine through.

Name: Oku
Description: The owner-chef opened a counter restaurant specialising in unagi after studying Japanese cuisine. The theme is ‘unagi and sake’, so the fare consists of the unagi set menu only. The menu uses fresh vegetables to impart seasonal moods. Ingredients are boiled, fried or straw-smoked for a unique sensibility. Unagi on rice brings the meal to a close, delighting the palate with rice freshly steamed in clay pots. The owner-chef’s experience also shines in the endless variety of vessels.

Name: Otsuki
Description: Do everything to the best of your ability, his mentor taught him. The chef takes those words to heart, channelling all his skills to offer fresh-from-the-grill aromas and flavours. The menu strikes a delightful balance between seasonal fare and creative cuisine. New items are constantly added, rewarding every visit with fresh sensations. Eager to satisfy expectations, the chef caters to diners’ preferences, adjusting portions to focus on customer satisfaction.

Name: Claro
Description: The chef creates modern Spanish fare with Japanese ingredients. Uniting two cultures, the chef combines foodstuffs like tortillas with seaweed, while other dishes feature elements such as sherry sauce and Daitokuji natto. Paella made with Japanese rice is another example: ingredients such as firefly squid, eel and crab tell of each season. The all-black interior is stylishly appointed with modern art. While lacking a bright mood during the daytime, it is nicely relaxing.

Name: Grand rocher
Description: Through the glass façade we spy a marble interior oozing elegance, right down to the decorative plates from Hermès. The chef fashions French cuisine from Japanese ingredients. Sauces, for example, are flavoured with sake and yuzu citrus; and Japanese mustard is used in place of European mustard. We recommend a table if you’d like to linger; the counter to enjoy the performance in the kitchen.

Name: Wakasugi
Description: The chef honed his skills in a wide variety of restaurant formats including ryotei, kappo, and caterer, cultivating his discernment. Lunches are omakase set menu only, while à la carte is available in the evenings, with fare running the gamut from hometown cooking to creative inspirations. Pacific herring with aubergine arrives tender, its flavours in harmony. Heshiko, or eel fermented in-house in salt and rice bran is served grilled. Potato salad of smoked salmon and herring roe stands out as a speciality. Nostalgia and novelty mingle agreeably.

Name: Kanzan
Description: Kazuma Yagi learned the spirit of devoted customer service at a succession of high-profile ryotei and ryokan. He thinks about his menus as he visits the fields of Shugakuin Imperial Villa in Kyoto. His vegetable takiawase impart the flavours of the season using the rich aroma of freshly harvested ingredients. The son of an antique store owner in Gion, Yagi also expresses the seasons through the elegant antique vessels on which he presents his dishes. Appetiser platters are served on rafts and baskets made by his own hands. Sincere devotion to details unseen by the eye underpins the cuisine here.

Name: Le progrès
Description: The chef and sommelier, who apprenticed at the same restaurant, opened this place together. Their aim is to present French cuisine that conveys Japan’s climate and culture. They pursue originality by applying French technique to Japanese ingredients in season. The menu is written vertically, inspired by kaiseki. Pairings with Japanese tea spring from the house’s Japanese soul. Le Progrès is a restaurant that ‘progresses’ through the passion of its two partners.

Name: macua
Description: ‘Macua’ is a contraction of three French words: magnifier, to make larger: cuisine; and agréable, enjoyable: cuisine that magnifies enjoyment. Amuse-gueules are enjoyed as a variety of dishes, each telling its own story. Rossini Burger, inspired by the classic dish of beef with foie gras, is a new taste sensation. Colourful dishes prepared with edible flowers engage the eye with beautiful shades and tones.

Name: Kitashinchi Okurano
Description: The menu, incorporating seasonal ingredients when available, changes each month. The head chef, whose passion is cuisine that sparks conversation, respects tradition while sneaking a little playfulness into his menus. Even familiar items are presented with ingenuity: the crab croquettes, for example, are suffused with the aroma of toasted crab shells to add the flavour of baked crab to the creamy fillings. The counter features sleek, modern design and five private rooms are available. Guests are graciously attended by kimono-clad staff.

Name: Naniwakappo NOBORU
Description: ‘Flavour first’ is the watchword at this kappo-style restaurant, where food is prepared before your eyes. The chef also serves generous helpings of smiles and conversation. Orders are placed in kaiseki fashion but varied by the mood of the day and guest preference. ‘Shinjo o hakari, ninjo wo kurau’— words from the restaurant where the chef apprenticed, serves as an exhortation to be thankful for the good fortune of providing what the diner desires. The craftsman spirit of a Naniwa (Osaka) kappo is enshrined in the name.

Name: UPSTAIRZ
Address: 2F, Zentis Osaka, 1-4-26 Dojimahama, Kita-ku, Osaka, 530-0004, Japan
Description: All-day dining supervised by the chef of Craftale in Tokyo. The extensive menu is based on French cuisine. For lunch, Western-style curries, vegan salads and other casual fare are served. At dinnertime the menu switches to snacks, à la carte items and an authentic, modern French prix fixe. With each dish, the chef aims to raise the bar a notch or two, hence the name ‘Upstairz’.

Name: Nila
Description: Located in the heart of El Sauzal, next to the San Pedro Apóstol church, this pleasant family-run restaurant occupies a property where you’ll find a relaxed ambience, lots of personality and an interior that is striking for its vintage decor (wood, a female mannequin, rock and roll memorabilia, ceramic crockery made by the owners etc) and charming terrace. The à la carte, which usually changes every week, is highly varied and adapts to what is available in the market, so don’t be surprised to find dishes such as amberjack sashimi, sea bass ceviche, squid lasagne, Nilo’s truffled eggs etc on the menu... all designed with sharing in mind.

Name: TonTon
Description: The first thing you notice at this restaurant, located in the city’s Chamberí district, and which describes itself as “a playful space with a minimal-intervention mentality”, is its eclectic and industrial look, which is dominated by large wooden beams and open brick walls. The French chef at the helm, Alice Reydet, was trained in leading restaurants and now focuses on commonsense cooking combining French and Mediterranean influences that is contemporary in style but with lots of personality, and incorporates seasonal ingredients and the flavours of traditional cuisine. The à la carte, featuring interesting dishes designed for sharing (such as sea urchin, brioche, salted butter; sea bass, citrus, piparra peppers; and sweetbreads, shallots, pomegranate and red wine), is complemented by an Omakase-style tasting menu called Carte Blanche.

Name: Pedra Furada
Address: Rúa Do Comandante Fontanes 6, A Coruña, 15003, Spain
Description: Located a stone’s throw from the Playa del Orzán, Pedra Furada can be viewed as a sibling of the successful Morrofino de Vigo as it shares the same culinary philosophy thanks to its fun, contemporary and meticulous dishes that also place a little more emphasis on top-quality ingredients inspired by the sea (e.g. flame-seared mackerel with cosium and a citrus jus with yellow chilli, and the grilled squid, onion sauce and delicate saffron cream). The à la carte, which is designed for sharing, is complemented by two menus entitled Pedra and Orixe, both served to the whole table.

Name: El Bajío
Description: This restaurant takes its name from a lowland region on the Central Mexican plateau that encompasses several of the country’s states, and is the international figurehead for a hotel group that has been in business for over half a century and has numerous ventures in the country. The up-to-date Mexican à la carte includes dishes such as “panuchos yucatecos” (stuffed corn tortillas), prawn “molcajete”, “huarache”, and sea bream with a green pepián salsa. The menu is well balanced and adapted to Spanish palates and includes perfect dishes that are always overseen by “las mayoras” – legendary Mexican women who ensure that the country’s traditional flavours are fully respected.

Name: Hikari Japanese Roots
Address: Buenos Aires 16, Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, 35002, Spain
Location: Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, Spain
Description: Located just a few minutes’ walk from the San Telmo park, this small Japanese-inspired eatery has a dining counter for just nine guests (the best option in our view) and several tables, where experienced chef David Rivero takes us by the hand on a journey across the best flavours found in Japanese cuisine. He does this via a single surprise Omakase menu (with an extra main course option available for a supplement) that he explains in detail to every guest at the same time, hence his requirement for customers to be punctual. Because of the restaurant’s success, we recommend booking in advance.

Name: Acebuche
Description: Located inside the Puerta de la Luna hotel along one of the narrow cobbled streets of Baeza’s old quarter, this gastronomically focused modern restaurant has strong links with the world of olive oil, as highlighted in its name (“acebuche” is the Spanish name for a wild olive tree). The couple at the helm in the kitchen (he is from Brittany in France, his partner from Castellar, a small town nearby at the foot of the Sierra Morena), showcase their strong personal style here having previously worked in leading restaurants in France and Spain. Their cuisine is a fusion of sauces and techniques heralding from classic French cooking coupled with the best local ingredients from Jaén province, and with a constant nod to olive oil and traditional recipes from the surrounding area. Choose between the à la carte and two set menus (Estaca and Olivo). In fine weather, make sure you eat on the pleasant patio-terrace.

Name: Freilager La Cucina Colaianni
Description: Celebrity chef Antonio Colaianni runs this stylishly designed fine dining restaurant in the Albisrieden neighbourhood with maître d' Marco Però, and it makes for a perfect complement to their Trattoria, which is housed in the same building. Born in Italy, he wows diners with Italian and French dishes, balancing tradition and innovation with finesse. This is beautifully showcased in his five-course menu featuring dishes such as "Tonno Rosso" – bluefin tuna and king crab, or "Tre Volte Manzo" – fillet, shoulder and essence of beef with Périgord truffle. Made by his mother Maria, the orecchiette warrant a special mention. He serves these with polpettine and tomato sauce. The chef makes a point of visiting tables personally and usually brings his dishes himself. Open Thu-Sat. Things get underway at 6.30pm with an aperitif, and dinner starts at 7.15pm. Motorists are advised to use the adjacent multi-storey car park (entrance at Flurstrasse 116).

Name: IGNIV by Andreas Caminada
Description: Another member of Andreas Caminada's IGNIV family. Designed by Patricia Urquiola, this restaurant in Andermatt's Reuss district showcases impeccable taste and modern elegance, with artwork by Gina Fischli, David Renggli and Philip Taaffe adorning the walls. Chef Valentin Sträuli, a young talent, who trained under Andreas Caminada and previously worked in the kitchen at Schloss Schauenstein, maintains allegiance to the IGNIV tradition while weaving in his own culinary vision. The result is extremely intense and punchy dishes, such as the super-fresh whitefish cut into fine strips and marinated in a green leche de tigre made from puréed jalapeños and sansho leaves, accompanied by an exceptionally delicate celeriac cream. The highlight is the four-course "Sharing Experience", which you have the option of supplementing with further dishes. Led by sommelier Hannah van den Nieuwenhuizen, the excellent service team guides you with charm and expertise – and for the finale, you can look forward to the "Candy Store". Take the opportunity to sample the cocktail creations in the bar area – or coffee and cake in the afternoon. The terrace is the ideal spot for an aperitif or digestif. On Saturdays and Sundays, there is a "Sharing Lunch". Tip for motorists: Andermatt Reuss Parking.

Name: Beefbar Grace Hotel
Description: The globally renowned "Beefbar" concept, which originated in Monte Carlo, has now arrived in St Moritz, at the luxurious Grace La Margna hotel. Open in the evenings, this restaurant has an elegant interior with a DJ providing the perfect musical backdrop. The waitstaff are courteous and professional. The international menu is dominated by premium charcoal-grilled meat cuts, but select fish and vegetables also feature in seasonal dishes. The impressive wine list is complemented by a fantastic cocktail menu.

Name: Château Attisholz - Brasserie la Source
Description: With this brasserie, the Châeau Attisholz presents a chic alternative to its fine dining restaurant (Le feu). Contemporary design meets a period cross-vaulted ceiling and pillars made of 18C Solothurn stone to form a harmonious whole. The menu features fresh seasonal cuisine rooted in classic recipes, with a preference for regional produce. At lunchtime, the options are reduced to a two-course set menu, to which a dessert can be added. There are elegant spaces on the first floor for events. Comfortable overnight accommodation available.

Name: La Miranda Gourmet Stübli
Description: At the wonderfully elegant yet cosy fine dining restaurant of Chasa Montana hotel, chef Bernd Fabian and his team conjure up a surprise menu comprising three to five courses. Each dish celebrates an extraordinary diversity of exceptional and predominantly regional produce, showcasing them in modern and precise dishes. The desserts are equally phenomenal! With its limited number of tables, the restaurant ensures friendly service – the chefs serve and explain the dishes personally, and even the head chef is on hand to engage with diners. The fantastic wine list boasts an impressive range of renowned labels. Your host and sommelier, Daniel Eisner, embodies a passion for wine shared by the whole team.

Name: Notre-Dame
Description: Chef Maxime Arnold creatively combines fresh regional ingredients in dishes such as beef tartare with black garlic, porcini carpaccio and preserved lemon focaccia. The atmosphere and decor reflect a love of music, compounding the charm of this already cosy setting. In summer, the small terrace is the perfect for a tasty tipple, whether a non-alcoholic cocktail or a glass of wine from the exclusively Swiss selection.

Name: Ankôma
Address: 5F, Kam Lung Commercial Centre, 2 Hart Avenue, Tsim Sha Tsui, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Description: This compact joint offers two seating areas – the counter overlooking an open kitchen serves a 10-course season-driven tasting menu that melds Japanese flavours with European techniques; the terrace serves upmarket steakhouse favourites like Wagyu sandwich, caviar with blinis, and truffle fries. Butter-aged lobster seared on a lava stone is velvety and flavoursome. Roast three-yellow chicken in a vin jaune sauce is ideal to share and worth pre-ordering.

Name: Udatsu Sushi
Address: GF, Stable Block, FWD House 1881, 2A Canton Road, Tsim Sha Tsui, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Description: At a counter made out of an ancient cypress tree that only seats 12, this sushi-ya endeavours to offer a global experience, including jazz playing softly in the background. The first overseas outpost of its Tokyo namesake is helmed by chef Nakamura, a protégé of chef Udatsu. The single omakase menu showcases quality ingredients, mostly from Japan, alongside some local fish and veggies. Rice is dressed in one of two vinegars depending on the fish.

Name: Citrino da Yoshinaga Jinbo
Address: 2F, 18 On Lan Street, Central, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Description: In 2024, Hong Kong’s CBD welcomed the arrival of Citrino, the brainchild of the Ryota Kappou Modern team and of chef Yoshinaga Jinbo. The decor overflows in Italian luxe, circa 1950s with rich, tactile finishes. On the menu, Italian dishes are given a Japanese spin, featuring many signatures from the chef’s flagship in Japan, such as smoked bagna cáuda with 30+ seasonal organic vegetables, as well as a pasta tasting menu with five primi choices.

Name: Kicho
Address: Shop 2B, 1F, Manning House, 48 Queen's Road Central, Central, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Description: This outpost of Tokyo’s famous yakitori kappo restaurant also champions a farm-to-table concept, sourcing free-range kuro-Satsuma chicken exclusively from a farm in Kagoshima. The breed is known for the even marbling and firm texture of its meat. The omakase dinner menu includes 10+ courses featuring various cuts of the chicken, mostly skewered and chargrilled. The chicken neck seduces with smoky aromas and bouncy, juicy, oily flesh.

Name: Drunken Fish
Address: 1F, Wynn Hotel, Rua Cidade de Sintra, NAPE, Macau, Macau
Description: Curved glass aquariums provide visual cues as to the oceanic theme that also dominates the seafood-led menu. Another recurring concept is the Chinese liquor Moutai. The young Beijingese chef melds global influences in dishes like leopard coral grouper in Moutai and Guizhou sour soup, or drunken freshwater prawns blanched in Moutai. Even the house-made chilli sauce is laced with the prized liquor. Order Moutai cocktails to start or finish your meal.

Name: Snack Baby (Central)
Address: 93-95 Hollywood Road, Central, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Description: Strict vegans and anyone who is lactose intolerant will adore this gelato store with 10-plus animal-free and lactose-free options. The pistachio crunch flavour made with cashew milk boasts a silky texture and crunchy bits.

Name: Té Bo
Address: 2F, Two Taikoo Place, 979 King's Road, Quarry Bay, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Description: A perfect spot for sophisticated food in an unpretentious space. Chef Sebastian, a Hong Kong native with Swiss-Filipino roots, honed his craft in some prestigious kitchens. In keeping with his eclectic background, he combines a reverence for classical French technique with Asian accents. His Wagyu short rib ravioli bursts with juices, creating a contrast with silky black truffle mashed potato enveloped in pasta dough. Ask the sommelier about wine pairings.

Name: Lord Stow's Bakery (Rua do Tassara)
Address: 1 Rua do Tassara, Coloane Town Square, Coloane, Macau
Description: For over 30 years, the store has prided itself on its Portuguese egg tarts that have a crisp shell and silky, smooth filling. Tarts are made from scratch, baked throughout the day and sold fresh from the oven. Takeout only.

Name: Ngao Kei Ka Lei Chon (Macau)
Address: GF, 1 Rua de Cinco de Outubro, Macau, Macau
Description: Don’t judge a book by its cover because the underwhelming signs outside reflect neither the quality of the food nor the service in this friendly, well-run noodle shop. The key draw is the swimmer crab congee – crabs are dressed on the spot and burst with seafood umami, while the creamy congee is rich in crab roe aromas. Curried beef brisket, noodles tossed in crab roe sauce and springy pan-fried cuttlefish patties are other standouts.

Name: Manuel Cozinha Portuguesa
Address: 90 Rua de Femão Mendes Pinto, Taipa, Macau
Description: After a spot of renovation for cosier feel, authenticity and hospitality remain the establishment’s hallmark. The friendly owner-chef has revamped the traditional Portuguese menu, now arranged by key ingredient. Using only top-notch seasonal produce, most dishes are barbecued traditionally. Grilled codfish and fried rice with squid ink are the must-tries. Check out the daily specials on the blackboard before ordering.

Name: Chesa
Address: 1F, The Peninsula Hotel, 22 Salisbury Road, Tsim Sha Tsui, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Interesting wine list,Valet parking,Wheelchair access
Description: Even since it was opened as a ‘pop-up’ restaurant by the Swiss-born manager back in 1965, Chesa has been the go-to place for those craving Swiss home-style fare. The Alpine chalet-inspired décor more than compensates for the room’s lack of windows, while the menu covers all the bases: fondue, raclette and the famous Chemin de Fer wines. Many dishes are designed for sharing; the set menu for two is a steal.

Name: Fong Kei
Description: A longstanding shop offering Chinese cakes and biscuits. The almond cakes and egg rolls stand out.

Name: Celestial Court
Address: 2F, Sheraton Hotel, 20 Nathan Road, Tsim Sha Tsui, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Description: This hotel restaurant furnished in rich wood accents is a firm favourite with the locals. Prime ingredients are turned into culinary gems such as sautéed lobster with egg white and caviar, and crisp silver cod in sweet and spicy sauce. For larger parties, consider pre-ordering the whole roast suckling pig with pearl barley and Yunnan ham. The windowless room may lack views, but it more than makes up for that with comfort, character and ambience.

Name: Above & Beyond
Address: 28F, Hotel Icon, 17 Science Museum Road, Tsim Sha Tsui, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Great view,Interesting wine list,Valet parking,Wheelchair access
Description: The stylish décor, sweeping harbour views and extensive menu make this restaurant a popular choice for Cantonese dining. The chef puts a new spin on the dim sum tradition by melding imported ingredients with authentic local flavours. Signatures such as steamed Alaskan king crab dumplings, and scallop rice flour rolls with cordyceps flowers are nothing short of ingenious. The set lunch can be ordered individually with a vegan option.

Name: Fat Boy
Address: 3 Hau Fook Street, Tsim Sha Tsui, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Description: Hong Kong-style snacks including octopus, pork liver & turkey gizzard marinated in soy sauce. Sweet sauce and mustard add to the flavour. The combo set offers great value with three signature items.

Name: Mak Kee (May Ka Mansion)
Address: Shop 1, May Ka Mansion, 21 Fort Street, North Point, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Description: This shop serves Shanghainese delicacies made fresh daily, such as pot-stickers, pan-fried pork buns and sour and hot noodle soup. Scallion pancakes are available from 3pm until they run out.

Name: Involtini
Address: 11F, The L. Square, 459-461 Lockhart Road, Causeway Bay, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Description: The young chef, an alumnus of Otto e Mezzo, attracts a loyal following with his fresh pasta, handmade in-house daily. Italian eggs and flour are used in the dough which is rested overnight to give it a lovely al dente texture. The signature tagliolini with springy carabineros red prawns boasts a rich sauce loaded with seafood flavours. The pasta menu is updated from time to time to keep it fresh and reflect what’s in season.

Name: Mandarin Grill + Bar
Address: 1F, Mandarin Oriental Hotel, 5 Connaught Road Central, Central, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Counter dining,Interesting wine list,Valet parking,Wheelchair access
Description: Perfect for power lunches and romantic dinner dates, this is the place for updated steakhouse classics. There is something for everyone on the menu. Raw oysters on the half shell from around the world start the meal on a decadent note, followed by quality meat from the U.S., New Zealand and Australia, chargrilled to perfection. The classic tasting menu experience also features French favourites like dover sole Véronique and tournedos Rossini.

Name: Ippoh
Address: 39 Aberdeen Street, Central, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Description: Now run by the fifth generation, this family business rooted in Osaka still strictly follows the traditional rules of making tempura. The owner-chef insists on battering and frying every morsel himself without delegating his duty. Seafood is flown in daily from Osaka and Toyosu fish market and they use flavourless safflower oil, so as not to overpower the ingredients’ natural tastes. The sauce is made to a secret recipe. Omakase is the best way to go. Bookings are essential.

Name: The Merchants
Address: 43-45F, Forty-Five, Gloucester Tower, Landmark, 15 Queen's Road Central, Central, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Description: The top three floors of a prestigious office tower in Central have been remodelled into a swanky restaurant with drop-dead harbour views. Green velvet is a prominent feature, with contrasting splashes of orange on the semi-circular banquettes. Well-crafted traditional Shanghainese and Jiangzhe classics like braised wheat gluten, sautéed “dragon beard” shredded mandarin fish, and osmanthus honey glazed Jinhua ham. Ask for dishes that need pre-ordering.

Name: Beanmountain
Address: GF, 1 Canal Road East, Causeway Bay, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Description: For over 20 years, sugar fiends have been getting their fix of Chinese-style sweets here – from traditional crowd-pleasers such as put chai ko and Hakka tea cake made with stinkvine to novelty treats like mango sticky rice ball.

Name: Jee
Address: 2F, 8 Lyndhurst Terrace, Central, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Description: A veteran Cantonese chef has paired up with a local chef well-versed in Western cuisine to reimagine local flavours using modern techniques. Their 8- or 10-course menu embodies a creative take on Cantonese classics that is pleasantly surprising at every turn. Crispy Silkie chicken in Moutai liquor sauce is loaded with deep aromas; soft-shell turtle aspic highlights the meat’s umami and rich collagen. Ask the sommelier about Chinese alcohol pairing.

Name: Carna by Dario Cecchini
Address: 39F, Mondrian, 8A Hart Avenue, Tsim Sha Tsui, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Great view,Interesting wine list,Valet parking,Wheelchair access
Description: The swanky room creates a Tuscan vibe with gracious arches and exquisite stained glass. It also commands breathtaking harbour views visible from almost every table. The Italian steakhouse, brainchild of the famous butcher Dario Cecchini, champions a nose-to-tail concept with a focus on beef from Italy, Australia, the U.S., Japan and Ireland. Premium U.S. Wagyu steaks stand out in particular. The Italian wine list practically covers the entire country.

Name: A Lorcha
Address: 289 Rua do Almirante Sergio, Macau, Macau
Description: Business is booming at this friendly restaurant near Barra Temple with a retro nautical theme – locals and tourists just can't get enough of its hearty Portuguese fare. Start with the obligatory salted cod fritter. Besides barbecue dishes cooked over a charcoal grill, the extensive menu includes specialities such as sautéed pork and clams Alentejo style, mixed seafood rice, and Macanese coconut and turmeric chicken. Reservations recommended.

Name: Mrs. Fong Chinese Desserts
Address: 198 Temple Street, Jordan, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Description: This busy family-run shop moved here in 2022. Over 10 Chinese sweets are made from scratch daily, such as red bean cake or put-chai cake. Black sesame roll is especially prized for its soft-springy texture and deep flavour.

Name: Magistracy Dining Room
Address: GF, Central Magistracy, Tai Kwun, 1 Arbuthnot Road, Central, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Description: If yours is a larger party, you can book the semi-private table in what was once the public gallery, but the best seats are the curved oxblood banquettes in the middle of this former court. It’s now a handsome room, with its wood panelling, high vaulted ceiling that radiates a palpable sense of history. There’s a distinct British accent to the menu, with everything from roast beef to dressed crab and soufflé Arnold Bennett. Be sure to order the confit potatoes, inspired by London’s Quality Chop House restaurant.

Name: Yi
Address: 21F, Morpheus, City of Dreams, Estrada do Istmo, Cotai, Macau
Description: Established on the 21st floor of a sky bridge, Yi boasts a knockout location with stunning views matched by impressive architecture and an exotic interior. The seasonally driven tasting menus, which refer to the 24 solar terms of the Chinese calendar, incorporate quality produce from around the world. Rare, premium ingredients such as seasonal marine fish from Japan and A4 Wagyu from Miyazaki are deftly and creatively crafted and artfully plated.

Name: Yi Shun (Macau)
Address: 381 Avenida de Almeida Ribeiro, Macau, Macau
Description: A longstanding shop offering traditional desserts, such as pineapple with crushed ice and sweet lotus seed soup with egg. Milk custard and ginger milk pudding are house specialties, to which you can add lotus seeds or red beans for extra flavour.

Name: Kika
Address: GF, 11A Travessa da Sé, Macau, Macau
Description: Pop in for an artisan Japanese gelato. Customers are spoiled for exotic choices here – crown melon from Shizuoka, Hokkaido 3.6 milk, Hojicha, and, of course, their famous ultra-strong matcha green tea for die-hard tea lovers.

Name: So Kee
Address: Shop 15, GF, Block A, Ho Shun Yee Building, 9 Fung Yau Street East, Yuen Long, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Description: There’s just one item on the menu – double-steamed egg white custard with milk, boasting a silky runny centre under a firmer crust. Order the chilled ones if you’re in a rush, or wait patiently as the hot ones are made to order.

Name: Man Kee Cart Noodles (Sham Shui Po)
Address: 121 Fuk Wing Street, Sham Shui Po, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Description: The number of topping choices can be overwhelming, but Chinese chive dumplings and Swiss chicken wings are especially good. Fancy a spicy kick? Try the house-made chilli sauce over your noodles.

Name: Yuè (Gold Coast)
Address: LG, Gold Coast Hotel, 1 Castle Peak Road, Gold Coast, Tuen Mun, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Garden or park,Valet parking,Wheelchair access
Description: It’s not often one can enjoy Cantonese food surrounded by verdant scenery but here on the ground floor of the Gold Coast hotel that’s exactly what you get as this comfortable restaurant looks out onto a delightful garden. The menu includes both traditional and more contemporary dishes and it’s worth seeking out the chef’s specialities such as barbecued pork and double boiled pork lung soup with almond milk and fish maw, and deep-fried chicken with shrimp paste.

Name: Lei Garden (Wan Chai)
Address: 1F, CNT Tower, 338 Hennessy Road, Wan Chai, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Description: An inventory of restaurants in Wan Chai wouldn’t be complete without a Lei Garden. This branch is bigger than most and boasts a busy, bustling atmosphere, particularly at lunchtime. It follows the group’s tried-and-tested formula of offering an extensive menu with luxurious dishes alongside less elaborate but classic Cantonese specialities. Seafood enthusiasts should consider pre-ordering the Alaskan king crab or Brittany blue lobster.

Name: Ki Tsui
Address: 135 Fa Yuen Street, Mong Kok, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Description: Despite the small size, this shop offers a wide array of Cantonese traditional puddings and pastries like Xiaofeng cake and walnut cookies.

Name: Luk Yu Tea House
Address: 24-26 Stanley Street, Central, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Description: Large numbers of both regulars and tourists come to Luk Yu Tea House for the traditionally prepared and flavoursome dim sum, and its three floors fill up quickly. The animated atmosphere and subtle colonial decoration are appealing but no one really stays too long; the serving team in white jackets have seen it all before and go about their work with alacrity. Popular dishes are crispy deep fried chicken and fried noodles with sliced beef.

Name: Hyde Park Garden
Address: 44 Hoi Pong Road Central, Lei Yue Mun, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Description: The owner also sells seafood from the opposite stall so diners can pick from a dazzling selection flown in daily. Ask servers for the best way to cook your meal; for instance, razor clams are typically stir-fried in chilli black bean sauce, and abalone with ginger and scallion in a claypot. The signature fish soup is simmered for hours with freshwater fish and tofu. Try also the deep-fried eggplant, and tofu skin sweet soup with pearl barley.

Name: Hing Kee
Address: 1F, Bowa House, 180 Nathan Road, Tsim Sha Tsui, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Description: It started two generations ago in Causeway Bay but the family’s reputation for Boat People style cuisine was made in Tsim Sha Tsui. Elder sister heads the serving team; younger brother runs the kitchen. They are famous for their stir-fried crabs with black beans and chilli, roast duck and rice noodles in soup and congee. You can decide level of spiciness for some dishes. Guests aren’t seated until everyone in the party has arrived.

Name: Jardin de Jade (Wan Chai)
Address: G3-4, GF, Sun Hung Kai Centre, 30 Harbour Road, Wan Chai, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Description: The first Hong Kong venture of the renowned Shanghai restaurant group is certainly not lacking in grandeur, with its double-height ceiling and striking chandelier. Shanghainese classics and dim sum are made the traditional way but with updated presentation. The xiao long bao with beautifully pleated paper-thin skin, soupy filling and spot-on seasoning is the jewel in the crown. The seasonal menu covers regional specialities from beyond Shanghai.

Name: Carbone
Address: 9F, 33 Wyndham Street, Central, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Description: A nod to Manhattan’s American Italian diners circa 1950s, this colourful venue celebrates the era in everything from the floor tiles and chandeliers to the cutlery and staff uniforms. Similarly, the menu embraces the classics, such as their signature Tasmanian lamb tomahawk and Caesar Alla ZZ, its famous mixed salad prepared tableside with jumbo croutons. The portion sizes are more American than Italian and ideal for sharing.

Name: Leela
Address: Shop 301-310, Lee Garden Three, 1 Sunning Road, Causeway Bay, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Location: Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR China
Description: The room, furnished in a neoteric Indian style, sports a balcony for pre- or post-prandial drinks. The Indian head chef champions a menu starring specialities from all over India, with contemporary, creative twists. Every course tells a story and diners can truly experience India’s food culture from different perspectives. Try the tandoori dishes from the custom-made oven. With firm yet tender flesh, monkfish imported from France works a treat in the curry.

Name: The Mews
Address: 1F, The Londoner, Estrada do lstmo, Cotai, Macau
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Interesting wine list,Wheelchair access
Description: Diners are bowled over by the high-ceilinged room adorned in colourful lanterns and wood carving, all of which on a mews (stabling for horses in historic London) theme. The native Thai kitchen team reinvents specialities from their homeland with a contemporary spin. Try the mouthwateringly juicy grilled Wagyu beef with red curry and chakram leaves, or the tangy sunflower chicken tom kha soup. Thai-inspired nibbles and cocktails are also highly recommended.

Name: Pin Yue Xuan
Address: Shop 1016, 1F, The Venetian, Estrada da Baía de Nossa Senhora da Esperança, Cotai, Macau
Description: The high-ceilinged room, which sports a smart modern Chinese vibe, is the quintessence of stylish flair. The Hong Kong head chef, who has been honing his skills in Macau for many a year, imbues the mostly Cantonese menu with creative touches and luxe delights, such as crispy quinoa on smoked tofu skin rolls, and steamed savoury custard made with Breton blue lobster and Japanese Ranou eggs.
