The appetiser assortment consists of bounty from sea and soil prepared with Chinese techniques. The joy of cooking creates the joy of eating.

Name: Alternative
Description: Alt-rock is rock music that doesn’t fit any particular category or is born of a spirit of breaking down established concepts. Noting the free rein Gallic cuisine enjoyed during his sojourn in France, the chef named his restaurant ‘Alternative’ to signal his determination to create new value. He lays the foundations of classic French theory and technique before adding elements from Japanese and Chinese culinary traditions. The venue, the former premises of a neighbourhood workshop, also expresses the chef’s individualism.

Name: Chugokusai HINA
Description: Counter-style Chinese committed to natural deliciousness. The husband, schooled in the kitchens of Yokohama and Shanghai, focuses on the cooking, while his wife serves guests. The inherent flavours of the ingredients are held paramount, interpreting the seasons of Japan through Chinese cuisine. Each dish is seasoned with restraint and elegance. In a novel twist, instead of Shaoxing wine, items are paired with well-aged Japanese sake or organic wine.

Name: Kabukizaura Masashi
Description: Diners are greeted by the open owner-chef and the graceful proprietress. The playful riot of colours on the wall is a tableau on the theme of people’s relationship with food. In this vision stretching from the past to the future, faces are drawn in kumadori, the shaded kabuki makeup fitting for a restaurant ‘behind the kabuki theatre’ (kabukiza-ura). The omakase set meal abounds in changes in inflection: two pieces of nigiri and two types of fried items (tempura and deep-fried) highlight contrasting textures. The chef’s experience with Chinese cooking bursts from his baked gyoza. For the best drink pairings, let the proprietress choose.

Name: DAN
Description: Casual French dining by a chef with deep experience in gastronomy. The counter forms an arc around the kitchen, dissolving the barrier between host and guest. Traditional recipes cooked with Japanese ingredients highlight the affinity between the two. Risotto, for example, is a perennial favourite, being a rice dish. The intimate establishment and cheerful circle of guests make Dan a step up.

Name: Chez Inno
Description: Chez Inno is a creation of Noboru Inoue, a name engraved in the history of French cuisine in Japan. Junji Koga runs the kitchen under Inoue’s tutelage. Items such as lobster terrine and lamb baked in pie crust are traditional recipes given a brush-up with the next generation of chefs. Sauces prepared with dollops of wine are the pride of Chez Inno. The chefs seek the essence of French cuisine while remaining mindful of the changing times.

Name: Takumi Sushi Owana
Description: Kenji Oana and his fellow artisans work with practiced synchrony, alternating servings of nigiri and drinking snacks. Rice is seasoned with either red or white vinegar; sushi of tuna and pickled daikon radish is shaped like o-hagi (rice cakes coated with sweet red bean paste), a legacy inherited from his mentor along with the shop’s name. Snacks are delightfully inventive: baked and steeped barracuda and eggplant, for example, or conger eel grilled with Saikyo miso. Never knowing what to expect accentuates the fun.

Name: Akebonobashi Kazu
Description: In search of cuisine that only his native country could conceive, the chef devoted himself to the path of Japanese cuisine. The menu observes the basics of kaiseki while imparting creative flourishes. Wanmono include items with fishcake that complements the broth. Fish in season is salted and grilled over charcoal. Takikomi-gohan, served at the end of the meal, is attuned to the seasons as well. He prizes simplicity yet spares neither ingenuity nor attention to detail.

Name: Ishibashi
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Cash only,Shoes must be removed
Description: Ishibashi began as a butcher shop in the early Meiji period. The owners also kept a sukiyaki shop next door, and this restaurant has passed down its original flavours through the generations. The fifth-generation owner-chef chooses wagyu beef by its marbling and the quality of the red meat. Seating is tatami-mat only; cooking is done exclusively by one hostess. In a unique touch, the meal ends with ojiya (flavoured rice gruel) made with fluffy eggs. The old-fashioned atmosphere adds to the flavour.

Name: Wakiya Ichiemicharo
Description: The flagship restaurant of Yuji Wakiya, renowned pioneer of nouvelle chinois cuisine. With “tradition and creativity” as his motto, Wakiya professes a new style of Chinese cooking. The starter, ‘Nine Joys Assorted Appetiser’, is so named because nine is a number believed to bring good luck in China. The restaurant name means ‘once a day, let’s relax, laugh and have tea’. Cuisine and hospitality to bring a smile to your face.

Name: Shunka Nakamura
Description: Relentless curiosity is the driving force of this chef. After going to Hong Kong to study Cantonese cuisine, he then worked at a kappo to learn about Japanese food. He calls the marriage of these two shunka, which roughly translates as ‘Chinese food with a seasonal sensibility’. Spring rolls of pike conger or conger eel are one example. The steamed chicken is a secret recipe passed on from his Hong Kong mentor. He presents the home-cooked flavours that Hongkongers love.

Name: Lyla
Description: The name is an amalgam of the French words ‘lyrique’ and ‘laboratoire’. Leveraging his poetic creativity, the chef showcases the fruits of his research in his prix fixe offerings. The first half of the proceedings is steeped in playfulness, beginning with a balloon-shaped cocktail. In the second half, we get back to essentials, with fish and meat dishes dressed in sauces. Foodstuffs from Kyushu reflect the chef’s roots in Oita Prefecture. Be sure to try Oita’s famed kabosu citrus and its wines.

Name: Sudachi
Description: This Japanese restaurant offers puzzles and coded menus! The puzzles rely on a coded-language tradition called goroawase, so if you know a little Japanese, they are sure to raise anticipation. Counter seating, which affords a view of the food-preparation process, adds a touch of fun as well. The eatery’s name can mean ‘leaving the nest’, and indeed the young cooks create a cheerful atmosphere. Puzzle-solving is for evenings only; lunch is traditional kaiseki, finishing with sea bream rice with green tea poured over it.

Name: Bistro YEBISU
Description: The key to happiness here is the blackboard menu. Sea urchin with new onions, whitebait quiche, veal cutlets and other offerings are chalked simply on the board. The chef is a fount of knowledge; ask about the fare and conversation flows, heightening anticipation of the meal to come. The bistro is run by a couple whose concept is a restaurant that makes people happy. Spend a warm and comfortable time in this casual scene.

Name: KOKYU
Description: A genre-defying cuisine paired with tea-based cocktails. While rooted in French techniques, the chef seamlessly weaves in elements of Chinese and Japanese cuisine. The duck dish, for instance, is prepared by ladling hot oil over the skin, much like Peking duck. The tradition of serving tea and sweets after a meal, known as ochauke, reflects Japanese hospitality. Chef and mixologist work in harmony, refining the distinctive world of ‘wither and decay’ or ‘kokyu’.

Name: PONTE DEL PIATTO
Description: ‘Ponte’ means ‘bridge’, while ‘piatto’ means ‘dish’. The earnest desire of the chef is to build bridges among people through food. Prix fixe menus express the seasons of Japan, but cooking methods and flavours are Italian through and through. Ribollita is a vegetable soup from Tuscany. Tiramisu is raised to a new level. Beautiful, modern arrangements attest to the chef’s many years of honing his craft.

Name: L'allium
Description: The basement dining room has the air of a concert hall. The conductor, on stage in his brightly lit kitchen, is Chef Yoshiaki Shindo. To ensure that the character is unmistakably French, caviar, foie gras and truffles are staple offerings. Poêle of foie gras is the centrepiece of the prix fixe menu. Guests are encouraged to choose their meat and fish, reflecting the restaurant’s core commitment to freedom of choice.

Name: Shokudo Uyuki
Description: The characters for ‘shokudo’ (dining hall) can be read as ‘jikido’: in Buddhist terminology, a hall where monks take their meals. The name reflects a desire to put people at ease through cuisine. Through dedication to improvement and hard work, Shokudo Uyuki creates simple, honest fare to calm the soul. Though he runs his restaurant alone, the Aomori-born chef devoted himself to preparing hot meals for survivors in Rikuzentakata, Iwate Prefecture, following the 2011 earthquake and tsunami. Mellow jazz plays in the background. Good-humoured service stimulates lively conversation.

Name: Tempura Nakagawa
Description: The chef learned his tempura from a master versed in the old ways. The first tiger prawn is fried at just the right heat to bring out its aroma; the second is served rare to elicit sweetness. Conger eel is fragrantly fried with minimum sesame oil. Nakagawa’s trademark theory is that ‘tempura is a process of drying-out’, by which he means ingredients are steamed and grilled in their batter to remove moisture, bringing their flavour to the fore.

Name: IL GiOTTO
Description: In this white-walled detached house facing Komazawa-Koen Avenue, with its cosy, wood-lined interior, sounds of food preparation from the open kitchen, and the atmosphere of a shop run by a couple, guests feel invited into a home. Chef Naofumi Takahashi specializes in meat dishes, such as bruschetta with home-cured ham and simmered tripe. He takes special pride in his slow-aged, char-grilled meats. Beef, aged to enhance umami, is seasoned with salt and pepper.

Name: Shintomicho Yuasa
Description: The character for ‘food’ (食) is composed of the components for ‘person’ (人) and ‘good’ (良), signifying the power of food to make a person good. Daisuke Yuasa, who puts great store by the principles of a balanced diet and good food for good health, creates dishes he hopes will support his patrons’ health in both body and soul. Another of his wishes is that food should be fun, so he gained a sommelier qualification to help customers expand their enjoyment.

Name: Akasaka Watanabe
Description: Dressed in white and sporting a bow tie, Yujiro Watanabe greets his guests with a smile. His spirit of graceful service is ‘delicious, fun and welcoming’. Sesame ground in a large bowl, karasumi (salted and dried grey mullet roe) shaved before customers’ eyes and the staging of the kitchen are three shared moments. Rice from Niigata, produced by his sister and her husband, is used. Sea bream chazuke (green tea poured over rice) is a legacy from his mentor. The gratitude is palpable, the conversation lively.

Name: unique
Description: Fine dining in a casual setting and price range is the concept. Masaaki Nakai interprets the classics to conjure a cuisine that is unique, hence the restaurant’s name. Stately presentations such as smoked terrine of foie gras and orange-fleshed yam or Asian black bear grilled in pie crust argue the case persuasively. Game such as fowl and rabbit are a seasonal speciality. Enjoy à la carte with a well-aged wine.

Name: Sakuragi
Description: The ‘counter kappo’ format was adopted to serve food as fresh as possible from the kitchen. Dried bonito is shaved and dashi is made for the soup right before your eyes. Fish is char-grilled and roasted on straw. Keeping a watchful eye over his kitchen, the chef serves each dish at just the right temperature and with an alluring aroma. Fresh-cooked rice can be savoured topped with raw egg or seasoned minced chicken. Though presentations range widely, each one conveys a desire to satisfy and delight guests.

Name: YAUMAY
Address: 2F, Nijubashi Square, 3-2-3 Marunouchi, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo, 100-0005, Japan
Description: A specialist in dim sum, popular in cities around the world. The red exterior belies the classic dining experience within, which is lively on every visit. Enjoy the culture of dim sum with Chinese tea to your heart’s content. The full complement of authentic dishes includes jasmine-smoked pork, steamed scallop siu mai dumplings, steamed shrimp gyoza dumplings and rice-noodle rolls wrapped in fried tofu skin. If the weather’s nice, taking in the local ambience on the terrace is recommended.

Name: sio AOYAMA
Description: When the chef speaks of ‘Italian of points,’ he means Italian cuisine cooked to just the right temperature, with just the right flame level and so on. Arrangements of pasta and risotto are simple, but with unique variations. Meat dishes may be cooked in any of three ways: grilled on an iron plate, oven-baked, or grilled over firewood. The light touch brought to cooking, guest relations and ambience, according with the mood of today’s diners, is appealing. A harmonious triangle of three points.

Name: Yakitori Hinata
Description: The owner-chef is passionate about the locally raised chicken of the Tamba-Sasayama region. The concept of yakitori with wine suggests some intriguing pairings; particularly compatible with wine are seared chicken breast dusted with salt from Guérande and liver brushed with balsamic sauce. The appetiser is chicken-liver pâté. The restaurant’s name hearkens back to the names of areas and relatives with whom the couple shares a bond; it connotes a ray of sunshine on a Kurayamizaka, which translates to ‘darkness hill.’

Name: COMME À LA MAISON
Description: Yuji Wakui faithfully recreates the cuisine of southwestern France, taught to him by a chef from Landes. From pâté de campagne to terrine de foie gras and duck confit, all are prepared with heartfelt affection. But Wakui reserves a special fondness for soupe de garbure, a simmered mélange of ham, duck, white kidney beans and other ingredients that spreads the flavours of Landes to a ready audience in Tokyo. Unwavering faithfulness to tradition wordlessly expresses Wakui’s gratitude to his mentor.

Name: Ginza Adachi Naoto
Description: This restaurant values traditional techniques honed at a ryotei. The painstakingly prepared appetisers are a must-try. Seasonal iimushi, mochi rice topped with fish and steamed, is served as an amuse-bouche, paired with seasonal tastes such as sea urchin, salmon roe and chestnut. Instead of rice, the meal closes with konnyaku soba (devil’s-tongue noodles), to relieve uncomfortable fullness after the meal. Meticulous food preparation eloquently conveys the spirit and feeling of the owner-chef.

Name: Ishibashi
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Notable sake list,Shoes must be removed
Description: Near the edge of the Kanda River stands a traditional detached house. The red-brick wall harks back to a time when such things were regarded as symbols of Westernisation. Unaju (broiled eel on a bed of rice in a lacquerware box) includes a whole eel; the Deluxe version includes one and a half eels. With only a small difference in price, we recommend the latter. The eel is cut and slowly steamed only after you order, so expect to wait an hour for your dish to arrive. Spend the time absorbing the restaurant’s history, learning about eels or enjoying a snack or two with drinks.

Name: APICIUS
Description: The name is a tribute to an epicure of ancient Rome. Masterpieces by Maurice Utrillo and Bernard Buffet decorate the art nouveau interior, creating the atmosphere of a salon. A particularly recommended menu item is the mousse of sea urchin, caviar and vegetables, a speciality handed down from the restaurant’s first chef. Interior, cuisine, wine, service: the quintessential elements of a great restaurant are here in abundance.

Name: hatsune
Description: The chef works alone in this tiny restaurant. At lunchtime the predominant theme is noodle dishes, such as dandan noodles and hot-and-sour ramen. In the evening, both à la carte and set menu dining are available. Be sure to order the appetiser platter, as it’s packed with variety and the time and effort taken to prepare it are apparent. The spring rolls, a finger food, are also recommended. The ‘Yellow Mapo Tofu with Seafood’ intrigues with its unusual name and distinctive yellow colour.

Name: Tanakada Nishiazabuten
Description: From the Rosanjin crockery to the retro Showa-era coasters, Tadaaki Tanaka’s restaurant is an interplay between authenticity and playfulness. The comments on the menu are easy to understand, enticing with delicious descriptions. When the chef exclaims “Tabetenshai!” meaning “let’s eat” in the Hakata dialect, it makes you want to eat what you like, as much as you like. The courteous staff of this high-grade izakaya, a step above a kappo but not quite a ryotei, ensure you’ll enjoy your visit.

Name: Sushi Marufuku
Description: Aged sushi prepared with originality and passion. Yutaka Isayama rests fish to bring out aroma, tenderness and flavour, focusing closely on ageing technique to impart a certain wildness of taste. Snacks are interspersed so as not to jade the palate with a succession of intensely flavoured sushi toppings. Aged sushi pairs well with sake, so ask the proprietress, an accomplished sake sommelier, for suggestions.

Name: Kappo Yuichi
Description: This counter-style restaurant hangs out its shingle in a corner of the roundabout in front of the north entrance to Ogikubo Station. Chef Kotaro Tachibana bases the menu around vegetables, showcasing the depth of Japanese cuisine. Takiawase highlight the ever-changing faces of nature, with colourful vegetables that cool you in summer and warm you in winter. Appetiser platters arrayed with salad with mashed tofu dressing, seasoned boiled greens and vegetables dressed with sesame sauce calm the soul still further with their savoury flavours.

Name: Kiyosumi Takahara
Description: Kyoto cuisine has left its mark on chef Shimon Takahara. Like his father before him, he apprenticed as a chef in Kyoto, devoting himself to his gastronomical studies. Guided by the teachings of his mentor, Takahara dedicates his heart and soul to creating dishes that offer a sense of the seasons and reverberate in the senses. Each day’s appetiser, prepared from what is most seasonal, shows this devotion. In spring, expect dishes laden with the colours and aromas of daily variations such as bamboo shoots and asparagus.

Name: Sushi Kobayashi
Description: Guests are greeted in Edo dialect with a hearty “Irasshaimashi”. A short shop curtain hangs under a market-stall roof, lending the shop an Edo-era food-stall ambience. Expect steaming hot towels, piping hot tea and gracious service. Influenced by two mentors, the owner-chef prepares fish patiently in the time-honoured way and uses red vinegar to form rice portions. His aim is to be his patrons’ every-day sushi stop. An old-school, no-nonsense sushi shop in both appearance and demeanour.

Name: Ristorante ACQUA PAZZA
Address: 2F, Passage Aoyama, 2-27-18 Minamiaoyama, Minato-ku, Tokyo, 107-0062, Japan
Description: Chef Yoshimi Hidaka has broadened the horizons of Neapolitan hometown cooking. Acqua pazza, the poached white fish dish that so thrilled him in Naples, is both the restaurant’s name and its signature dish. Prepared by fishermen, it began as fish and tomatoes simmered in seawater but here freshwater is used and Manila clams are added for saltiness. The synergy of umami from inosinic acid in the fish, glutamic acid in the tomato and succinic acid in the Manila clams is classic Yoshimi Hidaka ingenuity.

Name: Sushi Ichigo
Description: A chance encounter with a single book sparked a lifelong connection with sushi for this chef. His omakase unfolds like a ninjo rakugo performance—beginning with light snacks, before moving into the main story: sushi. The sushi itself progresses like a narrative, a light opening act with squid, building through tuna, cresting with gizzard shad, and tapering off with egg to end the meal. Occasionally, the chef interjects a playful remark to his guests, much like a rakugo performer engaging the audience.

Name: Oryori Horiuchi
Description: The starting point for Mrs. Sayaka Horiuchi is her early life lived amid natural beauty. Considering that ‘the mountains water the village and feed the ocean,’ the dishes are prepared with a spirit of gratitude for ingredients from land and sea. Horiuchi nurtures relations with food producers nationwide who share her vision. Local vegetables are from farmers in Nerima, clams from fishermen in Kyoto. Her famous chicken offal stew is home cooking from her native Yamanashi Prefecture.

Name: Tsurutokame
Description: The name means ‘crane and turtle’ and derives from a Japanese folktale in which a crane from the wider world (the guest) befriends a turtle in a pond (the chefs). It reflects the ladies’ desire to spread Japanese culture through Japanese cuisine, so appetiser platters are arranged like the decorations of traditional events. The gracious service puts you immediately at ease. The crane and turtle are a symbol of good fortune. At birthday parties, happiness is sure to descend on your table.

Name: MATSUKI
Description: The husband-and-wife team of chefs make you feel at home. Inspired by life in the south of France, the couple strive to recreate the unpretentious flavours of the countryside. Vegetable soup, fragrant with basil, encapsulates the memories of both chefs. With onion tarts, stewed beef à la Provençal and couscous, visions of everyday life in France float before your eyes. Accompany your meal with one of their select organic wines.

Name: eman
Description: Drawing inspiration from Japan’s four seasons, the chef fuses ingredients with the cuisines of various regions of Spain. His choice to take the path of Spanish cuisine was set when he tried paella as a student. Obsessed with reproducing this epiphany for his guests, the chef offers Spanish and Japanese rice cuisine in tandem. Clams on rice is a Basque recipe, arranged in Fukagawa-meshi style. A deep dive into the hometown cuisines of Spain and Japan, in the heart of Kiyosumi Shirakawa.

Name: Sushi Kanesho
Description: Akira Watanabe inherited old-school sushi traditions but learned from his mentor the spirit of adding his own novel spin. Vinegared sushi rice is regarded as the most important component of great sushi, and Watanabe’s evolved over time through trial and error. The chef displays judgment and skill as he serves gizzard shad first, and his simmered conger eel and kurakake egg (egg straddling the rice like a saddle) reflect his personality. He confides that he tries to ‘investigate the old and understand the new’.

Name: Maeshiba Ryoriten
Description: The speciality is charcoal-grilled beef and sauce only. On this, the French cuisine of Taira Maeshiba is focused. Ingredients whose producers are listed by name, finely disciplined flame-tending techniques, and traditional yet distinctive sauces combine to form menus only Chef Maeshiba could compose. The fare is simple, the work meticulous.

Name: BAMBAKUN
Description: Two people known only as ‘Bamba-kun’ and ‘Bamba-chan’ offer an interlude of fun at this charming patisserie. To heighten the deliciousness of the prix fixe dessert menu, the sweets are preceded by a light, slightly salty meal of soup, salad and sandwiches. French dessert recipes are interpreted through fruits in season and Japanese ingredients. Baked sweets are misted with awamori, wreathing the creation in a sake aroma.

Name: Uisane
Description: What Kohei Ikeda tries to do is mix freewheeling imagination into traditional fare, an approach taught by the head of Kikunoi during his apprenticeship there. Fine examples include sea urchin wrapped in sea bream and spring rolls of glass shrimp. He focuses on ingredients from his native Ehime, the better to share its wonders with the world. Born and raised in Uwajima, Ikeda dreamed of becoming a chef in his youth. He never forgets to carry out this ‘original intention’, a phrase reflected in the name of the restaurant.

Name: ETHICA
Description: The chef’s love for Mesoamerican jewellery made him a fan of cowboy culture. As he travelled the American Southwest, Tex-Mex cuisine won him over. In Oaxaca and the Yucatan Peninsula, with their large indigenous populations, his studies convinced him to put down roots in the food of those regions. By marrying eco-friendly ingredients with Mexican tradition, ETHICA seeks to create a culture all its own.

Name: Tinc gana
Description: To convey the gastronomy of contemporary Spain, the chef adopted the concept of Barcelona's local cuisine with a modern sensibility. Pan con tomate is just one Catalan tradition. All ingredients are painstakingly selected to whet the appetite with their lightness. The restaurant’s name means ‘I’m hungry’ in Catalan.

Name: Hibinoryori Viola
Description: A mother-daughter team opened this restaurant out of a desire to spread Japanese culinary culture. The chef and author of the menu is the mother, herself the daughter of the head of a tea ceremony school. The guiding principle is to base the fare on daily Japanese home cooking. Soup stock is drawn with painstaking care from select seasonal ingredients. The salad of cooked vegetables in season is generously portioned, while steaming fresh-cooked rice is served with Japanese comfort food. Home-style fare infused with the spirit of kaiseki.

Name: Ichiu
Description: A door of cedar bark, roof tiles for a nameplate, and a rope curtain with the same diagonals as the ceiling. ‘Ichiu’ means ‘under one roof’, and the ceiling is shaped like a roof to emphasise this point. The menu is faithful to the spirit of Chef Koichi Hamano, a man experienced in Japanese cuisine, particularly sushi. The evening begins with a cup of sake; soup and steamed dishes are then served. After the sushi, takikomi gohan - rice with a variety of ingredients concludes the meal.

Name: UDATSU SUSHI
Description: A fresh intersection between sushi and art. The walls of this modern space are hung with paintings by artists, giving the feeling of dining in a gallery. Bright and colourful side dishes include herb rolls, smoked tuna and veggie rolls. Nigiri technique hews close to the basics, but with some tempura-inspired creative touches, such as sea urchin and fried nori. A sushi restaurant for a new age.

Name: Clos Des Gourmets
Description: In his primary school graduation yearbook, the future chef wrote, “I want to be a chef”. He studied gastronomy in Paris, developing his most intimate relationships with a restaurant in the 7th arrondissement. The chef’s culinary philosophy, his restaurant’s name and his signature cuisine are all inherited from his mentor. One representative dish is tête de cochon, grilled cuts from a pig’s head. In this intimate eatery, guests are in close proximity with the chef, as if invited by a friend.

Name: Nogizaka yui
Description: The chef is passionate about ‘the ties that bind’. He chose the name ‘yui’, meaning ‘ties’ or ‘connections’, to mark his restaurant as a place that links guests with food producers; people with people. The gracious service by the warm-hearted proprietress also conveys that spirit. Cuisine based on Sichuan traditions combines with vegetables delivered directly from farms. Nogizaka yui connects with Japan’s seasons as well, evidenced by sour soup of bamboo shoots and beef in spring and soy-sauce stir fry of organic maitake mushrooms in autumn. Seasoning is restrained to place ingredients centre stage.

Name: Sushidokoro Yamato
Description: The spare interior reminds us of a tea hut, its shelves casually stocked with water jugs used in the tea ceremony. On one earthen wall, an implement used to pierce bags of rice to take samples hangs like a flower arrangement. Omakase set menus place the accent on nigiri. First up is gizzard shad, an item notoriously difficult to get right. Boiled squid, conger eel and egg follow, each accomplished in proper sushi shop fashion. Refined, no-nonsense sushi, the way it’s meant to be.

Name: RISTORANTE Al Porto
Description: Mamoru Kataoka is a pioneer who has broadened the appeal of Italian gastronomy in Japan. His passion for seafood stems was inspired by the seafood restaurants he encountered on a visit to Milan in the 1960s. Al Porto’s famous pasta is a seafood ragù prepared with lashings of clams and shrimp. Kataoka manages the kitchen and restaurant with his son. When time allows, father and son circulate among the tables, ever mindful of the importance of graceful service.

Name: Sushi Rinda
Description: The unconventional restaurant name is in honour of the owner-chef’s daughter; probe further, and you find that Rinda is also the name of a song by the chef’s favourite rock band. With such rock-star inspirations, it’s no wonder that the young cooks are such a blur of motion. The fatty flesh of tuna is sliced thin and piled high before the sushi is moulded so the fat will melt faster. ‘Rindamaki’ is a sumptuous roll sushi of tuna, sea urchin and salmon roe. The lively enthusiasm of the restaurant’s team is sure to lift your spirits.

Name: malca
Description: The restaurant takes its name from the signboard of the chef’s grandfather’s fish shop on Awaji Island, marked with a hiragana ‘ka’ inside a circle (maru). Opening the menu reveals a wide array of dishes, each with its place of origin listed. The selection changes daily, reflecting the day’s catch and the chef’s deep connections with producers. While a set course is available, guests can also delight in the freedom of ordering à la carte, with portions adjusted to their preference.

Name: Oryori Ichiho
Description: The name is a play on ‘ho’, which could mean ‘step’, as in ‘stepping forward’ or ‘bounty, prosperity’, reflecting chef Ryusuke Yamazaki’s desire that his restaurant blossom and prosper. The soup stock gets its umami from kombu, with a light flavour reflecting his Kyoto experience. Dishes such as fish steamed with grated turnip on top and dumplings made from bamboo-shoot derive from ages past, recounting the culinary culture of the ancient capital. Pike conger in summer and eddoes in winter are eagerly awaited.

Name: Fugu Club miyawaki Bettei
Description: Takashi Miyawaki is taking fugu (blowfish) cuisine to a new level. Thick-cut sashimi is dressed with caviar and olive oil; skin and milt become spring rolls. While the fare is strictly Japanese, Western ingredients and oils are added to good effect. Even pots of stew are served individually, for a special twist. Prices are set quite reasonably to ensure people see fugu as accessible. Now a much-loved dish especially on celebratory occasions, fugu brings happiness through eating.

Name: Kukuku
Description: A tea ceremony where Japanese sweets and tea are made for each other. The confectioner demonstrates his skills with pastries while the tea master draws tea one cup at a time for each item. ‘Hyoro’ is charcoal ice cream; ‘Rikyumochi’, a sesame rice cake favoured by wabi-cha founder Sen no Rikyu. Next to come is the main cake, followed by matcha tea. In deference to Sen no Rikyu, the patisserie is named ‘999’ (pronounced ‘kukuku’), one less than a thousand (‘sen’), and in hopes that the tea ceremonies can make one giggle (also ‘ku-ku-ku’ in Japanese).

Name: joujouka
Description: The restaurant’s name comes from an album recorded by a former guitarist of The Rolling Stones in the 1960s. The chef is not one to be swayed by fads, as his cooking attests. He pursues his own ideals in flavour, yet never strays far from the foundations of French cuisine. In roasting meats, vegetables and fish the chef prizes heat and aroma. No-nonsense, simple preparations make the results all the more impressive.

Name: KEI Collection PARIS
Address: 49F, Toranomon Hills Station Tower, 2-6-2 Toranomon, Minato-ku, Tokyo, 105-5549, Japan
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Counter dining,Great view,Wheelchair access
Description: A project by Kei Kobayashi – the chef who charmed the Paris culinary community. Billing his restaurant as a ‘grill with gastronomy’, he sends out his new wave in cuisine from the top of a skyscraper. In a first for him, KEI Collection PARIS focuses on à la carte items. Appetisers boast a spirit of playful creativity. Wagyu beef is grilled with grass over a traditional charcoal stove. The stylish interior and lights glittering like jewels create a real sense of being in the heart of the big city.

Name: TRATTORIA SICILIANA Don Ciccio
Description: ‘Don Ciccio’ is the nickname of a Sicilian Cosa Nostra boss in The Godfather. Used by those close to the Don, ‘Ciccio’ means ‘broad-shouldered gentleman’. The restaurant's name reflects the chef's aspiration of becoming a beloved ‘Don’ or culinary figure. He is a pioneer, dedicated to spreading the joy of Sicilian cuisine. This ‘Don Corleone of Sicilian cuisine’ conveys the flavours of the Mediterranean with lemons and herbs.

Name: Ginza Nominokoji Yamagishi
Description: This izakaya was opened by one of Kyoto’s most popular kappo. Ingredients are sourced from Nishiki Market, ‘Kyoto’s kitchen’, and even the water is famed water from the ancient capital. Service begins with a set of four items, such as decoratively arranged sashimi and soup dishes, followed by à la carte items to the customer’s taste such as oden, baked gyoza dumplings and squid fried noodles. Curry rice and ramen are typical ending dishes. The shop stays open late, so drop in without worrying too much about the time.

Name: UNE IMMERSION
Description: The chef runs UNE IMMERSION all by himself. To control all aspects of the restaurant, from cooking to service, the lunch and dinner shifts are limited to two parties each. Prix fixe starts with carp soup. Appetiser of turnip and squid, sculpted into the shape of a white rose, is an elegantly plated homage to the restaurant where he apprenticed. A modern tapestry weaving French gastronomy with the chef’s hometown roots.

Name: Regalo
Description: ‘Regalo’ is Italian for ‘gift’. Chef Tomomi Ogura uses Japanese ingredients such as bamboo shoots, sweetfish and Pacific saury to bring the seasons of Japan to his guests. Combinations of ingredients are to be kept to a minimum; set menus should offer variety . These two principles summarise cucina Ogura, which literally means ‘Ogura’s Kitchen’. A calculated minimalism creates precisely the desired effect.

Name: recte
Description: ‘Recte’ embodies the spirit of embracing things as they are. The chef uses hand-picked ingredients, prepared simply to showcase their vibrant flavours. The star of the show is the kamado cuisine, cooked over charcoal or wood in a traditional stone oven, or kamado. This method draws out the full potential of the ingredients with the power of far-infrared rays. Respect for nature, producers, and diners fuels the passion behind every dish.

Name: Noto Kanazawanosachi Ginza Furuta
Description: The couple in charge of this restaurant want to tell the world about the wealth of food from Ishikawa Prefecture. Fish arriving from Nanao, the proprietress’ place of birth, is prepared by her husband, the owner-chef. In addition to vinegared mozuku seaweed and rosy sea perch cooked whole, the restaurant serves mountain treats such as vegetables from Kaga and edible wild plants from the Noto Peninsula. The couple tour farms and sake breweries, building warm relations with producers.

Name: Ristorante HONDA
Description: Seasonal foodstuffs are the theme at this modern Italian restaurant. Tetsuya Honda’s culinary creations link the traditional cuisine of Italy with the seasons of Japan. The speciality, ‘Sea Urchin Tagliolini’, uses no cream, relying instead on lashings of sea urchin to achieve a rich, satisfying flavour. Honda strives to elicit the flavour of each ingredient.

Name: çayca
Description: A once-in-a-lifetime experience, welcomed by a tea practitioner and a patissière. The meal begins with a cup of matcha, imbibed while watching a simple tea ceremony. ‘Dessert a l'assiette’, works of patisserie art on a plate, are patiently assembled one-by-one before your eyes. In the manner of French confectionary, recipes are layers of many elements. The sweetness of fruit, the tartness of citrus and vinegar, and contrasting textures are gathered on one plate. The interior, a fusion of tearoom and Western-style house, is altogether novel.

Name: Haruka Murooka
Description: Dessert prix fixe by a restaurant pâtissière. Named after the owner, ‘Haruka’ comes from ‘fragrance of spring’, expressing her desire to move guests’ souls. Generous portions of fresh fruits from producers throughout Japan brighten the palate, with a vegetable dish served between the dessert courses. Each item is a work of delicate beauty, honouring the aesthetic heritage of the chef’s sculptor father and art lecturer mother.

Name: ESPRIT C. KEI GINZA
Description: Chef Kei Kobayashi, renowned for his 3 Michelin Stars in Paris, moves onto the next stage with this harmonious blend of tradition and modernity in Ginza. Based on the concept of a ‘gourmet laboratory’, he offers à la carte dishes bursting with creativity. The C. in the restaurant name stands for both ‘cuisine’ and ‘creation’. The spirit of KEI breathes new life into French cuisine.

Name: ABBESSES
Description: ‘Abbesses’ is the name of a train station in the Montmartre district of Paris. The damask patterns on the walls, red bench seating and antique furnishings conjure the atmosphere of a bistro from the good old days. À la carte menu items are meant for sharing. Popular items include mackerel marinated in vinegar and roast wagyu. The freshly cooked truffle soufflé omelette shares its fresh-cooked scent.

Name: Noyashichi
Description: Chinese cuisine overlaid with Japanese ingredients and techniques, such as kombu kelp and dried bonito flakes, is the theme here, with Shinya Yamamoto treading an original path that blends the two. The technique of steamed chicken with spicy sauce, for example, is applied to fish sashimi, which is spiced with chilli oil. Rice cooked in clay pots is topped with Sichuan-style bean curd or stir-fried beef. Kombu kelp in clear soup is an homage to Japanese preparation. Dishes are served on Japanese serving plates, highlighting the affinity between the cuisines.

Name: The Pizza Bar on 38th
Address: 38F, Mandarin Oriental Tokyo, 2-1-1 Nihombashimuromachi, Chuo-ku, Tokyo, 103-8328, Japan
Description: As the name suggests, food is served at a counter, which seats just eight. Prix fixe is made possible by starting each seating at the same time. A succession of different pizzas are baked, then cut into eight, allowing diners to enjoy a slice of each type. The dough is kneaded from organic Italian wheat and rested for hours, creating a moist crust with a light texture. This is a popular place, so make your reservations early.

Name: VERT
Description: Japanese tea is rich in pedigree and lore, and when it’s paired with the right sweets, the duo sizzles. Sweets of fermented fruit, for example, are paired with ‘sencha’ and ‘hojicha’, medium-grade and roasted green tea, respectively, as well as with black tea produced in Japan. The chef of Vert visits growers in person, even taking part in picking the tea, sharing the sweat of labour. Using ingredients with deep roots in the land, he expresses the character of each region through his menu. Yokan, a kind of jelly with added fruit, is the speciality here. Fermentation brings sweetness and sourness to just the right levels, placing Japanese tea in the limelight it deserves.

Name: Margotto e Baciare
Description: Whole truffles are on offer here, and indeed ‘Margotto’ is a creative spelling of marugoto, ‘the whole thing’. The concept is revolutionary: guests can choose a single bead of the truffle of their liking. The chef brings his Japanese cuisine experience to bear on a base of French cuisine. Consommé of kombu dashi is poured into wine glasses, the better to enjoy its fragrance. Truffles are even paired with fried eggs on toast and raw egg on rice. Enjoy this moment of mellowness to its fullest.

Name: Tempura Taku
Description: Tempura is required to be light. The flour is aerated as it is mixed with water to form a thin coating. Tempura pieces are fried in cold-pressed sesame oil to bring the flavour to the fore. Service alternates seafood with vegetable items, so flavours are constantly changing. In addition to favourites such as shrimp and conger eel, the menu includes a few novel tempura items. Sea urchin is served rare, so is wrapped in nori seaweed; asparagus tips and stalks are fried at different temperatures for the best texture.

Name: Le Bouton
Description: ‘Le Bouton’ is French for ‘the button’, and the chef loves to match dishes to wishes like buttons to buttonholes. Macaron de foie gras and pike conger pie are popular appetisers. Guests can choose salad or French fries to accompany their main dishes. Napolitan (Japanese ketchup spaghetti) and curry are not on the menu but may be available if you ask. A genuine desire to please makes this bistro a pleasure to visit.

Name: SIGNATURE
Address: 37F, Mandarin Oriental Tokyo, 2-1-1 Nihombashimuromachi, Chuo-ku, Tokyo, 103-8328, Japan
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Great view,Interesting wine list,Wheelchair access
Description: Pâté en croûte, fish bouillabaisse, lamb baked in pie crust: SIGNATURE breathes modern elements into recipes interwoven with French history. The chef reveres French sauces, while using herbs and vinegar for a light finish. From the dining room, decorated in blue throughout, the view is exhilarating. The service team’s pleasant demeanour also puts the mind at ease.

Name: La Lune
Description: Japanese elements are woven into French cuisine to evoke a sense of Japan. Amuse-bouches focus on seafood, a tribute to the abundance of the sea. Service on wooden trays with chopsticks adds a distinct Japanese touch. The shifting seasons are expressed through vegetables and fruit — pulses in spring, watermelon in summer, chestnuts in autumn, and Shogoin daikon in winter. Foie gras poêlé is a house staple, expressing the chef’s respect for tradition.

Name: ALTER EGO
Description: A ‘sugidama’, a traditional ball made from sprigs of Japanese cedar, hangs from the eaves of a house with a unique green décor. The restaurant is the creation of Milan-based Yoji Tokuyoshi and the concept is ‘Italian food with Japanese ingredients’. To draw out the delicious flavour of ingredients in season, preparations are kept simple. A menu focused on à la carte selections encourages guests to enjoy freely. The richly seasonal menu offers something new to discover on every visit.

Name: Ăn Ði
Description: Modern Vietnamese food from a chef trained in French cuisine. Ăn Ði combines seasonal Japanese ingredients with bánh xèo, raw spring rolls and phở to express the four seasons of Japan with Vietnamese cuisine. With a skilled sommelier at the helm, you can also expect perfect pairings that elevate each dish. The emphasis is on wines, but the restaurant also showcases a modern approach to pairing sake and shochu. The restaurant name means '’Bon appétit!’ in Vietnamese.

Name: Watanabe Ryouri-mise
Description: A chef who is a disciple of gastronomy opened this bistro. Keen on making French cuisine accessible to a general audience, Watanabe Ryouri-mise fosters a casual atmosphere, greeting guests with à la carte offerings. French techniques are on display in the charcuterie of pâtés and hams, and in the beef cheek stewed in red wine. Seafood offerings make full use of Japan’s advantages as a country surrounded by oceans. The chef draws on his experiences and lessons from working at Toyosu Market.

Name: Sushi Miyuki
Description: The owner-chef of Sushi Hashimoto opened this restaurant for young people to showcase the spirit and skills they learned from him. Sushi is cut thick and portioned generously. At lunchtime, only nigiri is served, but both nigiri and side dishes are offered in the evening. Hiroyuki Hashimoto keeps a watchful eye over his young charges, to see that they grow to become chefs in their own right. The name is an amalgam of one Chinese character each from Hashimoto’s parents’ names. Graceful service by artisans devoted to their craft.

Name: SAKAKI
Description: Sakaki was founded in 1954 as a restaurant serving Western dishes. The fourth owner-chef, Daisuke Sakakibara, who earned his culinary spurs in France, changed the format, serving Western fare for lunch and French cuisine in the evenings. Dinner is prix fixe but with a comprehensive menu leaving plenty of choice. Seafood appetisers reflect Sakakibara’s experiences in the south of France; main courses centre on traditional fare such as roast lamb and beef cheek stewed in red wine.

Name: gentil H
Description: The aim here is to offer refinement through the flavour of excellent ingredients. Placing harmony of flavours above all, it focuses on temperature, fragrance and texture. The menu lists producing regions and producers, conveying gratitude for the ingredients that make the restaurant’s cuisine possible. The chef personally serves the dishes, ensuring that the recipe’s intention and passion shine through. Name-brand tea and bread baked by a friend from the same graduating class are both from the chef’s native Shizuoka.

Name: Chez Olivier
Description: Chef Olivier Oddos arrived in Japan to teach at a cooking school and stayed to open a restaurant that would serve as a bridge between France and Japan. He pours his labours into selecting the right ingredients, cooking with just the right heat and preparing sauces. A red wine sauce called bordelaise and a small pastry called canelé are home cooking in his native Bordeaux. The restaurant’s simple, humble name expresses the warm atmosphere, while portraits by his mother watch tenderly over the room.

Name: Courage
Description: A canvas of artwork grabs the eye as you approach; open the door, and the owner greets you, resplendent with red pocket square. Red is the decorative theme of the interior, proclaiming that the restaurant is run by a woman. Chef Seira Furuya’s forte is light French fare. Never stinting on sauces, the soul of French cuisine, she aims for flavours that are light and delicate. Bright colours of edible flowers make good use of her experience in flower arrangement.

Name: Jfree
Description: French cuisine with a healthy dollop of Japanese influence, by a chef well versed in Japanese cuisine. Soup of locally raised chicken uses chicken dashi stock with char-grilled chicken thigh meat, prepared with Japanese techniques and scented with vermouth for a French sensibility. ‘Jfree’ means ‘free’ as in ‘free expression’. Prix fixe offerings centre on the bounty of Miyazaki Prefecture, dovetailing the chef’s love of good ingredients with his love of his homeland.

Name: Raisan
Description: The name derives from the masterwork of French epicure Jean Anthelme Brillat-Savarin, The Physiology of Taste, translated as Bimi Raisan. Raisan’s owner was deeply impressed by how timeless gastronomy is. His guiding purpose is to serve dishes light on salt that diners won’t weary of eating. Each dish uses a particular type of dashi stock, including shrimp, dried fish and shellfish. Raisan means ‘praise’, and we praise the warm spirit pervades the service here.

Name: Filemone
Description: The concept is an encounter between Italian home cooking and the seasons of Japan. Each dish combines Japan’s four seasons with the distinctive characters of Italy’s twenty regions. Ingredients come from Yamanashi and Nagasaki Prefectures, the home regions of the chef and service staff respectively, affording a surfeit of bounty from both mountain and sea. In the evening, the menu offers both the fun of choosing à la carte and generous portions; you can also order a number of single dishes and split them. Lunch is strictly set menus.

Name: farsi largo!
Description: The Italian-trained chef runs this restaurant with his wife. A chance encounter with a fishmonger in Shizuoka Prefecture made the seafood of Suruga Bay the star of this show. One fish dish after another is served, from fried fish to soup and carpaccio. Panna cotta of black truffle comes from the chef’s experiences in Piedmont. The name of the restaurant means ‘blaze your own trail’, and the cuisine wordlessly conveys the chef’s single-minded passion.

Name: Soan Mitate
Description: Mitate means ‘the three freshes’: freshly ground, freshly kneaded and freshly boiled. Like the chef, most of the ingredients come from Toyama, and his experience with Japanese cuisine is evident. The set menu includes buckwheat-flour galettes of tuna and caviar as well as an assortment of delicacies served before the soba, which is are slender, cleanly cut 100% buckwheat noodles. Watching his practiced movements as he prepares the soba is an added entertainment. An impressive list of champagnes is also offered.

Name: Kyoryori Aun
Description: Seasonal menus are supported by dashi broth drawn from ripened Rishiri kombu. Chef Eiji Onoyama uses dashi in everything, from appetizers to the final takikomi-gohan, rice seasoned with various ingredients. sashimi dishes are prepared in a jellied dashi broth style. They may be complemented with ume or nori seaweed, depending on the type of fish. Egg-yolk soy sauce is the secret ingredient that brings out the umami in tuna sushi. While the soup and takiawase add inflection, the focus is on the power of dashi broth to accentuate the flavour of the ingredients.

Name: ROPPONGI RIAN
Description: The concept of this kappo is ‘as much as you want of what you want’. Seasonal fruits and vegetables are lined up on the counter, ready to be cooked by your preferred method. The head chef honed his craft in Kyoto, so he uses rice and water from Kyotango. Pike conger and oysters are sourced from Nagasaki, reflecting his Amakusa roots. The champon served to close out the meal is a recipe from his mother, who runs a shop specialising in this noodle dish.

Name: Aoyama Ototo
Description: Char-grilled fish and rice cooked in an iron pot are the mainstays here. Set lunches of salt-grilled mackerel and sablefish saikyo-yaki (fish marinated in white miso and grilled) are popular. In the evening, guests can choose from a selection of meats and vegetables to grill. Pickled dried Nanko-ume apricots from the chef’s native Wakayama are the perfect companion to rice. À la carte offerings are plentiful, so pairing various fish and bar snacks with sake and wine is a fun way to dine.

Name: Washoku Ebihara
Description: The shopfront lettering sums up this couple’s approach: ‘Enjoy the season’. The proof is in the earnest cooking of the owner-chef and the cheerful disposition of the welcoming proprietress, his wife. Taking a page from his experience as a caterer of chakaiseki (tea ceremony cuisine with its roots in Kyoto), seasonings are both delicious and nutritious. Garnishes and pickled vegetables are inventive, teaching us that true flavour is found in the subtler notes.

Name: Le temps moelleux
Description: Just one colour, a bracing white, defines the décor. Decorative plates were crafted by the chef’s mother, featuring motifs that reflect the mother and daughter’s love for both food and poems by the Kenji Miyazawa. The seeds of Izumi Tanaka’s love for cuisine were planted when she was little; yearning to own her own restaurant, she set off for France. The vigorous flavours of French ingredients and the delicious ways they overlap enthralled her. Each month she creates a new theme for her prix fixe menus. Brimming with imagination and playfulness, the menus and their impish illustrations will have you grinning before you know it.

Name: L'EAU
Description: The whole restaurant is a canvas on which Takamitsu Shimizu expresses his love of nature. Driftwood and charcoal adorn the stone walls and the cuisine celebrates the seasons, stirring the senses. ‘Water, Leaf, Soil, Tree,’ an amuse bouche, drives this concept home. On dishes moulded in the shapes of mosses and plants are served bite-sized pieces of the bounty of mountain and sea. The appeal of each producing region and producer is on display here, appreciated through the chef’s own filter.

Name: Tomidokoro
Description: A place to feed on sushi to your heart’s content. The owner-chef, a man of few words, focuses strictly on sushi to maintain the proper tempo. True to his Obihiro roots, he cooks ancient varieties of Hokkaido rice in a broad-brimmed hagama pot. Fish is cut thick, so guests can enjoy the flavour to the fullest, and vinegared rice servings are generous to match. Standard lunchtime items are a bargain. The chef is generous both in sushi and in spirit.

Name: Ji-Cube
Description: The restaurant reinvents its offerings every month, with dinner courses featuring Japanese ingredients in odd-numbered months and dim sum-focused lunch courses in even-numbered months. The omakase dinner is an elaborate affair, showcasing the chef’s deep experience and refined sensibilities. As dishes are rarely repeated, many regulars return in eager anticipation of what comes next. His extensive knowledge is the result of a steady, dedicated journey, one that guests can savour with every bite.

Name: Piatto Mitsu
Description: Chef Mitsuaki Okamura opened his own place in Fukuoka, but love of Azabu drew him back here. He sources his ingredients from Kyushu, owing to the strong relationships he has built with producers there. The shop’s speciality is abalone, served deep-fried, oven-baked or in pasta. Hometown dishes are all the more impressive for their simple presentation. ‘Piatto’ is Italian for ‘plate’, while ‘Mitsu’ is part of Chef Mitsuaki Okamura’s name, hence the name suggests ‘Mitsu’s plates’; his own style of cooking.

Name: Shiomachi
Description: ‘Shiomachi’ means waiting for the right tide to push out to sea. The name expresses the owner-chef’s wish to create a shop where people congregate, just as fishermen gather to await favourable conditions. Yearning for the sea, the chef was drawn to a job where he handles fish. He visits Toyosu Market daily, ever on the lookout for that once-in-a-lifetime catch. He chats with brokers as he makes purchases and drains fish of blood to preserve freshness. Gather here to enjoy your fill of high-quality fish.

Name: Merachi
Description: The name means ‘creation of an artisan, pouring in heart and soul’. It was chosen to express thanks to his food producers, who grow his ingredients with care and effort. Preparations are no-nonsense, respecting the sanctity of domestic foodstuffs. Tokyo tomatoes are used to prepare sauces and mozzarella cheese from Chiba is paired with cured ham. Pastas express the joys of each season, such as pasta Genovese in summer and brown-mushroom pasta in autumn.

Name: SŌWADŌ
Description: SŌWADŌ is just past Ebisu Bridge, which crosses the Shibuya River, but there is no sign. Pass through a cheerless grey corridor, then be greeted by cooks in crisp whites working in a lively interior. The eye is drawn to the ‘Genshiyaki’, skewers of fish and meat grilled slowly over a charcoal brazier as in ancient times. We recommend the dishes with which the chef feels a special connection: Unzen ham cutlet, nanbanzuke and steamed squid dumpling, for example. All are from Kyushu.

Name: Ginza Yondaime TAKAHASHIYA
Description: This restaurant was founded in Sugito, Saitama Prefecture, in 1873, at the dawn of the Meiji period. Charmed by the allure of Tokyo, Akihiro Takahashi, the fourth proprietor, fulfilled a dream by hanging out his shingle in Ginza. As his main store’s concept was to be an ‘eel kappo’ he serves soup dishes and decoratively arranged sashimi in the kaiseki style. Eel is freshly cut, steamed and grilled to achieve a tender texture, in the Kanto style. Dipping in egg yolks, à la sukiyaki, is one of his creative ideas.

Name: Plaiga TOKYO
Address: M2F, Nihonseimei Marunouchi Garden Tower, 1-1-3 Marunouchi, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo, 100-0005, Japan
Description: The concept is ‘French cuisine on a journey through Japan’s four seasons.’ Seasonal ingredients are treated with French techniques to create a delicate cuisine. Dishes of vegetables that don’t fit Japan’s strict standards for shape and colour are served on vessels reimagined from discarded glass. The purpose of this sustainable odyssey, considerate of both food and environment, is to point to a future of new perspectives and destinations in which harmony with the environment is celebrated.

Name: OLD NEPAL
Description: The restaurant’s name is a shout-out to the culinary culture of Nepal in the good old days. Street scenes of the capital Kathmandu adorn the walls. Keen to convey the mood of old Nepal, the chef uses his own experiences to spin tales on the theme of journeys. Of particular note in his set menu is the creative flair of appetisers. They’re followed by Dal bhat, a dish enjoyed by mixing the flavours of lentil soup, rice and curries – a Nepalese journey of the palate.

Name: CIRPAS
Description: The restaurant’s name stems from ‘Circulation’—the flow of guests, producers, and food culture—and ‘Passion,’ the driving force behind it. One dish features crab and caviar. The presentation of seasonal vegetables changes throughout the year, with geometric cuts and striking colours that highlight each ingredient while maintaining perfect harmony. At its core, the cuisine remains classic French, yet it embraces new sensibilities, bridging the past and the present.

Name: Sushi Ikki
Description: The restaurant was relocated here for sentimental reasons: the chef had chosen this location to study sushi on his days off. The omakase menu is a judicious balance of sushi and snacks. Drawing on his expertise in other disciplines of Japanese cuisine, the chef serves traditional sushi-shop snacks as well as other flavours such as baked goma tofu, made with ground sesame paste. In search of the perfect match of sushi rice and toppings, the chef is constantly tinkering.

Name: Edomae Shibahama
Description: A stylish eatery serving the popular fare of Edo. To discover the original dishes of the city, Hiroshi Kaibara dived deep into the literature. ‘Mukimi-kiriboshi’ (dried daikon strips in clam soup stock), a staple of the restaurant, was widely enjoyed during the late Edo period as a favourite to pair with rice. Shiba shrimp, so named because it was originally caught in Shiba inlet, is served in soup as a fishcake. Soup stock brewed from dried bonito flakes, without using kombu, is another traditional taste of Edo cuisine.

Name: à table
Description: Owner-chef Yoichi Nakaaki pours his heart into creating cuisine that would win the approval of a person from France, the land of epicures. His classic dishes such as pâté en croûte, roast lamb and tarte Tatin are the result of painstaking research. He is especially adept at preparations of fillings, such as pigeon, foie gras and game, wrapped in pastry and dressed in sauces. Dishes here are meant for two, so reservations are for two people or more.

Name: Daikanyama Issai Kassai
Description: The warmly lit counter catches the eye through the glass walls – so Japanese in style, yet Western in mood. Having honed his craft in New York, the chef opened this izakaya to offer Japanese fare in a casual setting. The proprietress greets guests in kimono. Sashimi is served as a mixed platter. Potato salad and steamed shrimp siu mai dumplings are perennial favourites, as is the finisher of takikomi-gohan (rice dish with soy sauce and boiled with various ingredients). Every dish bursts with playful creativity.

Name: LA BOTTEGAIA
Description: Seasonal cooking and organic wine heighten the appeal of the Italian fare here. Japanese ingredients enliven dishes such as ravioli of clam and bamboo shoot and spaghetti with milt and dried mullet roe. From his experience with French cuisine, the chef favours sauces suffused with vermouth and port, serving as perfect complements to the wines. Wine pairings come with the prix fixe menus, but if you opt for à la carte, the staff will be happy to suggest wine by the glass.

Name: Spoon Restaurant
Description: A monumental building dating from 1890, formerly a bank, located on the picturesque Maasplein. In this elegant setting, you will find Sebastiaan Follong and his enthusiastic team. He trained at renowned establishments and demonstrates his mastery of the interplay between strong cuissons and liveliness, with exotic nuances here and there. Who can resist a piece of fresh turbot topped with a slice of crispy bacon, a slice of orange, pommes fondantes and a butter sauce enhanced with vadouvan and buttermilk to bring everything together? This chef enjoys himself, as he demonstrates by offering different types of spoons for dessert. And whichever one you choose, you will undoubtedly lick it clean.

Name: Ode
Description: Get ready for an ode to Friesland rooted in Dutch Cuisine principles – typically 80% plant-based and 20% animal-based. A fully open kitchen with marble worktops forms the centrepiece of the elegant black-and-white interior. On this culinary stage, Liudger van der Meer and team give free rein to their creativity. A penchant for fermented flavours meets the odd international influence and meticulous preparation. An array of asparagus textures – including a vinaigrette made from the vegetable blended with pine nuts oil – pair beautifully with an eel fillet, an asparagus tube filled with a crayfish farce, saffron and marinated stem lettuce. This is a playful ode to the riches of the local terroir, presented in a compelling multi-course set menu. Take the opportunity to get to know this tranquil gem of a city better by booking one of the lovely guestrooms.

Name: Café de Gaper
Description: Café de Gaper is delightfully laid back. A glance at details such as the exposed beam ceiling and the elegant apothecary cabinet reveals the building's rich history. The menu, divided into bites / raw / cold / hot / cheese / sweet, offers excellent value for money. The chef likes to give classic recipes a twist with fiery Asian seasonings. Think brioche with a salmon farce fine enhanced with chipotle, or briefly fried mushrooms and halibut with a crispy crust paired with a beurre blanc and dashi emulsion for a touch of umami. And to win you over completely, there is a nicely curated wine list.

Name: NEV
Description: Nilay Taşkıntuna and her team invite you to discover a fresh take on Turkish cuisine. Drawing on dishes from various regions, she values authenticity but adds her own playful twist – for example, minced beef in a deep-fried filo pastry cannelloni that pairs beautifully with a tangy yoghurt flavoured with paprika oil and smoked paprika powder. At this delightful establishment – nab a table downstairs if you would like a view of the kitchen – you can explore the richness of Turkish cuisine through a surprise menu or an appealing à la carte selection. Oenophiles will appreciate the all-Turkish wine list.

Name: Salty Seafood Restaurant
Description: As the name of their restaurant implies, chef Nino and hostess Aysen are dedicated to serving up fish and seafood. Their principal supplier is sustainable fisherman Hendrik Kramer from Urk, whose catch largely dictates the menu, which also features vegetables from their own garden. That commitment to local sourcing translates into top-notch ingredients, which are showcased in dishes such as mussels and slivers of squid with house-made kimchi and a tangy mussel broth with kimchi, or meaty langoustine delicately infused with vanilla and accompanied by fresh summer vegetables and a ginger marinade. This is a cuisine of subtlety and finesse that elevates its terroir.

Name: Create by Guido Braeken
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Garden or park,Valet parking
Description: Hotel Van Oys has transformed Oost Castle into the epitome of luxury. Housed in what was once the barn of this historical building, Create immerses you in elegance with a natural touch. Old meets new in the dining space, which features a striking tree truck across the ceiling. Every detail is carefully considered, from the valet's warm welcome to the attentive service at the table.Guido Braeken creates his distinctive culinary world with outstanding ingredients, refined, time-honoured techniques and subtle exotic nuances. His distinctively expressive cooking is technically flawless and bursting with vitality. The fact that the chef is a master of sauces becomes clear in creations such as a tarragon hollandaise or an Ibérico pork bouillon enriched with basil oil, both of which lend the dry-aged turbot remarkable intensity and roundness. Langoustine dishes – a speciality of his – are also not to be missed: One highlight is a magnificent tail, cooked to perfection on the Japanese barbecue, finished with lime zest and finger lime compote, and accompanied by glazed aubergine, vin jaune hollandaise and a winter truffle and shiro kombu dressing that adds exceptional depth. A rush of exquisitely harmonious flavours awaits you at Create.

Name: Bistro De Ertepeller
Description: The view of the Drierivierenpunt and the endless stream of boats always draws plenty of attention in this sleek yet cosy bistro. A glance at the tempting set menu reveals that the chef likes to elevate French cuisine with North African spices. From tender lamb neck served with a robust meat-based jus, to crisp pistachio-filled baklava accompanied by mint and yogurt ice cream – this cuisine is defined by precise technique, bold flavours and meticulous plating. The 250-label wine list, with a particular emphasis on Burgundy and broad international reach, is sure to pique your interest.

Name: GEM. by Soenil Bahadoer
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Garden or park,Interesting wine list
Description: Once you have made your way up the driveway, you are welcomed by the hostess with a drink. You then walk through the neat kitchen garden and, finally, enter the magnificent castle – a supremely elegant and chic stage for Soenil Bahadoer's cuisine. The terrace alone is enough to take your breath away! The chef is known for sensitively bringing his Surinamese-Hindustani heritage into dialogue with French cuisine and local ingredients. After earning acclaim for many years at De Lindehoeve, he shines just as brightly in this remarkable setting.His dishes are vibrant and utterly captivating. The flavours hit the mark and are sometimes complex, but always balanced. Premium ingredients such as turbot and foie gras feature prominently. European lobster, for example, is cooked to translucent perfection and elevated with a whirlwind of spices – sambal vegetables, harissa and orange sauce, pomtayer, okra tempura stuffed with tomato and sardine, kimchi cream and unripe papaya. This exotic blend of intensity and finesse is truly engaging, all the more so with the inspired wine pairings that add an extra dimension. And why not round off the experience in style with an overnight stay in one of the guestrooms?

Name: NORRA
Description: Lieke Nicole-Creemers of restaurant Le Nord in Bilthoven has opened NORRA, a stylish and somewhat fashionable establishment. The atmosphere is relaxed, and she provides charming service. In the kitchen, a passionate chef serves guests both an appealing à la carte menu and a delightful set menu (including vegetarian options). French cuissons, well-considered exotic influences and playful textures add zest. For example, he uses black-legged chicken in a juicy ballotine, which is further flavoured with a cashew nut compote, a vinaigrette with balsamic vinegar, pommes fondantes and plum. Be sure to leave some room for the cheese trolley, because it is really worth it.

Name: Testamatta Ristorante Enoteca
Description: You would probably walk right past this cosy ristorante, were it not for the vibrant energy emanating from it. The atmospheric decor, the bustle of the open kitchen at the back and the congenial service team immediately put you in the right mood. The chef demonstrates a deft hand with traditional fare, from house-made pasta with a bold lamb ragù to a fresh take on tiramisu bursting with those familiar rich flavours. A few surprises, like Dutch cheese or katsuobushi, give things a modern and international twist. Chef Roberto Borelli definitely puts his own stamp on Italian cooking.

Name: Petite
Description: Petite comprises a luxury bistro, a wine bar and two rooms upstairs. The seductive, updated vintage atmosphere is mainly cloaked in soft green and brown tones. Behind the stove is a chef who has put together a tempting menu and an extensive à la carte selection, in which he challenges his classical knowledge with flair. Think of a fresh cocktail of king crab with choron sauce, apple and grapefruit, or chicken fillet with a tasty aligot and leek velouté. This cuisine is perfect in every detail. The beautiful wine list also demonstrates that professional knowledge and excellent value for money are the specialities of the house.

Name: THE CLOUD by Käfer
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Interesting wine list,Valet parking,Wheelchair access
Description: Chef Jens Madsen serves up his extraordinary concept of "Culinary Nomadism", in which local ingredients meet global influences, at the equally special – and architecturally impressive – BMW Welt. For a year at a time, the spotlight is shone on a specific region of the world, its culinary traditions and techniques, spices etc. Each season brings with it change and progression – like a cloud moving through the sky. Inspired by his own trip to Africa, the chef takes you on a voyage of discovery of the flavours of East and South Africa. Top-quality produce goes into a tasting menu made up of eight elaborate courses promising a unique and immersive experience. In addition to wine, there are truly fantastic alcohol-free pairings. Extremely professional service is provided by a well-staffed front-of-house team – restaurant manager Mona Röthig (previously at Tantris Maison Culinaire) and sommelier Luigi Pecchia deserve a special mention. The interior is airy, light and minimalist, with upscale design. The large glass façade affords a view of BMW Welt. An illuminated cloud floating in the middle of the room reflects the movement and evolution of the food.

Name: PINK - DAS RESTAURANT
Description: Located in the Haus für Kultur und Sport, in a quiet yet easily accessible area in Schwalbach-Hülzweiler, this restaurant is very popular. The interior with modern lines is tastefully decorated in a palette of calm, cheerful colours, and the broad, glazed façade means the space is lovely and bright. The seasonal and Mediterranean-inspired food is cooked meticulously and with attention to detail. The excellent à la carte selection ranges from beef carpaccio to truffle pasta and fried halibut. There is also a children's menu. Attentive service with a personal touch comes courtesy of the competent team.

Name: Anders auf dem Turmberg
Description: From this impressive location high up on the Turmberg, the view over Karlsruhe and the Rhine Valley to the Vosges mountains is magnificent. Add to that tasty tapas-style cuisine – the smaller portions are perfect for sharing and sampling a selection. The food is cooked with quality ingredients, some regional, others Mediterranean. Dishes such as braised ox ribs on a corn cream with chilli or tuna with buttermilk and lime are fun to eat and showcase the skills of chef-patron Sören Anders, who is no stranger to the dining scene. The pared-back, modern interior with its large windows is attractive – tip: Aim to sit side by side so that everyone can enjoy the great view. During the day, small plates are served from the food truck in the courtyard.

Name: Brasserie Barbara
Description: Open from noon to 8.30pm, Brasserie Barbara is an appealing daytime alternative to the fine dining restaurant here at the Auerhahn "wellness hotel", which is just across the road from the lake, Schluchsee. The bright, friendly atmosphere is inviting. The completely open kitchen produces cleverly devised dishes that are both bold and pleasingly uncomplicated. Based on top-notch ingredients, they are deeply rooted in regional culinary tradition. Options on the appealing à la carte menu include starters such as "Black Forest croquetas" or beef tartare with french fries, followed by a main course of local trout with a pepper salsa or fried black pudding with apple and mashed potatoes.

Name: PEYSK
Address: Westendstraße 73, Frankfurt on the Main, 60308, Germany
Description: The name of this restaurant in the well-heeled Westend district is a Proto-Indo-European word meaning "fish", so it will come as no surprise that the cuisine is fish- and seafood-driven. The chef-patron spent time in Asia (including Singapore and Japan), before setting up shop here, and influences from his travels are reflected in "hamachi, wasabi, kosho, radish" and "octopus, mussel, curry, coconut, chilli, egg", for instance. The dishes are clearly structured and harmonious in taste, with interesting flavour combinations. There are also a few smaller plates, including oysters or sardines. The selection varies between à la carte options and a tasting menu of four or five courses. In summer, food is served on the terrace in front of the building – a pleasant, quiet spot in the shade.

Name: Grill Royal Hamburg
Description: Right on Ballindamm, with a view of the Binnenalster and its fountain, the restaurant boasts a superb location. Inside, the place has an appealingly relaxed yet stylish feel, and the service is friendly and professional. Top-notch ingredients are beautifully prepared to create attractively presented dishes – don't miss the steak cuts from the grill (eg Black Angus sirloin or a 900g porterhouse). There are also seasonal specials, and seafood such as oysters and grilled fish. Order sides and sauces of your choice to accompany the dishes – our top tip if you are having beef is the chimichurri! For fine weather, there is a small terrace on the pavement in front of the restaurant.

Name: Sonne
Description: The Rombach family (the business is in its seventh generation!) offer a cosy atmosphere in pretty rooms with wood panelling and exposed floorboards. The food is really good – a mix of traditional and modern ideas; the focus is on regional produce. Beautiful terrace. For overnight stays, the hotel of the same name has appealing, comfortable guestrooms.

Name: Mi Niña Lola
Description: This restaurant boasts an outstanding location on the slopes of Gibralfaro hill, once home to the La Coracha district, from where its terrace enjoys one of the best views of both the city and the Mediterranean. The chef at the helm in the kitchen, Pablo Rutllant, showcase a culinary concept that combines a global outlook and local cuisine in his small plates because, in his eyes, Málaga is a city “teeming with foreign influence” that has adopted gastronomic ideas from everywhere. The à la carte, featuring dishes such as black corm empanada with squid, leeks with Payoyo cheese, and mango with yuzu, is complemented by a tasting menu.

Name: Clómada
Description: Fancy a distinctly-feminine international experience? Here you can have one, as the Ecuadorian chef Claudine Paulson, well accompanied by a team that is made up entirely of women, brings to the table the different flavours that she has come to know around the world during her time as a professional tennis player (she was the number one tennis player in Ecuador), a career that she combined with her hotel and catering studies. Within the proposal, with numerous international influences that evoke her nomadic lifestyle, dishes such as the fish ceviche or the crispy sea bass stand out. The logo and the striking lamps play with the symbolism of hot air balloons!

Name: Vituco Gourmet
Description: This bright, stone-walled restaurant in the heart of Alacant is the dream come true of chef Javier Beltri, who named the restaurant after his father (Victor Beltri, known to his family as Vituco). After training at Le Cordon Bleu, the Basque Culinary Center and various prestigious restaurants, here he seeks to offer us an itinerant proposal that flutters between the Mediterranean and Peru (especially surprising in the rice dishes, seasoned with products from this South American country). Interesting dishes? The Ensaladilla with soy mayonnaise and aji amarillo, the Anticucho a la brasa, the Arroz de cerdo con aji panca y cebolla morada (pork rice with aji panca and red onion)...

Name: Tetsu
Description: What is most striking about this restaurant, which could be defined as a western teppanyaki (the griddle is the gastronomic epicentre of everything), are the two very young chefs behind the proposal (Miguel de Aguilar and João Kather), both under the tutelage of the MOM Culinary Institute but with incredible skills for their age. The restaurant, which is full every day for diners to enjoy its menu (which changes weekly) or the accompanying omakase menu, has a good Japanese-style bar and is clearly committed to market cuisine, often fusing Spanish and Asian flavours. Interesting dishes? We particularly liked their scallop, corn soup and black garlic combination.

Name: Smoix
Address: Ronda Nord, Ciutadella de Menorca, 07760, Spain
Description: Located next to the rural Sant Ignasi hotel and boasting a dreamlike natural setting; and no wonder, this is a Menorcan aristocratic estate that... dates all the way back to the 18th century! Chef Miquel Sánchez, together with his team, offers Mediterranean cuisine with a traditional base that comes to light through a small menu and two set menus: Smoix and Vegetal. A standout dish? We liked, for the tenderness and flavour of the meat, their beef onglet, confit shallot sauce with herbs and green beans.

Name: Meloxeira Praia
Address: Carretera San Vicente Do Mar 1100, O Grove, 36989, Spain
Description: The beach reference in the restaurant name doesn’t disappoint, given the stunning location of this gourmet “chiringuito” between the beaches of Seixeliño and Area da Cruz. Attractively furnished, it boasts superb sea views including the island of Ons on the horizon. Its cuisine, which can be enjoyed in the glass-fronted dining room or on its delightful terraces, focuses on traditional cooking with a modern touch, including some dishes cooked on the on the open grill, plus a section of the menu dedicated to rice and fideuá options.

Name: San Remo
Description: Behind its simple, somewhat old-fashioned façade lies a restaurant that lives and breathes gastronomy with a heated passion. Chef Alberto Villegas, who after studying at the Basque Culinary Centre took over the family business where he grew up, wants the restaurant to be seen today as ‘a haven for the senses’. He focuses on seasonal produce, offering a contemporary menu with dishes such as smoked eel with salsa verde and Palencia peas, red prawns and bisque made from their heads, and, for dessert, the surprising ricotta and mascarpone flan.

Name: O Loxe Mareiro
Description: Overlooking the Arousa estuary, and the curious sticks or poles that mark the cultivation parks where the famous Carril clams grow, O Loxe Mareiro has recovered an old traditional seafood restaurant. In this simple restaurant with a rustic-present-day atmosphere, which aside from the dining room has a charming terrace and a table in the kitchen, the proposal is totally focused on seafood products, always with a great deal of honesty and under the umbrella of both their small menu and a complete tasting menu (Arousa).

Name: Nazario Cano
